#111626. Mussels that live in total darkness have cells that still keep a daily rhythm

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1135 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Mussels that live in total darkness have cells that still keep a daily rhythm

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1135 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Deep-sea mussels live in total darkness, yet their cells kept a roughly 24-hour rhythm in the lab, offering clues to how life keeps time without sunlight.
  • Deep in the Atlantic, a mussel called Bathymodiolus azoricus lives where no daylight reaches, and the tides, not the sun, change its surroundings on a schedule.
  • Even so, the mussel’s cells kept a daily rhythm when researchers grew them in a lab refrigerator, far from the seafloor.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Deep-sea mussels live in total darkness, yet their cells kept a roughly 24-hour rhythm in the lab, offering clues to how life keeps time without sunlight.

Deep in the Atlantic, a mussel called Bathymodiolus azoricus lives where no daylight reaches, and the tides, not the sun, change its surroundings on a schedule.

Even so, the mussel’s cells kept a daily rhythm when researchers grew them in a lab refrigerator, far from the seafloor.

The finding suggests that genes that run daily clocks in flies and people also help keep time in animals that never see sunlight.

Audrey Mat, a researcher at the Alfred Wegener Institute in Germany and the University of Vienna, grew the cells from mussels collected on the Atlantic seafloor.

Her team has kept two of those cultures alive for more than three and a half years.

In a recent development, the mussels come from the Lucky Strike vent field on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, south of the Azores, about 5,600 feet (1,700 meters) down. The water pressure there is about 170 times what it is at sea level.

At hydrothermal vents, seawater seeps into the seafloor, moves through the rock below and flows back out as hot, metal-rich fluid. Some of it reaches about 660°F (350°C).

The mussels settle in cooler water nearby, between 39 and 48°F (4 and 9°C). The direction of the vent flow shifts with the tides, so the water around the mussels switches between vent fluid and ordinary seawater.

In a 2020 study, Mat and her colleagues reported that on the seafloor, the mussels’ behavior and gene activity followed mainly a tidal rhythm of about 12.4 hours.

A weaker daily rhythm showed up as well, though no clear day-night cycle reaches the vents.

Mussels from a shallower vent switched to a mostly daily pattern in a lab with lights on for 12 hours and off for 12 hours.

How an animal with no brain produces either rhythm has been unclear.

Lab cells are usually kept warm, close to body temperature. Mat tried something different.

“While cells in the laboratory usually thrive at 25 to 37 °C, our mussel cells grow in the fridge, at deep-sea temperatures,” said Mat, who first proposed the experiments.

“This technical advance is unique in the world and allows novel insights into the biology of these animals.”.

Recent findings suggest that the team tried cells from six tissues at three temperatures. At 77°F (25°C), fungi and other contaminants quickly took over.

Out of 63 cultures, cells from the mussel’s foot survived best. The foot is the muscular part a mussel extends from its shell.

Keeping whole mussels alive took work too.

About half of the animals collected in 2023 died within a month, likely from the stress of the trip to the surface and the flight to Vienna.

The remaining mussels lived for 13 months in an aquarium shielded from white light.

To look for a clock, the team put foot tissue from five mussels in culture and kept it in constant darkness at 39°F (4°C). Then they sampled the cells every four hours for two days.

Industry observers note that A pattern of gene activity that repeats about every 24 hours is called a circadian rhythm. Finding one is how scientists spot a clock at work.

According to recent reports, of 5,616 genes the team could track, 157 indicated a circadian pattern, about 2.8%. That’s close to the 2.5% the team found earlier in mussels on the seafloor.

So the cells kept time on their own, with no ocean and no daylight around them.

Across 10,000 reshuffles of the sampling times, none yielded at least 157 daily cycles while also recovering the same 66 transcripts that earlier research had identified as rhythmic.

The team also found 109 genes with a tidal pattern. That number was no higher than chance alone would produce.

In fruit flies and mammals, CLOCK teams up with a partner protein to turn on clock genes such as period.

The proteins those genes produce then dial back CLOCK and its partner, and the cycle starts again.

According to recent reports, no genome exists yet for this mussel. So the team compared three related deep-sea mussels and found two stretches of DNA, just upstream of period, that were nearly identical across species.

The researchers copied those stretches from B. azoricus and tested them in fruit fly cells that lack their own clock parts.

The mussel’s CLOCK and BMAL proteins increased the activity of a test gene controlled by one of those DNA segments.

In a recent development, A protein called CRY2 shut the signal down, and more CRY2 meant a stronger effect. The mussel’s PER protein had no effect on its own.

Added alongside CRY2, though, PER made the shut-off stronger and helped CRY2 build up inside the cell’s nucleus. A third protein, TIM, canceled PER’s effect.

The PER result matters because the period gene in these mussels rises and falls on a roughly tidal schedule.

The researchers suggest the balance between PER and CRY2 could switch the clock between tidal and daily timing.

The deep sea is one of the least explored ecosystems on Earth, and prepares for deep-sea mining are putting it under pressure.

Kristin Tessmar-Raible, who studies biological clocks at the University of Oldenburg and the University of Vienna, led the study with Marjolaine Matabos of Ifremer, France’s national ocean research institute.

“The fact that these ecosystems are mechanistically highly complex and possess timing systems as sophisticated as those at the surface underlines how worthy of protection they are,” Tessmar-Raible and Matabos noted.

“On land, we know that human activities such as light or vibrations disrupt circadian clocks. Deep-sea clocks are very likely just as vulnerable, with significant consequences for organisms and ecosystems.”.

The team noted that mining could affect the timing of deep-sea animals even from a great distance.

A dish of cells doesn’t capture everything happening inside a whole mussel at a vent.

The team also detected RNA from the period gene in mussel tissue, while levels in the cultured cells were below what the test could detect.

Either the cells with a tidal rhythm didn’t survive in culture, or conditions in the dish turned off whatever drives the tidal pattern of period, the researchers wrote.

According to recent reports, the next question is whether a mussel runs one clock that switches between tides and days, or keeps separate groups of cells that each follow one rhythm. The researchers wrote that their results fit either idea.

Genome studies and work locating the clock proteins inside mussel tissue could help tell those two ideas apart, the team wrote.

The full study was published in the journal EMBO Reports.

#111624. What to know about kratom and its powerful derivatives

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1295 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencenews ↗ Open Full Page

What to know about kratom and its powerful derivatives

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1295 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencenews

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that this is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • Recent findings suggest that for the past few years, addiction specialist Roopa Sethi has been seeing a fresh set of patients.
  • According to recent reports, kratom is a plant used for chronic pain relief and to help people stay off opioids.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Recent findings suggest that for the past few years, addiction specialist Roopa Sethi has been seeing a fresh set of patients. They show up at the University of Kansas Health System hospital in Kansas City with what looks like severe opiate withdrawal: nausea, vomiting and muscle aches. They’re extremely anxious and sometimes hallucinating. But they haven’t taken an opioid, like fentanyl or heroin. Instead, they’ve used something labeled as kratom, though it may not contain kratom at all.

According to recent reports, kratom is a plant used for chronic pain relief and to help people stay off opioids. But souped-up fresh versions with hyperpotent derivatives of the active compound are sold online and in gas stations. The derivatives act strongly on the body’s opioid receptors and are often far more powerful than the opioid drugs they are sometimes intended to replace. Kratom products — sold as pills, liquid shots, edibles and more — are often mislabeled, and state and federal regulations lag far behind.

A 2026 survey estimated that about 5 million Americans have used kratom or similar products, and the increased use has sent kratom-related exposures up 1,200 percent from only 258 exposures in 2015, according to the National Poison Data System.

Industry observers note that now, newer versions of the substance can produce withdrawal symptoms like nausea and vomiting, which are often so severe they bring people to the hospital. Here’s what to know.

Kratom comes from the dried leaves of Mitragyna speciosa, a tree native to Southeast Asia. Dutch scientist Pieter Willem Korthals first described it in 1839. But “without a doubt, it was used likely for centuries prior to that” in countries including Thailand, Indonesia and Myanmar, notes Oliver Grundmann, a pharmacologist at the University of Florida in Gainesville. “Wherever there is a stream, these trees are growing there.” People chewed the leaves for a stimulant effect and brewed them into a tea to treat pain,” Grundmann says.

According to recent reports, in the United States, kratom is billed pain treatment that is more “natural” than opiates like morphine, Sethi indicates. “When you take this product at low doses, it is used for waking up … but at higher doses it becomes opiate-like.” Others take it to treat withdrawal or cravings from opioid use.

It has been revealed that the leaf form contains more than 40 different naturally occurring chemicals called alkaloids that could have psychoactive effects. The most notable is mitragynine, which makes up two-thirds of the plant’s alkaloid content.

Industry observers note that mitragynine acts on the body’s mu opioid receptors. These receptors — found in the brain, spinal cord and gut — usually respond to natural peptide signals in the body such as endorphins, signaling cells to produce pain relief and release chemicals like dopamine. The receptors get their name from the most famous drug that binds to them: opium. Mitragynine is not derived from or related to opium or morphine but it binds partially to the receptor.

“It’s kind of like a dimmer switch versus turning on the lights,” says Mallory Pullman, a clinical toxicologist at the Mississippi Poison Control Center at the University of Mississippi Medical Center in Jackson. “You don’t fully light your room.”.

Mitragynine also hits receptors that bind norepinephrine, serotonin and dopamine receptors, says Grundmann. The activity at adrenergic receptors creates a stimulant-like effect. “Now I think when we look at mitragynine, it’s primarily kind of this duality of the adrenergic and the opioid receptor activity,” he says, producing stimulating and depressive results in turn.

What nature made, chemists and users are happy to tweak.

As the kratom leaf is dried, Grundmann claims, tiny amounts of mitragynine metabolize into another alkaloid, 7-hydroxymitragynine, or 7-OH. After someone takes kratom, the body also converts some mitragynine to 7-OH. The small chemical tweak changes the compound from one that binds partially to the mu opioid receptors to one that binds fully — like morphine or opium, Grundmann says. 7-OH binds 10 times more strongly to mu opioid receptors than mitragynine does. The resulting product is far more potent in its effects and addictive potential.

Industry observers note that when people use the leaves alone, the amount of 7-OH is extremely limited. But by the mid-2010s, scientists found products with more than 500 percent more 7-OH than in the plant alone, and now, consumers can buy products labeled as pure 7-OH.

While 7-OH can be described as “natural” because it can, in theory, occur in nature, toxicologists like Pullman are also seeing synthetic derivatives that are even stronger, including one molecule named MGM-15. MGM-15 is sold as a “research chemical” and is four times more powerful than 7-OH.

Industry observers note that what is in kratom products may not always be what’s on the label, leaving users in the dark about what they are taking. In a 2026 analysis of 44 different kratom products, including tablets, dissolvable films and edibles, Pullman and her colleagues found that 85 percent of the products had contents that did not match the label. Some advertised kratom but contained very high levels of 7-OH. Others had alkaloids that weren’t listed at all.

It’s “very concerning at a consumer level if you can’t trust what’s actually on the label,” Pullman claims.

Sethi started hearing the word kratom about 10 years ago in her work with people seeking treatment for opioid use. “I would have patients intermittently tell me about kratom use,” she indicates. People were using kratom to stay off opioids, or to treat pain, and didn’t report being addicted to the plant.

Now, it’s a different story, Sethi says.

Patients who started using kratom or 7-OH to get off opioids “now are having really bad withdrawal and cravings and ending up in the hospital,” she says. Some are seeking addiction treatment, not for opioids, but for kratom and 7-OH. In 2025, U.S. poison centers documented 3,434 kratom-related exposure reports, reported both by people who called the center and medical professionals. “I see less fentanyl and more kratom at this point, or more 7-OH,” Sethi says.

According to recent reports, in July of 2026, the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration temporarily classified some kratom derivatives as Schedule I drugs, meaning they have high abuse potential and no medical use. Those derivatives include 7-OH and another related kratom derivative, mitragynine pseudoindoxyl or MGPI, as well as MGM-15 and its powerful sibling MGM-16. The DEA re-upped the temporary scheduling of MGM-15 and 16 and MGPI in October. 7-OH was temporarily placed in Schedule I at any dose higher than that found in the kratom plant. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has also issued statements warning consumers not to use the products. None of these measures affect the legality of the kratom leaf itself.

Regulations vary at the state level: Twenty-six states don’t regulate kratom at all, while six states and the District of Columbia list kratom’s ingredients as a Schedule I controlled substance, like the current federal scheduling. A further 18 states regulate sale and manufacture in some way.

“I think there’s a lot more concern now, especially that there might be potential opioids out on the market,” Pullman says. Regulations are trying to thread the needle between banning the plant and banning high-potency derivatives, knowing that when one derivative gets smacked down, another will quickly appear in its place. That cycle is a familiar one, mirroring the evolution and development of synthetic opioids.

“There’s risk with everything,” she says. “I think it’s crucial to distinguish the difference between a synthetic product versus the natural, and that way we can clearly attribute where the risk lies.”.

#111623. Voyager 1's light-day milestone: See the photos behind the discoveries

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1471 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Livescience ↗ Open Full Page

Voyager 1's light-day milestone: See the photos behind the discoveries

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1471 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Livescience

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • 18), NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft hit a newly introduced space exploration milestone: The probe, which launched in 1977, became the first spacecraft to reach one light-day from Earth.
  • The milestone is largely symbolic, but it comes with practical consequences: While Voyager 1 cruises through interstellar space at roughly 16.1 billion miles (25.9 billion kilometers) from our planet, it now takes a full 24 hours for radio signals moving at the speed of light to get from Voyager 1 to Earth, and vice versa.
  • Sources indicate that the growing space between Voyager and Earth makes it increasingly hard to troubleshoot problems on the nearly 50-year-old probe.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Early Wednesday (Nov. 18), NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft hit a newly introduced space exploration milestone: The probe, which launched in 1977, became the first spacecraft to reach one light-day from Earth.

The milestone is largely symbolic, but it comes with practical consequences: While Voyager 1 cruises through interstellar space at roughly 16.1 billion miles (25.9 billion kilometers) from our planet, it now takes a full 24 hours for radio signals moving at the speed of light to get from Voyager 1 to Earth, and vice versa.

Sources indicate that the growing space between Voyager and Earth makes it increasingly hard to troubleshoot problems on the nearly 50-year-old probe. But with Voyager 1 still collecting data with two of its science instruments, which are expected to stay powered up into the 2030s, NASA scientists say one thing is certain: The spacecraft isn't done surprising us.

"What Voyager has taught me is to expect the unexpected," Linda Spilker, who joined the Voyager team in 1977 and is the mission's current project scientist, told Live Science in an interview. "So many times the ideas and theories we had, Voyager was able to prove them wrong.".

Here, we look back at some of Voyager 1's most groundbreaking discoveries, told through its incredible photos.

NASA's Voyager 1 probe launches atop a Titan/Centaur-6 launch vehicle from the Kennedy Space Center in Florida.

According to recent reports, NASA's Voyager 2 probe released before Voyager 1, on Aug. 20, 1977. Voyager 1 took off a few weeks later, on Sept. 5. (The two spacecraft took slightly different routes through the solar system, allowing Voyager 1 to reach interstellar space first after a gravity boost from Jupiter and Saturn.).

Spilker, who joined NASA right out of college, attended the historic Voyager 2 launch and recalls "that feeling of watching the rocket lift up off the launchpad, feeling the roar of those rocket engines and knowing this was a mission going to visit places I'd always been curious about.".

A few weeks after launching, Voyager 1 took this photo of a crescent Earth and moon from 7.25 million miles (11.66 million km) from Earth.

On its way to the outer solar system, Voyager 1 snapped this image of a crescent Earth and its moon, captured in the same frame for the first time ever.

Industry observers note that voyager 1 photographed Jupiter from January to April 1979, reaching a minimum distance of 174,000 miles (280,000 km) in March 1979, according to NASA. As the spacecraft zoomed closer to the giant planet, it snapped an image every 96 seconds, creating this incredible time-lapse animation of the planet's turbulent atmosphere.

A time-lapse animation of Voyager 1 approaching Jupiter over the course of one Earth month.

It has been revealed that the close-up view indicated that Jupiter is a far more dynamic world than previously thought. But Voyager also made key discoveries about the planet's many moons.

According to recent reports, while passing by the Jovian moon Io, Voyager 1 witnessed an explosion: the first volcanic eruption ever seen beyond Earth. This proved that there were other geologically active worlds in our solar system, opening up entirely upcoming avenues of inquiry and exploration.

A blue eruption on Jupiter's moon Io, the first volcanic eruption seen on another world.

In a recent development, "Going in, we thought that the moons would look a lot like our own moon: ancient dead worlds," Spilker stated. "And yet we found out they were very different worlds — like Io with active volcanoes. It was just an incredible change in our thinking.".

By viewing these eruptions, scientists saw parts of Io's surface being changed in real time. "As we got closer [to Io], scientists kept saying the surface is getting younger and younger, because they didn't see any massive craters, no medium sized craters, no little craters — until finally parts of its surface are just minutes old," Spilker noted.

A mosaic view of Callisto taken from Voyager 1 photos at a distance of about 250,000 miles (400,000 km).

Some of Voyager's close-up observations also confirmed old theories. For example, Voyager 1's flyby of the moon Callisto in March 1979 revealed vast fields of well-preserved impact craters, proving that Callisto was geologically dead.

Jupiter and its thin ring of dust backlit by the sun in a Voyager 1 image.

In a recent development, A final surprise at Jupiter came when Voyager 1 swooped around the planet's nightside, seeing the gas giant backlit by the sun. This view revealed a thin ring system around the planet, made partly of the dust particles Io spewed into space.

Voyager 1 reached Saturn in November 1980 and made its closest approach to the planet on Nov. 12 of that year. Four days later, the spacecraft took this image of the planet's nightside, showing a broad shadow cast onto the surrounding rings.

Recent findings suggest that "That is one of my favorite pictures: an outbound image, taken by Voyager looking at [Saturn] in a way you could never see from the Earth," Spilker remarked, noting that we can only ever see Saturn's sunlit side from our planet. "The rings just look so beautiful shining there, and you can actually see the shadow of Saturn on the rings themselves. It's a really, really special picture.".

In addition to discovering a previously unknown ring, Voyager 1 spotted five newly introduced moons around Saturn and took close-up photos of several other known satellites.

Voyager 1's closeup view of Titan revealed a dense, hazy atmosphere.

The mission required Voyager to swing by the moon Titan in order to bend the probe's trajectory, sending it away from the solar system's planetary plane and toward a rendezvous with interstellar space. Before that, Voyager 1 revealed Titan's atmosphere to be so hazy that it completely obscured the moon's surface. This showed that Titan's clogged atmosphere was far denser than those of Earth and Mars.

By 1990, Voyager 1 was so far from the planetary plane that our solar system's planets looked like little more than specks of light. But before turning off its camera for good, Voyager 1 looked back at our cosmic neighborhood and took some of the most iconic space photos of all time.

In a series of 64 images taken from roughly 40 times Earth's distance from the sun, Voyager snapped its solar system "family portrait," a mosaic of images capturing six planets together for the first time. The portrait included views of Venus, Earth, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune.

Frames from Voyager 1's family portrait showing Venus, Earth, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune.

The image of Earth from this collection is famously known as the "Pale Blue Dot.".

"We took the pictures of the planets in color, and that one is especially one of my favorites," Spilker mentioned. "There's Earth captured in a sunbeam. A tiny world less than a pixel in size representing all the life that we know in our solar system — just a very special image reminding us just how special and precious our planet is.".

Earth appears as a pale blue dot in this iconic Voyager 1 image.

In a recent development, voyager 1 turned off its camera immediately after taking these images, concluding its role as the greatest tourist in the history of our solar system. In 2012, Voyager 1 passed beyond the heliopause — the boundary where the sun's radiation gives way to the interstellar medium — becoming the first interstellar spacecraft in history.

Voyager 2 crossed the same boundary in 2018 and is expected to reach its own light-day in 2035. In the meantime, several science instruments remain active on both probes, allowing them to measure the strange and mysterious environment between stars.

Even way out there, the probes are still detecting whispers of the sun's power.

According to recent reports, "We are still seeing effects from the sun that come out, hit the heliopause, and send shocks and pressure fronts out into the interstellar medium," Spilker stated. "I wonder where we will finally reach the point where the sun doesn't influence what we're seeing, and we're in the pristine interstellar medium — and I hope that happens while Voyager 1 is still operating.".

He holds a bachelor's degree in creative writing from the University of Arizona, with minors in journalism and media arts. His interests include black holes, asteroids and comets, and the search for extraterrestrial life.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Taung Child is about 3 million years old, and a fresh study suggests some fossils long grouped with it may belong to a different species.

It has been revealed that A skull the size of an orange changed everything we thought we knew about human origins in 1924. Now, a century later, it’s doing it again.

Newly introduced research has pinned the Taung Child – the original specimen of Australopithecus africanus and the first fossil proof that humans evolved in Africa – to between 2.96 and 3.03 million years old.

A more unsettling finding was that many of the fossils long grouped alongside it probably don’t belong there at all.

The study was conducted by an international team led by Gabriele Macho from the Vrije Universiteit Brussel.

The experts combined uranium-lead dating, 3D dental morphometrics, brain development modeling, and fossilized pollen to argue that southern Africa’s early hominin landscape was far messier than textbooks suggest.

Here’s an uncomfortable fact that paleoanthropology has been skirting for decades. Australopithecus africanus – one of the most cited species in human evolution – has never been properly defined.

In a recent development, the Taung Child is its holotype, the original reference specimen. But no definitive diagnostic criteria were ever established for classifying other fossils into the same species.

According to recent reports, since the 1950s, researchers have lumped dozens of South African fossils under the A. africanus label. However, they used vague qualitative descriptors like “more rounded” and “less extreme.”.

Strictly speaking, the Taung Child remains the only unequivocal member of its own species.

“For over 100 years, we assumed the Taung Child was just one of many similar fossils from the era,” Macho noted.

“Our findings turn that on its head. The human family tree wasn’t a neat, straight trunk – it was a chaotic, tangled bush driven by climate shifts.”.

The team used 3D geometric morphometrics of the dentino-enamel junction – the boundary between enamel and dentine inside first molars – to compare Taung against other supposed A. africanus specimens.

This internal tooth structure forms early in development. Unlike bone, which remodels through life, it is under strong genetic control.

Taung’s molars fell at the edge of the A. africanus cluster in shape space, equidistant between Sts 18 (a presumed A. africanus) and SK 61 (a Paranthropus robustus).

Other fossils traditionally lumped with Taung – MLD 2 from Makapansgat, Sts 24 from Sterkfontein – looked nothing like it.

Recent findings suggest that the adult fossils assigned to Australopithecus africanus had braincase volumes ranging from 391 to 568 milliliters. That range is comparable to the variation seen within a single living ape species.

Braincase shape raised a different question. Using growth patterns in living apes as a guide, the researchers estimated how the Taung Child’s braincase might have changed by adulthood.

Taung could have developed a braincase shaped like those of two adult fossils, Sts 5 and Sts 60.

In a recent development, three others were harder to explain using the same growth patterns, suggesting that some fossils assigned to A. africanus may belong to a different species.

In a recent development, the team extracted fossilized pollen from cave infills at the Taung site. They found wetland sedges, grasses, and savanna indicators – but also Podocarpus, which is startling.

Today, Podocarpus forests are confined to the wet eastern Escarpment, roughly 400 kilometers northeast of Taung.

Their presence suggests ancient Taung was more wooded than the current dry grassland.

The area was likely a mix of riparian woodland and Bushveld-like savanna stretching across what is today semi-arid Thornveld.

The paper’s most ambitious move is linking all of this to climate.

Hydroclimate records from marine and terrestrial cores show that between 4 and 2.5 million years ago, southern Africa experienced pronounced wet-dry oscillations driven by orbital eccentricity cycles.

The region sits at a critical biogeographic junction, where the tropics bordering the temperate world meet.

That boundary shifted over millions of years as the Intertropical Convergence Zone migrated northward.

The authors propose that early human relatives followed shifting habitats.

As those habitats expanded and contracted, populations may have repeatedly split apart and reconnected, helping explain the diversity seen in the fossils.

According to recent reports, A century after its discovery, the Taung Child is still the only specimen that can truly be called Australopithecus africanus. Everything else might be something different.

The authors are blunt. Scientists should stop invoking “intraspecific variation” as a catch-all explanation.

Instead, they should re-examine the historical biases baked into how these fossils were sorted. They should also treat the eco-evolutionary dynamics of Plio-Pleistocene southern Africa as the primary engine of the diversity we see.

The Taung Child isn’t just a museum piece. It’s a provocation and a clear warning against tidy narratives.

The study is published in the journal npj Palaeoecosystems.

#111619. Could a wasp the size of a sesame seed help protect carrots and canola?

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1138 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Could a wasp the size of a sesame seed help protect carrots and canola?

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1138 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Scientists discovered Gonatopus quebecensis, a tiny wasp in Québec that attacks leafhoppers and might help protect crops naturally.
  • According to recent reports, some leafhoppers in Québec farm fields have a small sac stuck to their bodies.
  • Each sac holds a wasp larva that feeds on the leafhopper as it grows.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Scientists discovered Gonatopus quebecensis, a tiny wasp in Québec that attacks leafhoppers and might help protect crops naturally.

According to recent reports, some leafhoppers in Québec farm fields have a small sac stuck to their bodies. These insects are known to spread disease to carrots and canola.

Each sac holds a wasp larva that feeds on the leafhopper as it grows.

According to recent reports, the wasps were raised to adulthood by researchers, who found a species nobody had named. It has now been called Gonatopus quebecensis.

It belongs to a group known as pincer wasps and is about as long as a sesame seed.

The wasp is a natural enemy of a crop pest and was already living in the fields. The researchers do not yet know whether it kills enough leafhoppers to help a farmer.

Leafhoppers on the province’s farms have been studied by scientists at Université Laval in Québec City since 2021.

Study supervisor Edel Pérez-López said the sightings “sparked our curiosity about the natural enemies of these important agricultural insects.”.

In a recent development, the study itself is a description. Lead author Thomas Vinatier and five colleagues described the wasp’s body and read a stretch of its DNA. The insect it grows on was also identified. The wasp was not tested as pest control.

According to recent reports, in July 2025 the team collected leafhoppers carrying wasp larvae. The insects came from highbush blueberry fields in the Mauricie region of Québec.

According to recent reports, they were moved into a university greenhouse where the wasps bred on leafhoppers kept on potted barley. The room was held at 73°F (23°C) and the lights stayed on 18 hours a day.

Industry observers note that adult wasps emerged and the colony kept going. One female now serves as the reference specimen for the species. She was reared there in January 2026.

Sources indicate that for close study the researchers randomly picked 11 adults. Six were females and five were males. Seven more were dissected so the mouthparts could be examined under a microscope.

Sources indicate that the reference female and one male are now stored in Ottawa. They are kept in the Canadian National Collection of Insects, Arachnids and Nematodes. The other specimens stayed at the university.

The new species is named after Québec. A total of 55 Gonatopus species are now known from the Nearctic region. That region covers most of North America.

In a recent development, the female has no wings. She is mostly black with brownish-yellow on parts of her legs and antennae. At 0.12 inches (2.97 millimeters) long she could pass for a small ant.

Industry observers note that each of her front legs ends in a pincer. It is made of an enlarged claw and the last segment of the foot. A row of tiny plates is carried on that segment.

Pincers like hers give the family its common name. Females grab their prey with them. The family has 1,928 known species that attack leafhoppers and their relatives.

Recent findings suggest that the male is a little smaller at just under a tenth of an inch (2.41 millimeters). He is almost entirely black and has clear wings.

Males and females are hard to match in these parasitic wasps. The two sexes of one species can look very unlike each other. Matching them by eye is therefore unreliable.

Sources indicate that rearing helped because both sexes came out of the same colony on the same host. The match was supported by the DNA data.

Recent findings suggest that A short stretch of a gene was read from four wasps. Two were females and two were males. Biologists use that stretch as a DNA barcode because it differs from one species to the next.

Sources indicate that no named species in the public databases matched the four wasps. Two unnamed records did.

One was a larva from Québec that the same lab had raised earlier from the same leafhopper species. It was a 99.91% match.

Industry observers note that the other was an unidentified larva from Ontario. It was filed in a reference library of 1.5 million barcodes from Canadian invertebrates.

The Ontario larva’s barcode matched the females’ exactly and the males’ at 99.80%.

The wasp had therefore been collected and sequenced before in two provinces. It may have gone unnamed because no adult specimens were available.

Among the named species compared, Gonatopus pedestris had the most similar DNA barcode, at 95.74%.

Only one G. pedestris barcode was available for the comparison. It came from a specimen collected in Norway. The authors wrote that more samples are needed to show how the two species are related.

The wasp’s host is the aster leafhopper. This insect is about an eighth of an inch (3 to 4 millimeters) long.

The wasp’s larvae develop on the aster leafhopper and feed on it.

An infected aster leafhopper can pass along phytoplasmas as it feeds on a plant. Phytoplasmas are bacteria-like organisms that have no cell wall.

One result is aster yellows, a disease capable of heavy losses in canola and carrots.

Recent findings suggest that the aster leafhopper is abundant on Canadian farms. In Québec strawberry fields it was found more often than any other leafhopper in the team’s earlier surveys.

Spraying has not been a sure answer for these crop pests. Strawberry fields in eastern Canada were examined in a 2024 study by members of the same lab.

They reported that growers’ sprays may not have been keeping leafhopper numbers down.

Industry observers note that the search for the leafhopper’s natural enemies had a second motive. Pérez-López noted it was the province’s push to use less insecticide.

It has been revealed that the farming question was left open by the researchers. They do not yet know what share of leafhoppers the wasp attacks or at what time of year. It is also unclear whether other leafhopper species are used.

According to recent reports, wingless females are poorly sampled by the traps entomologists set for flying insects. Wasps like this one may therefore be undercounted across North America, the authors wrote.

It has been revealed that the team suggested repeating its own method in more places. Leafhoppers that carry wasp larvae would be collected and kept alive until the wasps emerge. The adults can then be matched by body and by DNA.

The authors wrote that such studies must come first. Only then can the wasp’s contribution to pest control be judged.

Three jobs are planned by Pérez-López’s lab. They are a full genome for the wasp, a closer look at its breeding and trials with other leafhopper species.

The full study was published in the journal ZooKeys.

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1085 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Brain scans reveal where fractions fit on the mental number line

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1085 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Brain scans show that adults use a shared mental number line to compare fractions and whole numbers, even as the brain distinguishes between them.
  • It has been revealed that A quarter looks more like four on the page, but its value is much closer to zero.
  • As adults compared fractions and whole numbers, brain activity followed a shared number line.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Brain scans show that adults use a shared mental number line to compare fractions and whole numbers, even as the brain distinguishes between them.

It has been revealed that A quarter looks more like four on the page, but its value is much closer to zero. In a upcoming brain scan study, that difference mattered.

As adults compared fractions and whole numbers, brain activity followed a shared number line.

The patterns still distinguished fractions from whole numbers, but numbers close in value tended to produce more similar patterns.

One idea about how the brain handles abstract concepts is that it files related concepts close together, so that similar ideas produce similar patterns of activity.

Numbers are a good way to test that, because everyone agrees on their order.

Daniela Valério and Stanislas Dehaene of the Inserm-CEA Cognitive Neuroimaging Unit, known as Unicog, led the study at the NeuroSpin center outside Paris.

People have long been known to carry a number line in their heads for whole numbers. The team wanted to know whether fractions, which children learn after years of schooling, get added to the same line.

Twenty-two adults took part, all right-handed native French speakers between 19 and 39 who had finished high school with a science track.

Two were excluded, one for a cyst found on the scan and one who had a panic attack in the scanner.

That left 20 participants in the brain scan analysis. A faulty response button reduced the number to 19 for the analysis of speed and accuracy.

Industry observers note that each person lay in a high-field MRI scanner run by the French research agency CEA. The numbers 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5 and the fractions 1/4, 1/3, 1/2, 2/3, 3/2, and 5/2 flashed up one at a time, each for one second.

For every number, the person pressed a button to say whether it was bigger or smaller than the one before.

In a recent development, each run lasted just under ten minutes, and every number followed every other number exactly once. The fractions were built from the same digits as the whole numbers on purpose.

That let the team tell whether the brain was reading 1/4 as a quarter or as a 1 next to a 4.

It has been revealed that fractions slowed people down. A comparison between two fractions took about 1.2 seconds on average, against 0.8 seconds between two whole numbers.

People also got 9.5 percent of fraction pairs wrong, compared with 3.7 percent of whole number pairs.

In an interview with Earth.com, Valério remarked fractions are harder for a few reasons.

Whole numbers follow a simple counting sequence, so 3 is followed by 4, while there is always another fraction between any two different numbers.

Industry observers note that the size of a fraction is also not always easy to judge from the numbers in it. “For example, although 5 is greater than 3, 1/5 is smaller than 1/3,” Valério stated.

In a recent development, numbers that were close together were also harder than numbers far apart, whichever kind they were. The closer two numbers were, the slower and less accurate people got, and the effect was strongest when both were fractions.

Psychologists have known this distance effect for whole numbers for decades, and here it held for fractions too.

Sources indicate that the team then laid out the speed and error data as a map. The 12 numbers fell along a single curved line in order of size, with the fractions among the whole numbers where their values belonged.

Recent findings suggest that the scans revealed the same thing. Across the brain regions that handle math, the pattern of activity for each number varied along two main directions.

According to recent reports, one separated fractions from whole numbers. The other ordered all 12 numbers by size, from small to large, and ignored whether they were fractions.

The size ordering was strongest in the intraparietal sulcus, a fold near the top and back of the brain that has long been tied to math.

Sources indicate that researchers have also linked this region to the ability to estimate quantities. In the latest study, patterns of activity in the hippocampus also reflected how close numbers were in value.

Then the team looked at single points on the cortex.

Industry observers note that within the front part of that parietal fold, many spots responded most to one particular number and less to its neighbors. The spots formed a map, with small numbers at the front and larger numbers farther back.

The map for fractions matched the map for whole numbers. Spots that preferred 0 also responded to 1/4, 1/3, and 1/2, and 1/4 ended up far from 4.

Valério mentioned that when people compare numbers, they have to focus on magnitude, meaning how large or small each one is.

“Our study demonstrates that the brain organizes this information into a shared map, much like a mental number line, “Valerio told Earth.com.

“This map brings whole numbers, such as 1 and 2, and fractions, such as 1/2 and 2/3, into the same system, according to their values.”.

The size map highlighted up in only 14 or 15 of the 20 participants, depending on the number type. The fractions also stopped at 5/2, short of the range the whole numbers covered.

Fractions and whole numbers were mixed in one stream, so people may have had to build a single line to keep up.

The authors wrote that if the two kinds had been shown in separate sessions, each might still have run from small to large. The two lines might not have lined up, though.

Sources indicate that valério said the study was not designed to explain why fractions are harder to learn or to find the best way to teach them. Other studies in her lab are working on that.

Her next step is to see how the shared map differs across people with different mathematical backgrounds and levels of education, and whether those differences go with mathematical ability.

How the brain represents fractions in children who are still learning them remains an open question.

The team has posted its data and code on the Open Science Framework. It wrote that longer scanning sessions could extend the map to more kinds of math.

The full study was published in the journal PLOS Biology.

Industry News: Hawaii’s 90-foot Hōlei Sea Arch was carved from lava that flowed about 550 years ago, and in late September it fell into the Pacific

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (805 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the 90-foot Hōlei Sea Arch in Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park collapsed in late September 2026.
  • For years, visitors who drove to the end of Chain of Craters Road in Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park could walk a short distance and see a 90-foot arch of lava rock reaching out from the cliffs into the Pacific Ocean.
  • In a recent development, that view is gone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the 90-foot Hōlei Sea Arch in Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park collapsed in late September 2026. Here is how it formed and why sea arches eventually fall.

For years, visitors who drove to the end of Chain of Craters Road in Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park could walk a short distance and see a 90-foot arch of lava rock reaching out from the cliffs into the Pacific Ocean.

In a recent development, that view is gone. The Hōlei Sea Arch was still standing on Wednesday, September 23, 2026. By the night of Sunday, September 27, it had collapsed into the ocean, the National Park Service unveiled on October 1.

Recent findings suggest that the exact time of the collapse is unknown. According to the park, it could have happened while the park was temporarily closed during Tropical Storm Nolo.

The arch stood about 90 feet (27.4 meters) high and extended from steep sea cliffs into the ocean along the park’s southern coast, on the Island of Hawaiʻi.

Sources indicate that it was carved into the cliff of an ancient lava flow from about 550 years ago, according to the park. The arch took shape through what geologists call differential erosion: some layers of lava are harder than others, so the sea wears them away at different speeds.

Visitors could see it by walking a short distance from the end of Chain of Craters Road, which the park described in 2020 as a 19-mile drive through some of the most spectacular scenery in the park.

Sources indicate that the park’s own page on the arch was clear about one thing. The formation was beautiful but temporary, with a limited life span, and it would eventually crumble into the sea.

It has been revealed that sea arches like Hōlei can be found along a wide stretch of Hawaiʻi’s southern coast. They are remnants of once-continuous sea cliffs, built where lava met the sea and added to the size of the island.

Lava meeting the sea can even build whole latest land, as it did when a new island rose from the sea off Iceland in 1963.

The moment that new lava cooled and turned to rock, it began to erode, the park explains. The seas on the island’s southern edge are known for rough water and violent surf, and the waves slowly break apart the rock and carve sea caves into the cliffs.

Sources indicate that when waves hit the back wall of a sea cave, the water bounces back and starts to erode the cave’s headland. Over time, that forms an arch.

The erosion does not stop there. Given enough time, the waves cause the remaining bridge of rock to collapse, leaving behind a pile of rocks known as a sea stack.

Volcanic coastlines are constantly being remade, and on the same island, Kīlauea has produced 55 lava fountains since December 2024.

The coastline around the arch had shown signs of instability for years.

Earthquakes during the 2018 Kīlauea eruption and summit collapse damaged the cliffs near the arch. In January 2020, fresh cracks and instability led the park to close the original viewing area and the short trail to it.

“This newly introduced development reminds us that Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park is an ever-changing volcanic landscape,” Rhonda Loh, then the park’s acting superintendent, said in January 2020.

A safer viewing area opened in March 2020, about 1,000 feet past the gate at the end of Chain of Craters Road and set back from the cliff edge.

Later that year, massive surf from Tropical Storm Darby broke off a chunk of rock from the lower part of the arch.

The park is urging visitors to stay back from the unstable cliffs, which drop vertically into the ocean and present a serious risk of falling.

After the collapse, photos on social media indicated people entering the closed area near where the arch once stood.

According to the park, that puts both the visitors and first responders at great risk of falling and drowning off the rough, wave-swept coast.

Visitors are required to stay out of closed areas and away from cliff edges, which can collapse without warning.

The park describes individual sea arches as an ephemeral feature of the island’s constantly shifting coastline.

Recent findings suggest that as the cliff slowly migrates inland, other arches will form and replace Hōlei, the park says. The park notes that erosion does not stop once an arch has formed.

The information was obtained from the National Park Service’s announcement of the collapse, its pages on Hōlei Sea Arch and how sea arches form, and its 2020 releases on the closure of the overlook and the new viewing area.

The U.S. just lost its measles elimination status. What now?

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1874 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencenews

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, this is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • After two years with nearly 100 measles outbreaks, thousands sickened and nearly a dozen deaths, the United States has officially lost its measles elimination status.
  • According to recent reports, the highly contagious disease is now endemic in the United States, the Pan American Health Organization declared November 17.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Updated November 17, 2026 at 12:50 pm.

According to recent reports, this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

After two years with nearly 100 measles outbreaks, thousands sickened and nearly a dozen deaths, the United States has officially lost its measles elimination status.

According to recent reports, the highly contagious disease is now endemic in the United States, the Pan American Health Organization declared November 17. Analyses of cases dated from when the first outbreak began in 2025 in West Texas through part of 2026 revealed the virus has been spreading uninterrupted for more than a year. That benchmark signals measles is no longer under control.

The United States is not alone. Mexico and Bolivia also lost their measles elimination status, PAHO unveiled; Canada had lost it in 2025. “Measles is resurging globally amid persistent gaps in vaccination coverage,” PAHO director Jarbas Barbosa said in a Nov. 17 news conference. “And this global trend is also affecting the Americas.” Countries will need to not only stop ongoing outbreaks, but also prove that no one caught measles within their borders for a full year to regain measles-free status.

In a recent development, that won’t happen overnight. But there is a way, experts say. Vaccinating people across the country, particularly in areas with low vaccination rates, will stifle the virus’s spread. But so far, the U.S. federal public health response has taken a back seat to efforts from state and local health departments to curb ongoing outbreaks.

Measles’s return “is an enormous black eye on the reputation of the United States,” mentioned epidemiologist Jennifer Nuzzo of the Brown University School of Public Health in Providence, R.I., in a Nov. 9 webinar hosted by the university. The Americas led the global campaign to control the virus, and in 2016 the region became the first to eliminate measles transmission from all its countries.

It has been revealed that “To lose [elimination status] means we’re going backwards… meaning decades of progress lost,” Nuzzo said. “It’s an indicator of our lack of protection. It is an indicator of our lack of preparedness for disease threats in general.”.

Industry observers note that PAHO’s verdict comes amid a surge of measles not seen in the United States since 1991. Health officials have recorded more than 7,000 cases since the beginning of the West Texas outbreak. That tally includes nearly 2,300 measles cases in 2025 and 5,412 in 2026 as of November 12, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Over 90 percent of cases have been in people who are unvaccinated or whose status is unknown. States report that 13 people have died, although the CDC so far recognizes only nine of those deaths.

While mild measles symptoms include high fever, cough and a rash, roughly 1 in 5 people will be hospitalized with complications such as pneumonia or brain swelling. Children younger than 5 years and adults over 20 are more likely to get sick, as are pregnant women and their infants. At least 13 babies were born infected, called congenital measles, since the beginning of 2025, researchers report November 16 in NEJM Evidence. Those babies are at risk for developing dangerous brain swelling that is almost always fatal later on in life.

Sources indicate that the measles, mumps and rubella, or MMR, vaccine helped eliminate measles from the United States in 2000. After that, cases still sometimes popped up. Those cases were mostly in unvaccinated people traveling from parts of the world where the virus still widely circulates. At least 95 percent of people in a community need to be vaccinated to prevent outbreaks.

Recent findings suggest that but widespread misinformation, including a disproven claim that the vaccine causes autism, means fewer children are receiving the MMR shot and more people are questioning its safety. According to the CDC, roughly 92 percent of kindergarteners across the United States had gotten the vaccine in 2025, down from 95 percent in 2019. And in 2025, 83 percent of U.S. adults viewed the MMR vaccine as safe, down from 86 percent in 2024, according to a survey from the University of Pennsylvania’s Annenberg Public Policy Center. Yet decades of evidence show the vaccine is safe and highly effective.

Industry observers note that that measles made a comeback is not a surprise, indicates Nathan Lo, an infectious diseases physician and epidemiologist at Stanford University School of Medicine. Until recently, outbreaks were largely isolated to communities with low vaccination rates and quickly contained. But now, outbreaks seem to be more likely to spill over into neighboring communities, Lo says. “There’s a lot of potential connectedness between the outbreaks.”.

In a recent development, what’s more, some infected people aren’t getting tested, making them invisible to officials who are now struggling to trace chains of transmission. An outbreak that hit Arizona and Utah, for instance, was far larger than official numbers suggest, researchers reported July 15 in a preprint at medRxiv.org. The roughly 1,000 confirmed cases may represent just 20 to 30 percent of the outbreak’s true size.

A functional surveillance system is crucial to keeping outbreaks under control, Jonathan Temte, a family medicine physician at the University of Wisconsin School of Medicine and Public Health in Madison, said in the Brown University webinar. Without good surveillance across the entire country, “we can miss pockets out there if people aren’t reporting, if people are hiding cases.”.

In a recent development, but surveillance alone won’t stop the virus from “popcorning across the country,” Nuzzo stated. “Measles has returned, and it’s going to take vaccination to stop it.”.

Over the last two years, measles outbreaks have popped up across the United States, sickening thousands of people since mid-January 2025. Most of those cases, shown by county where they were reported, are in people who are unvaccinated. Colors on the map indicate the relative number of cases reported. Green represents the lowest and red the highest number of cases. Notable outbreaks have appeared in Utah, Arizona, Texas, South Carolina, Wisconsin and Pennsylvania.

Michael Mitchell and Andrea Uhlig/Brown University School of Public Health.

Efforts to boost vaccine uptake could be targeted toward areas with low vaccination rates. Most places across the United States still have vaccination rates high enough to fend off measles, but not all. “Figuring out which ones are [high risk] can be a little tricky,” Lo says. “But if you do, then intervening in those places can be quite helpful to mitigate spread.”.

According to recent reports, homing in on school districts or individual schools could also help. State health departments typically report vaccination rates among school-age children by county. But that broad metric can hide high risk schools with low vaccination rates, epidemiologists Siyu Chen and Ana Bento reported in August in Nature Medicine. Computer simulations relying on data that included 50,000 schools across the United States indicated that school-level estimates best revealed where the virus could gain a foothold. That was true even if county-level vaccination rates were close to 95 percent.

Another element that influenced where measles took off was whether communities with cases were near other areas with low vaccination rates, the team found. The outbreak in Texas, for instance, may have ended faster because communities with low vaccination rates were farther away from one another compared with outbreaks in South Carolina and Pennsylvania, states Bento, of Cornell University. Neighboring areas where many are unvaccinated may face longer-burning outbreaks. “Which is what we are now seeing,” Bento says.

Measles elimination status can be regained. The declaration that the virus is endemic is “not a punishment,” Bento states. It’s a sign that something needs to change. That might include vaccine catch-up campaigns, community outreach or getting rid of nonmedical vaccine exemptions.

It has been revealed that local public health officials are “doing every last thing that you can imagine with limited resources,” health psychologist Noel T. Brewer stated in a Nov. 12 webinar hosted by the Association of Health Care Journalists. But a cohesive blueprint at the federal level could bolster defenses before the virus arrives in newly introduced states, noted Brewer, of the University of North Carolina Gillings School of Global Public Health in Chapel Hill.

Such efforts could be targeted toward areas with low vaccination rates. Most places across the United States still have vaccination rates high enough to fend off measles. “A subset [with low vaccination rates] are high risk,” Lo says. “Figuring out which ones are which can be a little tricky. But if you do, then intervening in those places can be quite helpful to mitigate spread.”.

Sources indicate that there’s also wiggle room in the childhood vaccine schedule to provide kids extra protection. Normally children don’t get their first MMR dose until their first birthday. But doctors can give infants an extra MMR dose at 6 months if there is an active outbreak in their area. Pediatricians can also offer the second dose a month after the first one, rather than waiting until around the time children start kindergarten. Adults, particularly those who received only one dose, can also get a booster. It’s unclear whether health officials will officially recommend such actions.

According to recent reports, “The problem is that there’s no trusted source for this vaccine decision anymore,” Lo says. Previous vaccine recommendations were up to the CDC’s Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices, which was disbanded in March after lawsuits blocked appointments made by Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. “Now, there’s a lot of different medical societies and initiatives to try and fill that void,” Lo says. But it’s unclear which would be best positioned to lead.

CDC director Erica Schwartz has remarked the health agency will not be changing its response to ongoing outbreaks. “We’re going to be doing the same exact thing that we’ve been doing today, which is working with the states,” she told Reuters. The CDC did not respond to Science News requests for an interview, but shared in a Nov. 17 statement that the agency will “encourage MMR vaccination, expand access to vaccines, and help communities close gaps in protection.”.

Eliminating measles again will take dedicated resources and more funding funneled to public health departments across the country, Lo says. “You see increasing measles outbreaks and a lot of time and resources to contain these outbreaks at a time where you’re slashing budgets,” Lo says, “that’s a really bad mismatch.”.

According to recent reports, public health responses to measles are expensive. Officials in Upcoming Mexico spent an estimated $5.4 million — over $53,000 per case — responding to a 2025 outbreak that was linked to West Texas. The CDC has provided an additional $100 million to states to help fight measles.

Other countries have beaten back measles after an unwelcome return. Extensive vaccination campaigns helped Venezuela and Brazil regain measles elimination status after briefly losing it in 2017 and 2019. The Public Health Agency of Canada also announced that its nearly two-year-long outbreak officially ended in October, though it’s unclear when the country might earn its status back.

“It is not hopeless,” Nuzzo mentioned. “It can be done, and I hope it will be done [in the United States].”.

Latest Update: A one-in-a-million catch in a New York harbor turns out to be a bright yellow burbot

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (663 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Fish and Wildlife Service crew caught a rare yellow burbot in Oswego Harbor, New York.
  • Fish and Wildlife Service were running a routine survey in Oswego Harbor, New York, on Lake Ontario, in October when they pulled up a fish they did not expect.
  • Sources indicate that the agency calls it a one-in-a-million catch.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, A U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service crew caught a rare yellow burbot in Oswego Harbor, New York. A genetic condition gave it the color, and it went to Cornell.

Biologists with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service were running a routine survey in Oswego Harbor, New York, on Lake Ontario, in October when they pulled up a fish they did not expect. It was a burbot, and it was bright yellow-orange.

Sources indicate that the agency calls it a one-in-a-million catch. The fish has xanthochromism, a rare condition that gives it a saturated yellow-orange color.

The agency noted the fish would make even the brightest fall foliage look pale in comparison.

It is also the first burbot ever documented during a fisheries survey in Oswego Harbor, although a few anglers have reported catching them there.

Xanthochromism is caused by a genetic mutation that suppresses normal pigmentation and produces the yellow-orange appearance.

According to recent reports, it is considerably less common in wild fish than albinism or melanism, according to the Fish and Wildlife Service. Unusual colors like this have surprised scientists before, as with a bright orange shark.

The place was a surprise too. Burbot populations in the lake are extremely low, and the species usually lives in deeper, cooler water than what is found inside the harbor.

Sources indicate that the crew was not looking for burbot. It came from the Lower Great Lakes Fish and Wildlife Conservation Office, and it was carrying out an Aquatic Invasive Species survey.

The program watches harbors, rivers and bays of the Great Lakes for invasive species on a watchlist.

Because invaders are often rare when they first arrive, the crews use several methods at once, including electrofishing, fyke nets, gill nets and environmental DNA, or eDNA.

Invaders are an old problem in these waters: the Great Lakes have been under invasion from one species for 70 years.

Most fish caught in these surveys are native species. Catching a rare native fish suggests the program may also detect newly arriving invaders when their numbers are still very low.

The agency summed it up as an effective survey strategy, along with a bit of luck.

Sources indicate that the burbot is a native fish of the Great Lakes. It tends to live on the lake bottom, and it is the only cod-like fish species in freshwater, according to a Fresh York Sea Grant fact sheet. The same fact sheet calls it a formidable predator.

In the Great Lakes, sea lamprey predation has been a common factor affecting burbot numbers.

According to recent reports, A 2006 study led by U.S. Geological Survey scientists found that burbot abundance in eastern Lake Erie increased significantly between 1987 and 2003.

The researchers, writing in Transactions of the American Fisheries Society, attributed the apparent recovery to effective sea lamprey control.

The same study suggested that a relatively high density of alewives, a small plankton-eating fish, probably held burbot numbers down in Lakes Ontario and Michigan at the time.

When U.S. Geological Survey fisheries biologists who know the species processed the yellow burbot, they noticed it was emaciated and looked to be in poor health.

According to recent reports, because of its condition, and because the reasons the species remains so scarce in the lake are still unexplained, the fish was sent to the Cornell University College of Veterinary Medicine for a health analysis. The agency has not reported the results.

The agency notes the catch could turn out to be lucky for the species too.

The rare fish may offer valuable insight into the health of burbot populations across the basin, and that could help guide how they are managed.

According to recent reports, the information was obtained from the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, a New York Sea Grant fact sheet and a U.S. Geological Survey study.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Thomas Massie of Kentucky told CQ Roll Call in late October that the Hegseth impeachment resolution would come up in the first week of the post-election lame duck session.
  • The lame-duck session of Congress kicks off this week as the House is expected to consider a resolution to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth while the Senate seeks to advance a bipartisan deal on permitting reform.
  • Last week’s midterm elections saw Democrats claim sizable majorities in both the House and Senate in the new Congress, and among the immediate questions is whether the demoralized GOP will face attendance woes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Departing GOP Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky told CQ Roll Call in late October that the Hegseth impeachment resolution would come up in the first week of the post-election lame duck session. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call file photo) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call).

The lame-duck session of Congress kicks off this week as the House is expected to consider a resolution to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth while the Senate seeks to advance a bipartisan deal on permitting reform.

Last week’s midterm elections saw Democrats claim sizable majorities in both the House and Senate in the new Congress, and among the immediate questions is whether the demoralized GOP will face attendance woes.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., the expected next speaker of the House, said Sunday that he would support the Hegseth impeachment.

“I'm a hard 'yes' on the Hegseth resolution,” Jeffries mentioned on ABC’s “This Week.” “The so-called secretary of Defense has abused his power, undermined our national security and engineered this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran, which has skyrocketed prices on the American people and made the country less safe. Pete Hegseth has got to go.”.

According to recent reports, departing Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., told CQ Roll Call in late October that the Hegseth impeachment resolution would come up in the first week of the post-election lame duck session.

It’s also orientation week on Capitol Hill for newly introduced members of Congress. House orientation got underway Sunday.

The Senate, meanwhile, looks to take up a bipartisan permitting bill that has the backing of President Donald Trump.

“This Landmark Permitting Reform Legislation will codify our America First Energy Agenda, and ensure that we can build Pipelines, Mines, and Power Plants faster than ever before, lowering Energy Costs for American Families, and creating High Paying American Jobs,” Trump posted on Truth Social.

Senate negotiators over the weekend released text of an amendment seeking to address remaining concerns.

According to recent reports, “I’m grateful for the input throughout this process from Senate and House colleagues, environmental and labor organizations, and Tribal leaders. Our manager’s amendment improves [the bill] and addresses the thoughtful feedback we have received,” Senate Environment and Public Works ranking Democrat Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island remarked in a statement. “Now it’s time to pass this bill so we can lower costs, juice the clean energy economy, build big things again in America, reduce pollution, and create tons of new well-paying union jobs.”.

Beyond the permitting bill, the Senate Republican majority may seek to use its remaining time trying to confirm more of Trump’s nominations before the control of the floor agenda passes to the Democrats.

Sources indicate that "We've got the farm bill, the NDAA, and we have that third reconciliation bill that we need to get across the finish line, and there are so many things that we need to get done and buttoned up," including nominations, departing Sen. Marsha Blackburn, R-Tenn., stated in a weekend Fox News interview. Blackburn, one of the Republicans who had success at the ballot box, is now governor-elect of Tennessee. But it's an open question how long lawmakers will want to stick around.

There’s also the matter of an imminent fight over funding the government and laying the groundwork for the newly introduced Congress. Republican leadership elections are scheduled for Tuesday, while Democratic leadership elections are expected in December. Democratic senators-elect are due on Capitol Hill Monday and Tuesday, according to the office of Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y. Schumer is widely expected to be the majority leader in 2027.

There have been some calls for Senate Republicans to delay their elections, though current Majority Leader John Thune of South Dakota has been widely expected to remain as the Republican leader.

Sources indicate that “One of the things I learned in business and the Army is that after a failure, you have to start with honesty, transparency, and accountability,” Sen. Dave McCormick, R-Pa., mentioned in a Sunday night statement. “As I’ve shared with Leader Thune, I don’t believe we should move to leadership elections until we have digested and debated the lessons of the midterms and how to move forward.”.

Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., has also been circulating a letter calling for a delay, and he has argued the election should not be held, in part, because the makeup of the Senate Republican Conference is not yet final. Senate races are still not called in Alaska and Mississippi.

Industry observers note that absent this week will be Sen. Christopher S. Murphy, D-Conn., who recently had a stroke.

In a recent development, “The doctors are very encouraged by the progress I’ve made so far. In order to take my recovery seriously and get back to work on the quickest timeline possible, I will be spending several weeks at a rehabilitation center after being discharged from the hospital today,” Murphy stated in a Friday statement.
