Industry News: A peanut by a lamp can make a city crow warier than a passing human

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1258 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • With a lamp base beside the peanuts, feeding odds fell to 0.53 for city crows and 0.76 for country crows in a Binghamton study of 20 crow families.
  • Industry observers note that in 2019 and 2020, a team led by biologist Dave J.
  • Recent findings suggest that on some mornings the peanuts had company: a rock, an ear of corn in its husk, a paper takeout box or a faux-wood lamp base.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With a lamp base beside the peanuts, feeding odds fell to 0.53 for city crows and 0.76 for country crows in a Binghamton study of 20 crow families.

Industry observers note that in 2019 and 2020, a team led by biologist Dave J. Colucci put out peanuts in the shell for 20 families of American crows around Ithaca, New York. Ten families lived in town, and ten in farm fields and natural areas of the nearby Town of Dryden.

Recent findings suggest that on some mornings the peanuts had company: a rock, an ear of corn in its husk, a paper takeout box or a faux-wood lamp base. Country crows held back more around the box, and city crows around the corn.

City crows were also less likely to eat next to the lamp, the study by Colucci and Anne Clark of Binghamton University found. Other urban-rural differences in the paper had only weak support.

Colucci earned a PhD at Binghamton in 2025. Clark is an associate professor emerita of biological sciences there, the Binghamton University release of November 16, 2026, notes. The paper came out online in Behavioral Ecology on October 22.

Recent findings suggest that each family’s territory got a feeding spot. The bait was 2 cups of raw, unsalted peanuts in a circle about 3 feet (1 meter) wide. They picked spots with little human traffic and no sign of predators or competitors.

Recent findings suggest that in town these were parking lots, dead-end streets and parks in Ithaca, Lansing and Cayuga Heights. Out in Dryden the sites were on private or public land.

Each family got three days with peanuts only and four days with an object, 140 trials in total, each starting between 6 and 8 a.m.

A hidden camcorder sat at least 10 feet (3 meters) from the bait. The observer stayed 164 feet (50 meters) or more away.

Sources indicate that the team ranked the objects by how often a crow in each place would have seen them. Rocks are everywhere and corn grows in Dryden, while takeout boxes are more common in town.

“What we wanted to show was that aversion would decrease with the amount of experience that we expected our crow to have had with these objects,” Colucci noted in the release.

To test the trash part, the team surveyed a 1-mile (1.61-kilometer) road route in each area weekly for three weeks. They counted 341 human-made objects, 169 in town and 172 in the country. Rural ones stayed put longer, 2.81 weeks on average against 2.27.

Recent findings suggest that the box cut feeding more for rural crows and the corn cut it more for urban crows. But the paper states the evidence for that switch was limited.

It has been revealed that crows that live near an Arby’s or a McDonald’s learn to recognize that chain’s boxes, Clark stated in the release. The box in the test was a plain one with no brand.

The lamp base was supposed to be new to every crow, in town or out. The authors chose it because it has none of the usual signs of a human-made thing, like bright colors, shine or sharp corners.

Sources indicate that with peanuts alone, nearly every visit ended in feeding, a probability of 0.99 in town and 0.97 in Dryden. Put the lamp down and it fell to 0.53 for urban crows and 0.76 for rural crows, according to the paper’s Bayesian model.

It has been revealed that how fast the birds came in was another matter. Timing for the boldest crow in each family was about the same in both places with the lamp out. That held for reaching 10 feet (3 meters) of the bait and for taking a first peanut.

It has been revealed that overall, the urban families did reach the bait sooner, at 4.23 times the rural rate. The authors attribute this to the rural crows partly reacting to the person on watch, since country crows are warier of people.

Earlier work had mostly found that city birds are bolder with upcoming things, which is why the release calls this somewhat surprising. Clark stated urban crows “are social animals” that watch one another. “In an area that has a lot of new opportunities, there are also new threats,” she said.

Industry observers note that the second test was about people. An experimenter walked toward single crows and noted how close the walker got before each one flew, a figure biologists call flight initiation distance.

One person did all 145 trials, in upstate Fresh York and in Quebec, in 2019, 2022 and 2023. The pace was a steady 2.7 miles per hour (1.2 meters per second). On some walks the experimenter looked at the crow, and on others tilted the whole face down.

It has been revealed that on average the crows took off when the walker was about 149 feet (45.3 meters) away. The walker got closer than 33 feet (10 meters) only 8 times. Where the walker looked mattered only in more crowded places.

Industry observers note that the model looked at areas with about 13,000 people per square mile (5,000 per square kilometer). There, it put the distance for a downward look near zero, about 82 feet (25 meters) shorter than for a stare. Rural crows left at about the same distance either way.

In a recent development, the authors warn that those predictions are uncertain. Human population within about half a mile (800 meters) of each trial predicted flight distance best.

Sources indicate that crow hunting is allowed in rural Upcoming York in a set season but prohibited within city limits, the paper notes. The release claims crows, seen as a nuisance, are more likely to be shot in rural areas.

It has been revealed that clark called the rural behavior “a blunt, anti-predator strategy” in the release. “Whereas in urban areas, if you were fleeing at every human, you’d never spend any time on the ground,” she said.

The authors compare the gaze result with earlier work on Seattle crows, where flight distance was on average about 10.5 feet (3.2 meters) shorter for an indirect gaze.

Separate University of Washington mask experiments found that wild crows learned the faces of dangerous people and passed the details to other crows. They remembered a threatening person for up to 17 years.

Separate lab work in Germany found carrion crows that made decisions about twice as fast as humans in a visual task.

It has been revealed that the town sites were really suburban, the authors say, not downtown. The litter count covered roadsides at one site per area, and the timing data on approaches came from 2020 only.

According to recent reports, one person ran every flight trial, and the approach timings may partly reflect wariness of the experimenter. Census numbers may also miss parks and shopping areas, where few people live but many walk through.

The lamp may not have been fully new to city crows either. It is perfectly symmetrical around its vertical axis, a shape rare in nature and common in things people make. So the town-country gap could be underestimated, the paper indicates.

Sources indicate that in Ithaca and Dryden, the 20 crow families got the same peanuts. What sat next to them, and who was walking by, changed what they did.

The full study was published in the journal Behavioral Ecology.

#111608. Industry News: Fossil teeth challenge a long-held idea about where early humans could live

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1200 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Fossil teeth challenge a long-held idea about where early humans could live

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1200 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Eight fossil teeth from two caves in southern China suggest that Homo erectus lived in rainforests and survived in the region longer than scientists thought.
  • Dense tropical rainforest was long regarded as a habitat that only our own species, Homo sapiens, had mastered.
  • Homo erectus, an extinct human relative, spread from Africa across Asia.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Eight fossil teeth from two caves in southern China suggest that Homo erectus lived in rainforests and survived in the region longer than scientists thought.

Dense tropical rainforest was long regarded as a habitat that only our own species, Homo sapiens, had mastered.

Homo erectus, an extinct human relative, spread from Africa across Asia. It was thought to need grassland and open woodland.

Fossil teeth from two caves in southern China suggest that Homo erectus lived in a rainforest landscape.

They are also far younger than any other firmly dated fossil of the species on the Chinese mainland.

According to recent reports, the study was led by Kira Westaway at Macquarie University in Sydney and Renaud Joannes-Boyau at Southern Cross University. Colleagues in China and Europe also took part.

Only a handful of teeth were found, and their dates span a broad window. By the team’s estimate, the species was present sometime between 324,000 and 184,000 years ago.

The two caves are known as Baxian and Naxian. Both are found in Guangxi, among steep limestone hills, roughly 9 miles (15 kilometers) from each other.

At the back of each cave sits a small chamber where fossils have been cemented into rock. More than 18,000 mammal fossils have been recovered from these chambers.

Porcupines may have brought many of the fossils into the caves.

Nine of those fossils were teeth from ancient humans.

Researchers assigned eight of the nine teeth to Homo erectus based on their shape, with ancient enamel proteins supporting the identification of four.

It has been revealed that researchers from the Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology in Beijing were part of the team. The institute also provided access to the excavated fossils.

Westaway’s team used five independent methods to date the teeth and the cave deposits around them.

It has been revealed that two of them work out when grains of sediment were last exposed to sunlight. The rest rely on uranium, which decays slowly in the teeth and in a mineral crust capping the fossils.

It has been revealed that in total, 45 ages were obtained. Forty-three of them were fed into a statistical model.

The model gave a 95% probability that Homo erectus was there sometime between 324,000 and 184,000 years ago.

It has been revealed that that span is a measure of how uncertain the dates are. It doesn’t mean the species stayed there for all 140,000 years.

The latest teeth date to between 324,000 and 184,000 years ago, making them younger than the previous firmly dated finds in China, which were about 400,000 years old.

“This is a fascinating discovery because it confirms the presence of Homo erectus in a location we were not expecting and at a time we hadn’t considered,” Westaway noted.

Elsewhere, the species hung on even longer. Fossils from the Indonesian island of Java show it there until roughly 117,000 to 108,000 years ago.

What an animal eats is written into its tooth enamel as chemistry. Carbon from trees and shrubs looks different there from carbon taken in from tropical grasses.

So by testing a tooth, scientists can tell whether its owner fed in forest or in open country.

No signature of tropical grasses was found in the teeth that were tested.

Sources indicate that many values were low enough to indicate a dense, closed canopy. A similar pattern has been recorded in forests of the western Amazon.

It has been revealed that the mix of species fits this picture. Orangutans, elephants, rhinoceroses and tapirs were found among the fossils. Most of the animals were forest dwellers.

According to recent reports, other chemical tests pointed to a humid climate. Conditions were wetter and cooler than in the region today.

Industry observers note that three Homo erectus teeth from Naxian were then tested in the same way. Their carbon values fell in the same forest range.

Those readings fell right where dense canopy gives way to more open forest.

Nicolas Bourgon, affiliated with the Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology in Germany, also took part in the research.

“In this case, the animal teeth and the Homo erectus teeth are telling the same story,” remarked Bourgon.

Sources indicate that strontium is locked into enamel as well. It’s picked up from local rock by water and plants, and animals take it in when they eat and drink. Each type of rock has its own strontium signature.

Teeth form in childhood, between the ages of 2 and 6. Their strontium therefore records where a child’s food and water came from.

Strontium was measured in four Homo erectus teeth. One came from Baxian and three came from Naxian. Each tooth carried signatures from more than one kind of rock.

So each child either moved between regions, or else ate food that had been gathered from several places.

A few of those signatures were consistent with the limestone near the caves.

Recent findings suggest that the most extreme ones best matched rock about 155 miles (250 kilometers) to the south. That area lies toward the Red River valley in northern Vietnam.

“This suggests these humans were far more mobile than previously recognized, moving across surprisingly large distances through a complex rainforest landscape,” Joannes-Boyau stated.

Still, the strontium evidence was called limited by the authors, and their reading of it tentative.

Rainforest has played a part in the debate over how Homo erectus died out.

In a recent development, on Java, the last known members of the species lived in open woodland. Rainforest was expanding around them at the time.

Industry observers note that it has been proposed that the spreading forest contributed to the extinction there. In this view, the species could not adapt to it.

The teeth from Guangxi complicate that idea. Homo erectus was “not ecologically excluded from rainforest environments,” the authors wrote.

Scientists use the word hominin for humans and our extinct close relatives.

“This is the first clear, direct evidence we have for another hominin living within these habitats,” said Patrick Roberts, also of the Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology.

The date range also overlaps with fossils of Denisovans, another extinct human group. Their remains have been found in Laos, on the Tibetan Plateau, in northeastern China and off Taiwan.

The authors wrote that several kinds of humans may have lived across the region during the same period.

The case for rainforest life rests on very few human teeth. Carbon values were obtained from only three of them, and all three came from one cave.

It has been revealed that the teeth show that Homo erectus could survive among rainforest animals. They cannot show that the species did well there.

The authors also wrote that rainforest may not have been its ideal habitat.

Industry observers note that it remains unclear whether this ability was limited to late survivors in southern China. It may also have been shared by the species more widely.

To settle that question, the same enamel tests will be needed on fossils from other sites of a similar age.

The full study was published in the journal Nature.

#111605. A compound used by dentists helped immune cells kill bacteria hiding inside them

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1706 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

A compound used by dentists helped immune cells kill bacteria hiding inside them

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1706 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In lab tests, K21, a compound used in a dental cleanser, helped some human immune cells kill bacteria that can survive inside them.
  • White blood cells protect the body by swallowing and breaking down bacteria.
  • A new study found that K21, a chemical used in dental cleaning products, helped certain human immune cells kill more bacteria in laboratory tests.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In lab tests, K21, a compound used in a dental cleanser, helped some human immune cells kill bacteria that can survive inside them.

White blood cells protect the body by swallowing and breaking down bacteria. But some bacteria survive inside these cells, making them harder to get rid of.

A new study found that K21, a chemical used in dental cleaning products, helped certain human immune cells kill more bacteria in laboratory tests.

Interestingly, the cells continued to kill more bacteria even after researchers removed K21, suggesting that the chemical had changed how the cells worked.

The researchers also found that K21 increased the breakdown and recycling of mitochondria, the tiny structures that provide energy to cells.

When they tested the chemical on small worms, the treated worms lived longer than those that received no treatment.

Christopher Rongo of the Waksman Institute of Microbiology at Rutgers University led the research.

Bhupesh Prusty of Riga Stradiņš University was a co-corresponding author, with other researchers working in Germany, Latvia, the UK and the United States.

In a recent development, the findings are interesting, but they come from cells grown in the laboratory and experiments with worms. Nobody has yet shown that K21 can treat an infection or help people live longer.

It has been revealed that the cells in question are macrophages. Swallowing germs, digesting them and keeping infections in check is their job.

In a recent development, they don’t all work the same way, though. Some are built for fighting infection, others for repairing damaged tissue.

Could K21 change how either type behaves? That was the question.

According to recent reports, blood came from healthy donors. Over nine days the team grew those cells into the two types of macrophages, and a small dose of K21, 0.28 micromoles per liter, sat in some of the dishes the whole time.

Recent findings suggest that enterococcus faecalis went in next. It lives harmlessly in the intestines, and it turns up in hospital infections.

That species was picked for one trait. It can survive inside a macrophage rather than being destroyed.

It has been revealed that the bacteria stayed with the cells for two hours. Gentamicin, an antibiotic, then killed off whatever remained outside them.

Bacterial DNA inside the cells was measured first. Treated and untreated macrophages held much the same amount.

So K21 wasn’t simply making the cells swallow more bacteria.

The macrophages were broken open next, to count the bacteria still alive inside.

Whatever spilled out went onto a gel. Living germs grow into visible colonies there, which makes counting possible.

The infection-fighting macrophages needed no help. Almost nothing survived in them, treated or not.

But the macrophages involved in tissue repair told a different story. Untreated repair cells let more bacteria live. Where K21 had been present earlier, far fewer came through.

Rongo mentioned the treated cells were “much more robust at killing and clearing that bacteria.”.

That was the first real clue. Whatever K21 did to those cells outlasted the chemical itself.

There are standard ways to check whether an immune cell has changed.

One is the chemical messages cells send each other. Another is the set of proteins on their surface, which marks what kind of cell it is.

The team checked both, expecting to see some obvious differences.

In a recent development, most of it came back unchanged. Of the two messages measured, one moved: repair-focused macrophages put out less of a substance that normally calms inflammation.

The surface proteins barely changed either.

Industry observers note that so the repair cells had not simply been turned into the bacteria-killing type. Whatever K21 did was subtler than that.

To find what they were missing, the team read gene activity inside thousands of individual cells, one at a time.

This time, differences appeared.

Two groups with stronger inflammation-related activity grew more common under K21. One group of repair-focused macrophages thinned out.

Three genes caught the team’s attention: IDO1, IDO2 and KYNU.

All three help break down tryptophan, a substance we get from food. Serotonin is built from the same amino acid.

The connection was worth exploring, although the study did not show that K21 changed serotonin levels.

Sources indicate that measuring serotonin in animals given K21 is what the researchers want next. That would show whether the gene activity means anything inside a living body.

The team also noticed something interesting about mitochondria.

They produce a cell’s energy. Like anything else in there, they wear out and need replacing.

Cells handle that themselves. They break mitochondria into smaller pieces and recycle the damaged ones, through a process called mitophagy.

The researchers wondered whether K21 was affecting this cleanup system.

Macrophage mitochondria are hard to examine closely, so two other types of human cell took the imaging.

In both, K21 left the mitochondria more broken up. Signs of recycling grew stronger too.

Other chemicals push cells into recycling their mitochondria. K21 was not working the same way.

In a recent development, it increased a protein called Drp1, which helps mitochondria split into smaller pieces. Similar activity turned up in the macrophages, though only in the cells associated with tissue repair.

That was especially interesting because these were the same cells that had become better at killing bacteria.

Industry observers note that could changing how mitochondria are maintained help explain the stronger response to bacteria? The results point in that direction, but they don’t yet prove how the two changes are connected.

According to recent reports, rongo’s laboratory already works on mitochondria and on how animals cope when oxygen runs low. That gave the researchers another way to investigate K21.

They turned to Caenorhabditis elegans, tiny, transparent worms that scientists often use to study basic processes inside living cells.

The team added K21 to the worms’ food and watched what happened.

The worms did what the human cells had done. More breaking down and recycling of mitochondria, and the mitochondria themselves came out shorter and rounder.

Worms missing certain genes for that process were tested too. In those animals nothing changed.

That suggested K21 depended on the worms’ normal machinery for dividing and recycling mitochondria.

The researchers then asked a different question. Would any of this affect how long the worms lived?

They followed 151 worms given K21 and compared them with 128 untreated worms across three experiments.

Recent findings suggest that the difference was clear. Worms that received K21 lived significantly longer.

But there was something the team needed to rule out first.

A worm on short rations lives longer, which has been known for years. Reduced feeding would have been the dull explanation.

Sources indicate that the researchers checked, and the opposite happened. Worms given K21 actually fed a little faster.

The chemical also did not appear to affect their growth, body size, reproduction or ability to survive through development.

There were many changes happening inside their cells, though. K21 increased the activity of 1,848 genes and reduced the activity of another 1,312.

Even so, Rongo warned against reading too much into the lifespan result. Helping a tiny worm live longer is very different from helping a person live longer.

There are still some important gaps in the research.

The immune cell changes showed up only in cultures holding a mixture of cell types. Take the mixture away and the effect went with it.

Much of the detailed work on mitochondria also took place in cells that weren’t macrophages.

The researchers used HUVEC cells, which come from the lining of blood vessels, and U2-OS cells, which come from a bone cancer cell line.

Industry observers note that the bacterial experiments were limited too. The team tested one bacterial species, using one K21 pretreatment schedule, with three replicates.

They did not give K21 to an infected animal or test whether it helped a human wound heal.

Sources indicate that there was a reason wound healing had attracted their attention in the first place. Earlier research by Gulve and colleagues, beginning in 2016, had reported faster wound healing in animals.

Those findings helped lead the team toward the immune cells examined in this study.

Industry observers note that the worms bring another problem when thinking about human health. They don’t have macrophages at all, and roughly a billion years of evolution separate them from people.

According to recent reports, so the worm experiments can tell scientists something about basic cell processes. They cannot tell us whether K21 would have the same benefits in humans.

The researchers also disclosed where their funding came from.

It has been revealed that part of the work was supported by the National Institutes of Health. The remaining support came from FiteBac, the manufacturer that markets K21.

FiteBac also supplied the material used in the worm experiments.

Rongo has no ownership stake in the manufacturer and no patent on K21, although he received a pilot grant from FiteBac. Prusty received a research grant.

These details matter because the company has a commercial interest in the compound. Independent studies would help establish whether the findings can be repeated.

Even after all these experiments, the team still doesn’t know exactly what K21 attaches to inside a cell.

Its chemical structure offers one possible explanation.

K21 has four fatty acid chains attached to a central structure known as quaternary ammonium silane. Together, these give the compound properties that might allow it to collect in the fatty membranes surrounding mitochondria.

The researchers suspect that could help explain what they observed.

But they have not identified a specific molecule that K21 binds to, so the idea remains unproven.

The researchers now want to test K21 in living animals. They proposal to measure serotonin levels to see whether the gene changes found in cells also matter in the body.

They could also give K21 to infected animals and check how many bacteria survive. This would help show whether the compound can fight infections outside the lab.

So far, K21 has helped human immune cells kill more bacteria and made tiny worms live longer. Whether it can benefit people remains unknown.

The study is published in the journal Life Science Alliance.

#111604. Cracks in public health grew in 2026

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 16m • 📚 Deep Dive (3188 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencenews ↗ Open Full Page

Cracks in public health grew in 2026

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3188 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencenews

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that this is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • It’s tough to tally the injuries or deaths that don’t happen thanks to seat belts, lead testing, smoking bans and vaccines.
  • But when disaster strikes — say, an outbreak or a pandemic — people take notice.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Public health is invisible — until it’s not.

It’s tough to tally the injuries or deaths that don’t happen thanks to seat belts, lead testing, smoking bans and vaccines. “It is the invisibility paradox,” notes Georges Benjamin, CEO of the American Public Health Association in Washington, D.C. “We are invisible because when our best work is done, nothing happens.”.

But when disaster strikes — say, an outbreak or a pandemic — people take notice. This year’s outbreaks of measles, Ebola, hantavirus and cyclosporiasis brought recent federal reductions into focus — and exposed cracks in a system that aims to keep people healthy. For years, that system functioned “reasonably well” despite chronic underfunding, Benjamin indicates. “But since the Trump administration has come on board, they have really made the system at all levels much more dysfunctional.”.

In 2025, the second Trump administration instituted sweeping federal funding cuts and layoffs, dismantled the global health–focused U.S. Agency for International Development and withdrew the United States from the World Health Organization. Officials reversed some of those changes in the wake of lawsuits and public backlash. But the damage persists.

According to recent reports, two stalwarts of U.S. public health — the Food and Drug Administration and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention — have lost between 20 and 30 percent of their staff, due largely to layoffs and early retirements. They have had to scale back, pause or cancel crucial disease-tracking programs at home and abroad. Some CDC divisions don’t have enough staff to function. And both agencies have cut funding to the local governments and nonprofits that shoulder much of the nation’s public health work.

Combined with deep cuts to international aid, that has stymied efforts to contain infectious disease outbreaks around the world, with Ebola in particular going undetected for months, public health experts say.

According to recent reports, domestically, 2026 saw a record-breaking measles outbreak, with some 5,412 confirmed cases as of November 12. That’s more than double last year’s count, and it is the highest number of annual cases since 1991. In mid November, the Pan American Health Organization determined that measles is again endemic to the United States and has stripped the country of its elimination status.

Against a backdrop of shifting federal vaccine guidance, fewer children are receiving the MMR shot that prevents measles. Roughly 92 percent of kindergartners across the United States had gotten the vaccine in the 2025–2026 school year, down from 95 percent in the 2019–2020 school year, according to the CDC. At least 95 percent of people in a community need to be vaccinated to prevent the measles virus from sparking an outbreak.

“The fact that we are spending so much time and energy [on measles] when we have a reliable vaccine is very disconcerting,” claims Lori Handy, a pediatric infectious diseases physician and associate director of the Vaccine Education Center at Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia.

The CDC has not responded to Science News requests for an interview.

Such challenges do not bode well for the future. Public health is tested during times of crisis, and the world will eventually face another pandemic, notes Michael Osterholm, director of the Center for Infectious Disease Research and Policy at the University of Minnesota in Minneapolis. “We’ve not responded [to the 2026 outbreaks] in a way that would give me confidence that the public health system … is prepared for what’s coming down the pike.”.

It has been revealed that on the heels of multiple 2025 outbreaks, measles continued to wallop parts of the United States this year. Communities in South Carolina, Utah and Wisconsin have been among the hardest hit, with sporadic outbreaks also popping up in other states. Until August, however, none of this year’s outbreaks had turned deadly. That all changed in Pennsylvania.

About a quarter of this year’s cases stem from an outbreak in central Pennsylvania, where the virus has spread widely in communities with low vaccination rates. Since April, seven people in the state have died, including two infants too young to be vaccinated. The CDC has so far attributed just six deaths to measles, despite the insistence of Pennsylvania state public health officials. Three children died of measles in November in New York and Wisconsin.

As of November 12, U.S. health officials recorded 5,412 measles cases for 2026. The last time this many cases were recorded was 1991, nearly a decade before the disease was eliminated from the country.

Measles spreads like wildfire, and one sick person can infect more than a dozen others in an unvaccinated community. While milder symptoms include fever and a hallmark full-body rash, infection can lead to pneumonia, brain swelling and even death. Statistically, the virus kills one to three out of every 1,000 infected people.

The United States eliminated measles in 2000, thanks to the MMR vaccine. “Elimination” means the virus was not spreading widely, and any outbreaks were controlled within a year. But dropping vaccination rates have reestablished the conditions to sustain multiple outbreaks — and may have done so as early as 2022, researchers reported in August in Nature Medicine.

It has been revealed that in the wake of losing measles elimination status in November, beating back the the virus again “will take a true change in the public’s trust of health care,” Handy claims. That means figuring out how to get people vaccinated — and to encourage them to work with public health officials on testing and contact tracing after exposure.

According to recent reports, during the 2009–2010 school year, 20 states had MMR vaccination rates equal to or above 95 percent among kindergartners. Just 10 states hit that threshold for 2025–2026, and 18 states had vaccination rates below 90 percent.

It has been more than three decades since measles caused widespread outbreaks in the United States, and many have never experienced the devastation it can cause. When one community hears about an outbreak halfway across the country, “it still feels very foreign,” Handy says. When the threat feels far away, people are not likely to line up to get a vaccine. Yet measles is so contagious that one unvaccinated traveler can bring the virus back home and spark an outbreak in their own community.

Even with the recent spike in cases, there is hope vaccination rates can catch up, indicates Cornell University epidemiologist Ana Bento. She points to California and Upcoming York, which experienced outbreaks in 2015 and 2018; they ended non-medical exemptions for school vaccinations shortly thereafter. Both states now have vaccination rates above 95 percent in kindergartners. “This is not a tipping point where there’s no coming back,” Bento says.

If measles exposed the consequences of long-simmering vaccine hesitancy, then this summer’s cyclosporiasis outbreak was a quick lesson in food safety screening.

In June, Michigan detected its first cases of the foodborne illness. By August 31, contaminated lettuce had caused the largest outbreak of explosive diarrhea ever in the United States, with 12,883 cases reported across 21 states. By the time the CDC declared the outbreak over on September 11, some 570 people had been hospitalized and two had died. Another 8,113 cyclosporiasis infections have not been traced back to any source. “[This] was one of those events where you felt like the cracks showed,” Handy indicates.

But it isn’t easy to track the origins of foodborne illness. Typically, local and state public health officials report cases to the CDC — and investigate the outbreak, with the agency lending support as needed. If patient interviews reveal the culprit to be produce, dairy or packaged food, the CDC contacts the FDA, which identifies the producer and the distribution area — and coordinates recalls. The FDA also conducts on-the-ground investigations at the farms and processing facilities that supplied the food.

Industry observers note that it can take weeks to identify which contaminated foods are behind a foodborne illness outbreak. Each outbreak is different and timing can depend on the pathogen, laboratory evidence and availability of records, an FDA spokesperson told Science News. After Michigan health officials notified CDC that something was amiss on June 25, it was another 21 days before federal officials confirmed a possible culprit: shredded lettuce ultimately traced to a Taylor Farms processing facility in Mexico.

Of more than 20,000 cyclosporiasis cases reported this year, nearly 13,000 occurred across 21 states, with the preponderance of them in the Midwest.

Sources indicate that the FDA aims to complete investigations as soon as possible. But delays in agency reporting early in the investigation led to unnecessary confusion about which foods to avoid in which states, stated Sarah Sorscher, director of regulatory affairs at the Washington, D.C.–based Center for Science in the Public Interest, at a July 16 news briefing. “It’s a perfect storm for viral news. A lot of people have been posting on social media about avoiding fruits and vegetables, which is not good public health messaging.”.

Sorscher applauded the dedication of public servants working to contain the outbreak. But she noted they were working with inadequate support. “These programs are completely overwhelmed by the scale and scope of the work of solving and communicating these novel emerging outbreaks with a dwindling set of resources.”.

Due in part to funding squeezes, in 2025 the CDC stopped mandatory surveillance of six foodborne pathogens, including the single-celled parasite that causes cyclosporiasis, Cyclospora. Speaking at the July 16 news briefing, epidemiologist Barbara Kowalcyk of George Washington University’s Institute for Food Safety and Nutrition Security in Washington, D.C., noted that half of CDC’s food safety budget goes to states to support surveillance and other programs. Yet that budget has remained flat for nearly a decade.

Sources indicate that FDA investigations have also been impacted, with foreign food inspections at historical lows. In the case of cyclosporiasis, delays gathering testing supplies and getting clearance from the Mexican government meant it took nearly a month for FDA investigators to arrive in Mexico once the source of the outbreak was identified, according to the Newly introduced York Times. Once there, inspectors found the parasite in a wastewater tank at a Taylor Farms processing plant — and in a drainage ditch at a farm that supplied the lettuce. Since Cyclospora infects only humans, the probable contaminant was sewage from a source that has yet to be identified.

It has been revealed that without knowing the source of the contamination, it’s hard to know how to stop the parasite from reaching produce in the future, notes Francisco Diez-Gonzalez, a food microbiologist at the University of Georgia in Athens. “It leaves us with the feeling that we most likely are going to have something similar next year.”.

Starting in 2027, FDA aims to increase surveillance of produce historically associated with Cyclospora and boost laboratory capacity in Mexico to speed up investigations.

Outbreaks of other foodborne pathogens — including Salmonella, Listeria and E. coli — have popped up this year, but not at a rate that’s out of the ordinary, indicates Diez-Gonzalez, who served on the U.S. National Advisory Committee on Microbiological Criteria for Foods before the Trump administration disbanded it in 2025. That suggests the sky isn’t falling, though he and others are concerned about our future ability to promptly contain outbreaks.

“We may see [fewer] cases, but it’s not that they are disappearing,” Diez-Gonzalez says. “We will not be able to detect them because we don’t have the resources.”.

When the WHO unveiled in May that an Ebola outbreak had erupted in the Democratic Republic of Congo, the virus had been simmering for months. People in the mining town of Mongbwalu, where the outbreak was first detected, began falling ill in January or earlier, according to reporting from Science. Armed conflict in the region has made the outbreak response difficult, states the WHO, and some aid workers and health facilities have been attacked.

Recent findings suggest that confirmed Ebola cases as of November 15, 2026. To date, 5,593 people have died, and 3,109 have recovered.

It has been revealed that as cases and death counts soared in May, health officials scrambled to test a backlog of patient samples for Bundibugyo virus, the species behind what has become the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak ever recorded. As of November 15, there were 11,432 confirmed cases and 5,593 deaths. Roughly 3,109 people have recovered. Cases have also been detected in France, Uganda, Kenya and Nigeria.

Before the outbreak, the United States significantly scaled back international aid that once flowed from USAID and the CDC. Such cuts may have hampered Ebola monitoring before the outbreak was declared — and affected infection control measures such as contact tracing, says infectious disease physician Krutika Kuppalli of UT Southwestern Medical Center in Dallas.

Sources indicate that kuppalli led an Ebola treatment unit in Sierra Leone during the 2014–2016 outbreak, the largest ever recorded. At the time, the CDC sent 1,450 physicians, epidemiologists and other experts to help out in affected areas. So far around 500 CDC employees stationed in the United States and abroad have responded to the current outbreak.

Sources indicate that by September, the U.S. State Department pledged $887 million toward the purchase of personal protective equipment and the building of fresh Ebola treatment units. That’s roughly a third of the total amount sent during the 2014–2016 outbreak. Still, earlier investments in public health could have saved lives and helped minimize transmission, Kuppalli says.

Recent findings suggest that information-sharing has also been a huge problem, Kuppalli notes. Prior to the second Trump administration, U.S. health officials were in constant contact with WHO teams that shared information about cases and contact-tracing efforts. After the United States withdrew from the WHO in January 2025, CDC officials had to coordinate with other groups such as UNICEF, the United Nations Children’s Fund.

Nevertheless, there has been some progress toward developing treatments and vaccines. Researchers in Congo are testing whether antivirals and engineered antibodies can stave off severe disease and death in people infected with Bundibugyo virus, and whether those treatments can protect people after exposure. In October, a large clinical trial began testing a vaccine that is already approved against the species that caused the 2014–2016 outbreak. Kuppalli and colleagues argued in September in the Lancet Infectious Diseases that the vaccine’s potential for cross-protection merited its use in high-risk situations.

Two Bundibugyo-specific vaccines are poised to join the new trial after early evidence in animals and people showed the shots are safe — and suggested they may be protective.

According to recent reports, conditions have improved in some parts of Congo, according to the WHO. But there are still hundreds of newly introduced cases per week, and other countries should be prepared to respond quickly if the virus crosses borders. “The longer this outbreak continues, the more opportunities the virus has to reach new communities,” Kuppalli says.

In a recent development, the M.V. Hondius was in for a rough voyage the moment it set off from Ushuaia, Argentina, on April 1. A passenger on the small ship had contracted Andes hantavirus, a rodent-borne disease that can cause severe respiratory illness and death. By the time the outbreak was contained, 13 people were infected and three people had died. Public health experts say a lagging U.S. response let other countries take the lead — and suggests the country is not prepared for future epidemics.

In a recent development, it’s unclear how the first patient, who died on April 11, was infected. Another patient died on the ship, and a third — who was allowed to board a plane — died in South Africa.

In a recent development, more than 300 high-risk contacts, including people who spent more than 15 minutes with an infected individual, were quarantined and monitored across 33 countries and territories. None of them got sick. Nor did another 336 low-risk contacts who had brief encounters with someone who fell ill, and who monitored themselves for symptoms.

The United States’ severed relationship with the WHO “in many ways hampered the [country’s] hantavirus outbreak response,” indicates Benjamin, of the American Public Health Association. Before 2025, U.S. experts frequently received information about emerging health threats from the organization. But confusion over who government officials could talk to likely resulted in knowledge gaps and communication delays, Benjamin says. “CDC was not engaged as early on as they needed to be on that outbreak.”.

Sources indicate that instead, other countries including Spain, South Africa, Argentina and Chile played leading roles. After scientists in South Africa determined that Andes hantavirus was behind the outbreak on May 2, passengers disembarked in mid-May in Tenerife, Spain, where health officials screened for symptoms and helped people travel home.

“Outbreak response depends on the knowledge and the relationships that already exist.”.

According to recent reports, the CDC didn’t set up a response team until after May 2, according to the Upcoming York Times. And controversy erupted over uneven U.S. quarantine practices, with some people forced to remain for weeks in quarantine units in Omaha, Neb., while others remained at home. “There was nothing standard” about the protocols, Osterholm says. “Almost everybody got a different approach.”.

The outbreak, which ended July 2, was quickly contained in part because Andes hantavirus isn’t very contagious. Of more than 50 known hantaviruses, Andes hantavirus is the only one known to spread from person to person. Although some rare superspreaders transmit the virus to others through casual contact, transmission typically happens through close contact, such as spending long periods of time together or kissing. It would have been harder to stop a pathogen that spreads easily through the air, Osterholm notes. “By the time that they recognized what was going on, transmission would have already occurred.”.

The international collaboration had some successes, says virologist Gustavo Palacios of the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai in New York City. Experts in South Africa “kept digging when everything was negative,” he says, until they finally identified Andes hantavirus as the cause.

Hantavirus infections are also relatively rare in the Americas, for now. Studies suggest climate change will increase the likelihood that hantaviruses — and other zoonotic illnesses like Ebola — will make the jump from animals to humans. Dense cities can make it easier for diseases to spread. And such threats don’t disappear when funding for studying them dries up.

“The strongest lesson [from the M.V. Hondius] is that outbreak response depends on the knowledge and the relationships that already exist before the event,” Palacios states. Of the billions of viruses on Earth, just a few hundred pose threats to people. With enough resources, researchers can work together to learn as much as possible about those pathogens and be better prepared when a new one emerges — just as previous work on coronaviruses made the rollout of COVID-19 vaccines possible within a year of the pandemic’s start.

“We will not always know in advance which [pathogens] will become important,” Palacios says. But by not tracking rare threats that could one day become larger problems, “we are shooting ourselves in the foot.”.

#111602. Tech Report: What could make a giant planet disappear? Astronomers may have the answer

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1124 w)

Tech Report: What could make a giant planet disappear? Astronomers may have the answer

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1124 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A giant planet stopped crossing its star as seen from Earth, and astronomers suspect an unseen neighbor tipped its orbit.
  • Astronomers had been watching a giant planet pass in front of its star for years.
  • In a recent development, the planet, TOI-2535 b, hasn’t gone anywhere.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A giant planet stopped crossing its star as seen from Earth, and astronomers suspect an unseen neighbor tipped its orbit.

Astronomers had been watching a giant planet pass in front of its star for years. Then, in March 2026, TESS looked again and saw no sign of a crossing.

In a recent development, the planet, TOI-2535 b, hasn’t gone anywhere. Its orbit has tipped, most likely from the pull of a second planet in the same system, one that astronomers haven’t detected directly.

TOI-2535 b, more than 1,000 light-years away, is the first confirmed planet around a single star that astronomers have seen stop crossing.

Samuel Yee, a postdoctoral fellow at UCLA, led the study with astrophysicist Erik Petigura.

Each of those crossings is called a transit. “The planet’s orbit is tilting so quickly that its transit disappeared while we were watching,” Yee said.

When a planet passes between its star and Earth, it blocks a little of the starlight.

The star dims for a few hours, and that small dip is how NASA’s Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) finds latest worlds.

A transit only indicates up if the star, the planet and Earth line up almost perfectly.

If the orbit tips by just a few degrees, the planet passes above or below the star as seen from Earth, and the star never dims.

TESS checked on the star, called TOI-2535, five times between April 2019 and March 2026.

It has been revealed that the planet orbiting it is a hot Jupiter, a gas giant that orbits very close to its star. It goes around once every 8.24 days. Mercury takes 88 days, more than 10 times as long.

To confirm the planet, the team used an instrument on the 11.5-foot (3.5-meter) WIYN telescope at Kitt Peak National Observatory in Arizona.

The experts tracked how the star shifted back and forth, and the measurements ruled out a small star.

Industry observers note that most planets that cross their stars keep a steady schedule. TOI-2535 b’s crossings came as much as six hours early or late. No hot Jupiter that circles its star in under 10 days has a bigger timing swing on record.

Over the years, the crossings grew shorter and blocked less starlight.

A planet blocks less light, for less time, as its path moves from the middle of a star toward its edge.

Over seven years, the path likely moved across more than half of the star’s face. It passed the middle, grazed the edge, then missed the star entirely.

From the ground, the team tried 15 times and caught a crossing only six times, because the planet kept arriving when it wasn’t expected.

When TESS looked again in March 2026, it found no crossing anywhere in the window where the planet could have shown up.

Recent findings suggest that so what’s pulling on it? Planets in the same system tug on each other. If two orbits are tilted relative to one another, those tugs slowly swing the direction each orbit faces.

The team’s computer models suggest the neighbor is at least as massive as Saturn, so it’s probably a second giant planet. The two likely move in a simple rhythm, such as one circling twice for every lap of the other.

By the models, the two orbits must be tilted at least 5 degrees apart to turn this fast.

Sources indicate that in most tightly packed systems, orbits stay within 1 to 2 degrees of each other. If this tilt holds up, the system will be one of only a handful so far out of line.

“We think of the universe as resembling clockwork, where everything is regular, but that’s not true. If there are multiple planets in a system, they can affect each other’s orbits,” Yee mentioned.

“We know of a few systems that are like this. This is the most extreme example we’ve seen because the two planets are interacting so strongly.”.

Petigura used Earth’s moon to explain it.

“If the moon’s orbit around the Earth was perfectly aligned with the Earth’s orbit around the sun, we would see an eclipse every month,” Petigura said.

According to recent reports, “But because the moon’s orbit is tilted, eclipses are less common. The tilt of the moon’s orbit is a relic of its violent formation history, which resulted from a collision with the early Earth.”.

The same geometry decides when TOI-2535 b will be back. The team calculated that each orbit goes through a full cycle every 30 to 50 years.

The researchers expect the planet to start crossing its star again within that span. Its hidden neighbor could start crossing even sooner.

According to recent reports, early planet formation models suggested giant planets need lots of ice to form. So hot Jupiters probably formed far from their stars and moved closer later.

How? Yee and Petigura see two ways. One is violent. A near-collision knocks the planet onto a stretched-out orbit, and the star pulls it in.

The other is slow. The planet drifts inward with other planets through the gas and dust around a young star. This way should leave the orbits flat.

If the suspected giant neighbor is there, the two planets likely drifted inward together through the gas disk around their young star.

It has been revealed that “Because TOI-2535 b has a close neighbor, it probably migrated by slowly spiraling in instead of getting flung in,” Yee said. “We may be seeing a formation channel that doesn’t happen very often but is very interesting.”.

According to recent reports, the tilt is still a loose end. The researchers think parts of the system may have tugged on each other later, tipping the orbits over time.

Hundreds of hot Jupiters are known around other stars. Few have a planet close enough to change their orbits. When one does, the neighbor is almost always much smaller. The only other known exception is WASP-148.

The team can’t say how massive the neighbor is or where it orbits. The crossing times also scattered more than the models predicted.

Industry observers note that the star’s back-and-forth motion was jumpier than expected for an old, calm star, too. Both clues could mean there’s more than one unseen planet.

TESS’s first four years of data alone couldn’t have clearly shown the shrinking crossings.

With no crossings left to time, the researchers wrote that the best way forward is to measure the star’s back-and-forth motion often. A neighbor as heavy as the models suggest should show up in that data on its own.

The full study was published in the journal The Astrophysical Journal Letters.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ron Johnson, R-Wis., walks through the Ohio Clock Corridor this summer.
  • After last week’s midterm elections saw them lose at least seven Senate seats and the majority, some Republicans are pushing for a reckoning, saying the conference should stop and think about its future.
  • It has been revealed that “After the stunning defeat [we] just can’t continue on business as usual.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., walks through the Ohio Clock Corridor this summer. Now he’s pushing to delay leadership elections for his conference, urging a discussion of last week’s larger than expected losses. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

After last week’s midterm elections saw them lose at least seven Senate seats and the majority, some Republicans are pushing for a reckoning, saying the conference should stop and think about its future.

It has been revealed that “After the stunning defeat [we] just can’t continue on business as usual. That kind of defeat demands change,” Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., stated on Monday evening.

It has been revealed that asked if he himself would want to run for Senate minority leader, the Wisconsin Republican responded with a question of his own: “That’s part of our problem. Who’d want the job? Would you want it?”.

In a recent development, though no hopeful had emerged as of Monday afternoon — at least publicly — to challenge current Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., for the top GOP post, the frustration was palpable as Republican senators returned to D.C. and grappled with the election results. Calls grew throughout the day to delay the conference’s leadership elections planned for Tuesday morning.

Sources indicate that “Well, I mean, I’m open to hearing what the arguments are for that,” Thune told reporters Monday when asked about the possibility of postponing the leadership votes. “I don’t know if that solves anything, but like I remarked, it’s going to be a decision that’s ultimately made by Republican senators. We’ll hear them out.”.

Recent findings suggest that johnson told reporters on Monday that if the election is held, he would “leave the room” and walk out. Either way, he seemed certain to at least get a “fulsome” discussion of the topic, as he requested in a letter he sent to Republican Conference Chair Tom Cotton, R-Ark. Four other Republican senators signed on to the letter, hitting the threshold to call a conference meeting under internal GOP rules.

Also signed by Sens. Mike Lee of Utah, Ted Budd of North Carolina, Rick Scott of Florida, and John Kennedy of Louisiana, the letter obtained by CQ Roll Call cites last week’s “stunning defeat” and reads in part: “Holding leadership elections without engaging in a robust discussion and evaluation of how those running for leadership intend to lead would be political malpractice.”.

Kennedy said Monday evening that he was asking to postpone the leadership elections because “we need time to talk to each other.”.

“We’re like a shop owner who’s losing his customers. It’s not the customer’s job to fix that. It’s the shop owner’s job, and I’m not looking for blame-shifting. I’m looking for self-examination,” he stated, adding that he wouldn’t consider running for minority leader himself.

In the letter, the group asked that at the time the leadership elections were set to begin, 9 a.m. on Tuesday, they instead “have a fulsome conference discussion and delay holding leadership elections until we all have a chance to hear from leadership candidates as to what type of collaborative conference governing model we should adopt and what our strategy will be to counter the emboldened Democrats.”.

Thune echoed that wording Monday as he spoke to reporters, saying, “I do think that we need to have a very fulsome, robust conversation about where we go from here, and then we’ll see what the consensus of the conference is.”.

It has been revealed that but Sen. Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va., who serves as chair of the Senate Republican Policy Committee, noted she has seen such requests released in the past and didn’t think it would do much to affect the ultimate outcome. “I think Sen. Thune will be reelected,” she said.

And several Senate GOP aides said that they suspected a “robust” conversation wouldn’t do much to delay the prepares and that leadership elections were still expected to take place Tuesday. They noted similar efforts from some of those same senators in previous years to sow discord in the ranks.

Industry observers note that that includes Scott, who unsuccessfully challenged Thune in 2024 and then-GOP leader Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., in 2022. But Scott told Fox News over the weekend, “I don’t want to run again. I’ve run twice.”.

Republicans “failed. We had a horrible night,” Scott stated. “Instead of having an [leadership] election, the first thing you do is you say, ‘OK, what are we going to change? We have to change something.’”.

Lee floated the idea of waiting until after the uncalled Senate races in Mississippi and Alaska are officially resolved.

An online pressure campaign was building in some of the same MAGA corners of the internet that have pushed to pass a sweeping voter ID bill, known as the SAVE America Act, that has stalled in the Senate. On Monday morning, influencer Scott Presler in an X post urged constituents to call their senators while praising the lawmakers who have already pushed for the leadership elections to be postponed. “Where is everyone else?” he wrote.

In a recent development, sens. Jim Banks of Indiana and Dave McCormick of Pennsylvania also called for a delay, though they did not appear on Johnson’s letter.

“A week ago, we had the worst election results in decades,” McCormick said in a post on X, calling Tuesday “too soon” to vote for leaders. “I know it’s been practice to go straight to leadership elections in recent years, but we should not rush it.”.

Banks similarly mentioned Tuesday was “too soon,” posting on social media, “Our conference needs to sit down and have a frank conversation about where we fell short, what we stand for, and what we’re going to do for the working families who sent us here.”.

In a recent development, one senator speaking out in Thune’s defense was Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, who competed with Thune for the top spot in 2024 but on Monday said the leader isn’t to blame for the midterm results.

“I think the president needs to look in the mirror and look at the flawed candidates that he endorsed, and the kind of environment that we’re in,” said Cornyn, who is still smarting from losing his primary to a challenger backed by President Donald Trump.

Industry observers note that cornyn’s loss means he has no say in the coming conference leadership elections. But he mentioned, “I think Thune’s a good man, and did as well as he could against a president and an environment that was pretty hostile.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:.

Scattered sparsely across Earth’s surface, from Nebraska to Mali to the Philippines, drilling rigs are rising from platforms surrounded by sheds and tanks. Each contains a tower 10 to 15 stories high. Only they aren’t pumping fossil fuels. While they’re reminiscent of machinery used to extract oil and gas, these rigs are on the hunt for a different type of gas—one trapped in microscopic pores of rock—that some researchers believe could help solve humanity’s clean energy needs for hundreds of years. Or at least offset our ever-increasing demand.

Industry observers note that natural stores of hydrogen gas exist throughout our planet’s crust on every continent. It’s colorless and odorless, and it frequently escapes into the atmosphere through natural seeps or during mining for metals like copper and zinc. But finding it in commercially viable quantities has always been difficult. Now, researchers and entrepreneurs think they have reason to hope this challenge can be overcome.

“There are places where we believe we’re going to find natural hydrogen accumulations, and in those places it’s going to be a very competitive energy source,” says Pete Johnson, CEO and cofounder of hydrogen exploration organization Koloma. The company intends to drill 20 wells in the next two years in some of “the best hydrogen systems” in the world, including in the U.S. and the Philippines.

Hydrogen is already a multibillion-dollar global industry. Fertilizer companies combine it with nitrogen to make ammonia. Oil refineries use it to lower the sulfur content in diesel. Metalworkers use it to prevent oxidation. Hydrogen is “an essential element for survival of humanity,” says Ukrainian geochemist Viacheslav Zgonnik, PhD. But nearly all of the hydrogen used in those processes is manufactured, and much of it from methane gas in an energy-intensive way. So energy intensive, in fact, that companies produce 9 to 11 tons of carbon dioxide for every 1 ton of hydrogen, according to the Environmental and Energy Study Institute.

Some companies are exploring ways to produce hydrogen with fewer carbon emissions. But even so-called green hydrogen still requires energy to produce and may never be economically viable at scale, states Zgonnik. That’s where natural hydrogen deposits enter the picture. And scientists and prospectors believe natural hydrogen could serve far more industries than just fertilizer and petroleum production. Some even envision it could help power the world with near-zero carbon emissions in the process.

According to recent reports, exactly how much hydrogen exists, however, is still up for debate. A 2024 U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) paper modeled the amount of hydrogen likely to percolate under the surface and found enormous amounts. The bulk is likely “impractical to recover,” according to the paper published in Science Advances, but if even a small fraction of the total amount could be captured, it “would supply the projected hydrogen needed to reach net-zero emissions for [about] 200 years.”.

A 2025 report from The Royal Society was more cautious, tempering the optimism of the USGS model by using currently available hydrogen survey data. But even that suggested hydrogen “could be a game changer.”.

Industry observers note that hydrogen forms naturally through at least two processes: chemical reactions between water and iron-rich rocks, and the splitting of water molecules by radiation in rocks containing uranium, according to the Royal Society paper. The gas then saturates porous rock, akin to an underground sponge sealed on the top by a dense layer of caprock such as clay or other sedimentary rocks. Stick a straw—or in practical terms a drill—into the sponge, and out comes the hydrogen.

It has been revealed that known hydrogen accumulations occur in the oldest and most stable rocks on Earth at the core of the continents. Researchers speculate it exists in places where Earth’s crust tried to separate, like the Midcontinent Rift, which stretches beneath portions of Kansas, Iowa, Minnesota, and Wisconsin, and the Great Rift Valley in eastern Africa. The gas has also been found in regions where tectonic plates collided, including parts of the Pacific Rim off the coasts of North America and Asia, says Canadian hydrogen researcher Barbara Sherwood Lollar, PhD.

Sources indicate that but natural underground hydrogen, also called gold or white hydrogen, has been discovered in plenty of other locations, too. In Mali, a country in western Africa, drillers searching for fresh water discovered a natural hydrogen system. Decades later, the Bourakebougou field, as it is called, began to produce enough hydrogen to supply electricity to a nearby village.

Local supplies of natural hydrogen could be among the gas’s first and most practical applications, says Lollar, who has studied natural hydrogen for decades, one of the few early researchers investigating hydrogen as a potential source for clean energy. In May, she coauthored a paper in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences detailing how more than 70 percent of the continental crust “has the potential for hydrogen generation.” That widespread distribution, she says, could make the gas a source of local and regional power.

Recent findings suggest that “Another one of the easy wins in all of this would be to use this hydrogen not just for a small community,” says Sherwood Lollar, a University of Toronto professor. “The same rocks that produce hydrogen and helium are the rocks that produce nickel, copper, gold, diamonds, critical minerals.” That means mining conglomerates could capture hydrogen already being vented and use it to power their facilities.

Industry observers note that johnson takes the idea a step further. Industries that require large amounts of power, such as data centers, or industries that require hydrogen, like fertilizer manufacturers, could relocate to places where natural hydrogen is abundant, reducing the need to transport the gas.

Companies like Koloma are already surveying for economically viable deposits around the world. Johnson indicates his manufacturer has identified several potential fields.

It has been revealed that assuming the hydrogen reservoirs are large enough to economically produce, the process would look much like drilling for natural gas, he notes. The timeline for developing the industry could be similar, too.

“We’re in some early innings right now,” Johnson claims. “I mean if you look at how long it took us to develop the concept of shale gas, that was a 20- to 30-year process.”.

In a recent development, then a few years after companies began drilling successful wells, the shale gas industry boomed. Natural hydrogen could follow a similar trajectory. Some companies are also exploring ways to stimulate hydrogen production underground by injecting heat and water into rocks before extracting the resulting gas. Those efforts, however, remain in their infancy.

Natural hydrogen could do more than help satisfy humanity’s insatiable appetite for energy—made worse by the buildout of energy-hungry data centers. It could also reshape the global energy map.

Sources indicate that “If the Philippines, for example, has domestic energy, what it means is that its neighboring countries like Taiwan, Japan, all these energy-poor countries may also have it,” Johnson says. “Anytime you find a fresh energy source in new places, it sort of rewrites the rules of geopolitics.”.

Recent findings suggest that he’s not certain exactly what role the gas will play in the world’s future energy portfolio. Will it render oil and gas obsolete, or will it become no more than a bit player? “That’s the question we’re trying to answer.”.

First, researchers and prospectors need to hunt down untapped hydrogen reservoirs and prove that they’re worth drilling.

Her work has appeared in National Geographic, Outdoor Life, The Atlantic, High Country News and New York Times, among others. She is also a 2025 Alicia Patterson Foundation fellow.

Bogong moths have a second compass for nights when the stars disappear

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Bogong moths use the tilt of Earth’s magnetic field to navigate at night, and their magnetic compass depends on violet-blue light.
  • Bogong moths use a magnetic compass to steer through the Australian night, much like migrating songbirds.
  • New experiments conducted by Lund University show that the moths read the tilt of Earth’s magnetic field and need violet-blue light to do so.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bogong moths use the tilt of Earth’s magnetic field to navigate at night, and their magnetic compass depends on violet-blue light.

Bogong moths use a magnetic compass to steer through the Australian night, much like migrating songbirds.

New experiments conducted by Lund University show that the moths read the tilt of Earth’s magnetic field and need violet-blue light to do so.

The research team included biologists Hui Chen, Eric Warrant, and Pauline Fleischmann.

According to recent reports, “It is remarkable that two such different groups of animals use the same basic principle to detect Earth’s magnetic field. This suggests that very ancient biophysical mechanisms have been conserved through evolution,” noted Warrant, a professor of zoology at Lund.

Sources indicate that A Bogong moth looks unremarkable: greyish-brown wings and a brain about one-tenth the size of a grain of rice. Yet each spring, these insects set off for mountain refuges they have never visited.

Their journeys can stretch up to 1,000 kilometers. They spend the summer dormant in cool caves in the Australian Alps, then return to their breeding grounds in autumn.

Sources indicate that the same moths make both trips, reproduce, and die. The next generation must find its own way.

It has been revealed that research published in 2025 highlighted that the moths use the stars as a compass. But they can maintain their course when clouds hide the sky, suggesting another guide is available.

To investigate, researchers caught migrating moths with light traps and brought them to a laboratory near Adaminaby, in southeastern Australia.

The building was constructed from non-magnetic materials to avoid disturbing the weak field the insects were being asked to follow.

Recent findings suggest that inside, tethered moths could fly and turn freely in an arena surrounded by magnetic coils. The apparatus recorded their headings during five-minute flights while the coils controlled the magnetic field.

In a recent development, overhead, a projected sky contained randomly arranged stars. It supplied light without the familiar celestial patterns that could otherwise tell the moths which way to go.

With the normal field present, spring migrants headed roughly southwest and autumn migrants roughly north-northeast.

Rotating the field horizontally by 180 degrees sent both groups roughly the opposite way.

When the magnetic field was removed, the moths lost their shared heading.

The crucial detail was the field’s tilt relative to the ground, known as magnetic inclination.

Industry observers note that flipping this tilt sent the moths the other way. Reversing the field’s polarity while leaving its axis unchanged did not.

This kind of compass distinguishes poleward from equatorward travel, roughly south and north in Australia.

A conventional compass needle responds to polarity. Some insects do too, but Bogong moths followed a different rule.

“The Bogong moth’s magnetic compass works differently from, for example, the polarity-sensitive magnetic sense of desert ants,” said Fleischmann, a biologist at Carl von Ossietzky University Oldenburg.

“This suggests that there are probably several types of magnetoreception, with migratory and non-migratory animals using the magnetic field in different ways.”.

The magnetic field was only part of the story. When researchers removed violet-blue wavelengths from the illumination, the moths no longer maintained their migratory heading.

Industry observers note that simply making the surroundings dimmer did not have the same effect. In outdoor tests, moths still oriented correctly with the full spectrum reduced to about one-eighth of its original brightness.

The team also checked whether removing those colors had prevented the insects from seeing well enough to fly.

It hadn’t. Given a realistic star pattern and no magnetic field, the moths could still navigate without the shorter wavelengths.

The problem was specific to their magnetic guidance. Their star compass remained usable.

Weak radiofrequency noise also disrupted the moths’ magnetic orientation. Together with the light experiments, that result points towards a proposed mechanism called the radical-pair mechanism.

In this explanation, light starts chemical reactions whose outcomes are influenced by the surrounding magnetic field. Those changes could give an animal information about direction.

Light-sensitive proteins called cryptochromes are possible candidates for the process. The experiments do not identify which protein provides the moth’s magnetic sense.

Pinning that down will require further work. For now, the results support a mechanism resembling the one proposed for migrating songbirds.

“What we see here is a navigational ability reminiscent of that found in migratory birds. Although insects and birds have evolved along separate paths for around 700 million years, they appear to be able to use similar biological solutions,” mentioned Chen, a biology researcher at Lund.

Having two compasses could help the moths keep going when one source of information becomes unreliable.

Clouds can conceal the stars, while disturbances in Earth’s magnetic field could interfere with magnetic guidance.

The experiments establish how moths choose a direction. Reaching a particular cave probably also involves local sensory clues encountered along the route.

How the brain combines those clues with its two compasses remains an open question.

“The next step is to understand in greater detail how this mechanism works and how it interacts with other senses when animals navigate,” Warrant concluded.

The study is published in the journal Nature.

Rebecca Pinals hadn’t planned to study neuroscience. But as she watched her grandmother decline from dementia, the chemical engineer decided to apply her talents to the human brain.

In a recent development, at the time, “one of the major questions was, ‘how do we get access to it?’” states Pinals, of Stanford University. “I thought nanotechnology could be an interesting and useful toolkit to answer those types of questions.”.

Recent findings suggest that one key access point is the blood-brain barrier, a dynamic microenvironment of cells that helps keep pathogens and other contaminants out of the brain. It’s so good at its job that drugs for treating dementia have a hard time penetrating it. It’s important for researchers to understand this barrier, Pinals says, but it is so thin and fragile that they can’t observe it in real time without risking patient health.

Recent findings suggest that pinals and colleagues re-created the blood-brain barrier on a microchip. The team reprogrammed stem cells engineered from human skin, then coaxed the cells to form the barrier in a small 3-D chamber on the chip.

Recent findings suggest that “As an engineer, this [system] is perfect,” Pinals states. “We love to take things apart and put them back together to learn how it’s made.”.

In a recent development, experts could use this scale model of the blood-brain barrier to figure out how to noninvasively access brains affected by neurodegenerative diseases. Pinals wants to use the device to investigate nanoparticles that could deliver drugs directly to patients’ brains.
