💡 Key Takeaways
  • Warm regions near the equator may have helped crocodile relatives survive the asteroid impact that wiped out the non-avian dinosaurs.
  • It has been revealed that when an asteroid struck Earth 66 million years ago, the non-avian dinosaurs died out.
  • A newly introduced study suggests their long association with warm climates may have helped them weather the aftermath.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Warm regions near the equator may have helped crocodile relatives survive the asteroid impact that wiped out the non-avian dinosaurs.

It has been revealed that when an asteroid struck Earth 66 million years ago, the non-avian dinosaurs died out. Some crocodile relatives survived.

A newly introduced study suggests their long association with warm climates may have helped them weather the aftermath.

Alfio Alessandro Chiarenza and Philip Mannion of UCL Earth Sciences led the work.

The evidence is computer models of past climate matched against fossils, so the maps show where the weather suited the animals, not how they lived.

“The asteroid did not make the whole planet equally hostile to every group,” Chiarenza said.

Crocodiles come from a line older and stranger than the animals on riverbanks today.

Its extinct relatives included armored plant eaters, land-dwelling predators that could move on two legs, and giants weighing more than 2,200 pounds (1,000 kilograms). The living ones look alike by comparison.

Chiarenza’s team gathered more than 7,000 fossil records covering over 400 of those species, living and extinct. They added about 130,000 records of where the 26 living species occur today.

The team compared all of it with 52 reconstructions of Earth’s climate and geography reaching back 245 million years.

In a recent development, through every warm spell and cold snap, the group’s preferred climate rarely changed. The animals went where that climate was.

According to recent reports, about 50 million years ago, the planet was roughly 18°F (10°C) warmer than today and the poles had no ice. Crocodile relatives lived far to the north in North America and Europe, and in Antarctica.

As the world cooled again, their range shrank back toward the tropics.

Rainfall turned out to be an even tighter rule than temperature.

In the models, a lineage that drifted from its usual rainfall returned to it more than four times faster than one that drifted from its usual warmth.

To test what the asteroid did to that habit, the researchers simulated the decades and centuries after the impact 66 million years ago.

They dimmed the sun by 5%, 10% and 15% to mimic dust blocking sunlight. They added layers of ash, raised carbon dioxide to mimic the volcanic eruptions underway in India at the time, and combined several of those at once.

Then they asked where a crocodile could still have lived. In every scenario but one, warm regions near the equator and in the subtropics stayed suitable.

Only a 15% drop in sunlight eliminated suitable climate everywhere, and the authors wrote that a cut that deep is beyond most estimates of what the impact actually did. Extra carbon dioxide, if anything, widened the suitable area.

The fossils fit that picture. Crocodile relatives from the first few million years after the impact turn up around the Gulf of Mexico, in northwestern Africa and in northern South America.

In a recent development, all of those places are inside the warm belts. From there, the group spread out again as the planet warmed.

The 2020 simulations found that the impact sharply reduced suitable climate for non-avian dinosaurs.

Sources indicate that “Crocodiles’ long-standing preference for warm environments may have placed survivors exactly where suitable climates held up best, like around the equator. These refuges could have sheltered populations that later recovered and radiated out,” Chiarenza said.

It has been revealed that the authors were careful not to make climate the whole story. A dinosaur and a crocodile living in the same place presumably tolerated similar air temperatures, they wrote.

Recent findings suggest that smaller bodies, a life split between water and land, a flexible diet and the low energy needs of a cold-blooded animal probably all helped. Other survivors of the impact fit the same pattern.

What the climate maps add is a geography: the places crocodiles already favored were the places that stayed livable.

The habit was not perfectly fixed. Twice in all that time, the models found a lineage whose preferred climate itself shifted.

According to recent reports, the first shift came about 94 million years ago, during one of the hottest stretches of the age of dinosaurs. Global temperatures then ran up to roughly 25°F (14°C) above today’s. Most of the family kept its old preference even then.

One branch near the base of the modern crocodile family did not. It moved its preferred temperature from around 73°F (23°C) to around 95°F (35°C), hotter than the line tolerated at any other time.

Industry observers note that the second came about 34 million years ago, as the planet cooled and Australia dried out. An extinct group of Australian crocodiles adapted to desert-like conditions.

Their preferred rainfall was about 9 inches (225 millimeters) a year, against a starting point for the whole group of about 76 inches (1,929 millimeters).

“Crocodiles are often called living fossils, but their ancestors and relatives changed enormously throughout their history, ranging from giants the size of a bus that could have devoured a T. rex, to small, cute animals with the face of a pug,” Chiarenza said.

“Our study shows that, despite all this diversity, what stayed surprisingly consistent was their relationship with climate.”.

The climate reconstructions come in steps of roughly 5 million years, so the models miss short events such as ice ages. The oldest maps also describe a world unlike any the living species have been measured in.

Gaps in the fossil record add more uncertainty. South America and Antarctica have stretches, around 30 million years ago, with suitable climate on the maps and few or no fossils.

The authors pointed to Jurassic-age rocks in India and Antarctica as places to search.

According to recent reports, and a suitable climate doesn’t prove an animal lived there. The authors wrote that their maps are a necessary part of the survival story, not a sufficient one.

Mannion remarked the pattern matters now. “If crocodiles mostly coped with past climate change by moving towards suitable habitats, today’s species will need room to move as the planet warms.”.

The loss of suitable areas to roads, farms and cities is making that harder, Mannion added.

Eleven of the 26 living species are already listed as threatened, and butterflies are shifting their ranges as the climate warms.

Whether a crocodile surrounded by farms and cities can do the same is a question these maps can’t answer. The models can show where suitable climate goes next. Whether the animals can follow it is up to them.

The full study was published in the journal Science Advances.

These ants grow enormous heads, but their antennae break a rule of biology

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1403 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Soldier ants grow heads twice as wide as a worker's, yet their antennae span exactly the same sizes, and colony signals help set them.
  • A bigger animal comes with bigger parts.
  • In one of the most diverse groups of ants on Earth, the soldiers don’t follow that pattern.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Soldier ants grow heads twice as wide as a worker's, yet their antennae span exactly the same sizes, and colony signals help set them.

A bigger animal comes with bigger parts. A substantial dog has a big head, big paws, and a big tail, and the same goes for nearly every creature biologists have measured.

In one of the most diverse groups of ants on Earth, the soldiers don’t follow that pattern.

Their antennae come in the same sizes as the antennae of the much smaller workers, and the colony’s own chemical signals help shape how substantial each antenna grows.

Recent findings suggest that A graduate student spotted it by accident under a microscope. Erica Vong, a researcher in Rajendhran Rajakumar’s lab at the University of Ottawa, indicated him the antennae of two ants, and the smaller antenna belonged to the soldier.

“Much like when you are getting your favorite latte, both castes have small, medium, and large sizes of overlapping antennae,” remarked Rajakumar, an associate professor in the university’s Department of Biology.

It has been revealed that the ants belong to Pheidole, the substantial-headed ants. Each colony has two kinds of worker: small minors and much larger soldiers whose heads are about twice as wide.

Soldiers defend the nest and mill seeds, and workers do most of the rest.

Industry observers note that rajakumar’s team measured 100 workers and 100 soldiers of one Florida species, Pheidole dentata. For body size they used the width of the thorax just behind the head.

For the antenna they used its first segment, the long stalk that gives an ant’s antenna its elbow shape.

Recent findings suggest that soldiers had wider bodies and far wider heads, as expected. Their antenna stalks, though, were the same length on average as the workers’, and the whole antenna followed the same pattern.

The two castes’ measurements overlapped so completely that the team couldn’t tell them apart.

Industry observers note that within each caste the old rule still held. A bigger worker had a bigger antenna than a smaller worker, and the same was true among soldiers.

Pooled together, the numbers revealed no link between antenna and body at all, and the trend only reappeared once the castes were split apart.

Queens were the exception, with larger bodies and larger antennae than either worker caste.

To see whether one species was a fluke, the team pulled published measurements for 565 Pheidole species from the Americas.

Across the 565 species, soldiers and workers often had antenna stalks of similar length, even though soldiers consistently had wider heads.

For each species, Rajakumar’s team divided the soldier’s antenna stalk by the worker’s. The most common answer was one, meaning no difference at all, with some species a little above and some a little below.

The same calculation for head width most often came out at 2 to 1, and no species came in under 1.4 to 1.

The team then measured ants from 14 other genera in three subfamilies, using live colonies, specimens from the Cornell University Insect Collection, and photographs from an online ant database.

In species with no soldier caste, and in most that evolved one on their own, antennae grew with the body as usual.

According to recent reports, the one exception was a turtle ant, Cephalotes varians, a close relative of Pheidole. The authors suggest the decoupling first appeared in the common ancestor the two groups share.

Whether a Pheidole larva becomes a worker or a soldier depends on how well it eats. A well-fed larva ends up with more juvenile hormone, and a high enough level turns it into a soldier.

Adult soldiers give off a pheromone that pushes the other way, so a colony with plenty of soldiers makes fewer new ones.

The team tested both signals on larvae from lab colonies collected in Gainesville, Florida, and kept at 77°F (25°C) on a diet of mealworms and crickets.

They dabbed some larvae with a synthetic version of the hormone and raised each one with either two adult workers or two adult soldiers, starting with 40 larvae per condition.

The larvae were about a twentieth of an inch (1 to 1.5 millimeters) long, young enough that either fate was still open.

Hormone-treated larvae raised by workers became soldiers with a normal spread of antenna sizes.

Larvae raised by soldiers without the hormone became workers smaller than any found in a natural colony, with antennae to match. The team calls them nanoworkers.

“Social signals and hormones do more than determine whether an ant becomes a worker or a soldier,” Rajakumar mentioned.

“They can also reshape how different traits grow and scale together (or decouple), within castes, between castes, and more broadly across species.”.

Larvae that had already passed the point of no return toward becoming soldiers gave the stranger result.

In a recent development, raised by soldiers, they emerged with soldier-sized heads on worker-sized bodies, and with antenna stalks shorter than those of the smallest natural workers. The team calls these nanosoldiers.

A developing soldier briefly grows a stub of a wing that never becomes a wing, and that stub acts as a signaling center that helps set the soldier’s big head.

When the team switched off a gene that drives that stub, the larvae grew into smaller ants with smaller heads. Their antennae came out at nearly one size, with almost none of the usual spread.

In a recent development, the team has not found a nanoworker or a nanosoldier in the wild. The authors suspect selection weeds them out.

A soldier’s head on a worker’s body may not be properly supported, and an antenna that small may carry too few sensory hairs to do its job.

The authors also allow that the hidden potential could be a side effect of selection on something else, and the question of which is open.

Recent findings suggest that an ant’s antennae are its main contact with the world. They pick up trail and alarm pheromones, touch, heat, humidity, and vibration, and ants use them to tell nestmates from strangers.

Industry observers note that the elbow stalk matters too, because an ant swings it to aim the sensitive tip at whatever it is exploring. The stalk’s length sets where that elbow sits, which affects how an ant probes and follows a trail.

A longer antenna carries more sensory hairs, and earlier work found that how an ant responds to an intruder depends on how many of those hairs it has.

So a colony whose members span a range of antenna sizes may span a range of sensitivities as well.

According to recent reports, rajakumar’s team offers one explanation for why the two castes share a range. When a Pheidole colony runs short of workers, its soldiers take on worker jobs, including caring for young.

Soldiers with the same spread of antenna sizes as workers may make that switch more easily. Once the next generation restores the balance, they can go back to defense.

“The antenna is not simply getting bigger because the ant is bigger,” Rajakumar noted.

“In these colonies, development preserves a flexible range of antennal forms that may help individuals compatibly respond together to changing environmental demands.”.

The authors wrote that the adaptive role of the decoupling is still unclear, and the job-switching idea is a hypothesis they haven’t tested.

Their hormone and pheromone experiments used one species, Pheidole dentata.

Roughly half the treated larvae died before reaching adulthood, which the authors attribute to raising each larva with only two adults instead of a full colony.

Antenna length was measured, not the sensory hairs on it, so whether a soldier’s small antenna senses what a worker’s does is still an open question.

Sources indicate that the evolutionary story also rests on a single turtle ant species. And 59 Pheidole species were left out of the genus-wide count because one caste or the other had no published measurement.

Checking the relatives is the next step the authors name.

If antennae turn out to be decoupled across the turtle ants and a third genus, Procryptocerus, the pattern would date back to the ancestor of all three.

Until someone measures those ants, the origin stays a hypothesis.

The full study was published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

Upcoming Congress will still be filled with losers

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (460 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Rollcall

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that the Capitol Dome is illuminated before dawn on Oct.
  • OPINION — Once again, the next Congress is going to be filled with losers.
  • This is not a personal judgment about their character or personality, but a simple recognition that many members have lost races before getting elected.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the Capitol Dome is illuminated before dawn on Oct. 13. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call).

OPINION — Once again, the next Congress is going to be filled with losers.

This is not a personal judgment about their character or personality, but a simple recognition that many members have lost races before getting elected. And the incoming class is no different.

I’ve written many versions of this column for more than a decade, and yet the lesson always seems to get lost, no pun intended. Parties routinely attack candidates who enter a race with losses on their record. And, of course, it happened this cycle as well.

Industry observers note that “We beat him once. We’ll beat him again,” National Republican Senatorial Committee Chairman Tim Scott declared when Democratic former Sen. Sherrod Brown unveiled his challenge to appointed GOP Sen. Jon Husted in the summer of 2025.

“Ohioans gladly sent him packing last year, and they’ll not hesitate to toss him aside again,” remarked a Republican strategist.

Brown lost reelection to Republican Bernie Moreno in 2024 but came back to defeat Husted for the state’s other Senate seat. And Brown is far from the only candidate to avenge a loss with an electoral victory last week.

The fact of the matter is that losing a race doesn’t have to be the end of a political career. Losses can lay the foundation for future success by building name ID or a fundraising network. Or sometimes it takes a change in the political environment or change in circumstances, such as running for an open seat instead of challenging an incumbent.

In addition to Brown, there are more than a dozen losers coming into the next Congress:.

In some instances, though, the losses are piling up.

Republican Rep. John James of Michigan now has three statewide losses on his record. He lost Senate contests in 2018 (taking 46 percent of the vote) and 2020 (48 percent) and came up short in his bid for governor this year (44 percent).

Sources indicate that republican former Sen. John E. Sununu of Newly introduced Hampshire, who lost reelection in 2008 to Democrat Jeanne Shaheen, fell in his comeback attempt for the open seat last week.

It has been revealed that but they could take heart from another repeat loser. Charlie Crist, a former Florida governor and congressman, has had a handful of high-profile losses over the years, including for Senate and two gubernatorial comeback bids. He was just elected mayor of St. Petersburg.

So even though I know it’s a futile request, let’s have a bipartisan agreement not to attack candidates for past losses, because losing doesn’t mean they can’t later pull off a win.

The Forever Chemicals Wreaking Havoc on Our Planet Are About to Meet Their Kryptonite

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, one of the most worrisome side effects of modern life is a class of chemicals called per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, or PFAS.
  • Today, nearly all humans, including newborns, have detectable levels of PFAS in their blood.
  • One promising approach to combating PFAS is to find a way to break their super-strong chemical bonds, then bake that chemistry into next-generation filters.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, one of the most worrisome side effects of modern life is a class of chemicals called per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, or PFAS. These man-made compounds show up in everything from non-stick pans to fast-food wrappers. They’re called “forever chemicals” because their carbon-fluorine bonds are so strong that they barely break down. The PFAS family includes nearly 15,000 different compounds, according to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, but the FDA tests food and animal feed for only a couple dozen of them.

Today, nearly all humans, including newborns, have detectable levels of PFAS in their blood.

One promising approach to combating PFAS is to find a way to break their super-strong chemical bonds, then bake that chemistry into next-generation filters. Right now, filters can trap a variety of PFAS but can’t destroy them, meaning the filters basically just move the toxic chemicals from one place to another. However, a study in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences describes a filter that uses hydrogen to attack carbon-fluorine bonds. When tested against six PFAS of regulatory concern, it worked on all of them.

Recent findings suggest that “PFAS are hard to break down, and normal processes that we use don’t work,” Arizona State University’s Bruce Rittmann, the senior author of the study, stated in a press statement. “We showed that this mechanism worked for all six. It’s a universal mechanism.”.

It has been revealed that hydrogen is essential for this process because once activated into a reactive form, it drives a process known as “hydrodefluorination,” stripping and replacing the fluorine and forming carbon-hydrogen bonds. To activate that hydrogen, Rittman and his team used palladium nanoparticles that can convert the hydrogen gas into its much-needed reactive form.

“The palladium attracts the PFAS molecule, and the palladium attracts the hydrogen and puts them together,” Rittmann said in a press statement.

Industry observers note that as hydrogen and PFAS travel through the membrane, both are attracted to the palladium catalyst. However, hydrogen isn’t simply added to the waste stream—instead, it’s fed directly into the membrane itself. This gives the filter the perfect opportunity to chemically dismantle those troublesome carbon-fluorine bonds. Over two months of continuous operation, the membrane broke apart most of the PFAS it captured. It removed 90 percent of the chemicals and stripped about 83 percent of their fluorine.

According to recent reports, that’s a huge advancement for combating the proliferation of PFAS in the natural environment, but a massive limitation will be cost. Simply put, palladium isn’t cheap, and Rittman estimates that roughly a kilogram of the stuff costs about $50,000. The upcoming approach could be paired with conventional treatments, which would first concentrate the PFAS into a smaller waste stream that the palladium membrane could then destroy.

“Decades of extensive deployment of PFAS in firefighting foams, oil- and water-repellent surfaces, non-stick cookware, and food-contact materials have created diffuse, chronic inputs into watersheds and drinking-water supplies,” the authors wrote in the study. “Hydrogen-driven hydrodefluorination offers a direct reductive route under comparatively mild conditions.”.

Darren lives in Portland, has a cat, and writes/edits about sci-fi and how our world works. You can find his previous stuff at Gizmodo and Paste if you look hard enough.

  • Industry observers note that in work published last year, after poring through nearly 30 years of telescope data, astronomers had found that the giant began brightening in 2018 and proposed that a smaller star was circling ever closer around a giant companion and had even slipped inside its outermost layers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

For seven years, a giant star in the Andromeda galaxy grew brighter. It swelled to more than twice its original size, even as its surface temperature barely changed. Then, in October 2025, it erupted. The slow brightening and sudden eruption tell a story of a smaller star orbiting inside of a massive star and what became of the pair, researchers report November 18 in Nature.

Industry observers note that in work published last year, after poring through nearly 30 years of telescope data, astronomers had found that the giant began brightening in 2018 and proposed that a smaller star was circling ever closer around a giant companion and had even slipped inside its outermost layers. Astronomers call this elusive phase of a binary star’s life common-envelope evolution.

According to recent reports, now, the astronomers have analyzed the system’s dramatic next developments, culminating in the October 2025 eruption. (The stars are nicknamed Little Bao and Big Bao as a nod to that event’s official designation, AT 2025abao.).

First, astrophysicist Viraj Karambelkar of Columbia University and colleagues revisited those years of brightening given the imminent eruption. One cause of the brightening could have been gas flowing away from the stars, giving off light as it slowed down. But even if all the energy of that moving gas turned into light, it still wouldn’t be enough to explain the glow.

Recent findings suggest that instead, the researchers determined that the binary hypothesis they had originally proposed fit better: As Little Bao orbited inside Significant Bao’s gas outer layers, the gas pushed back against the little star. That drag made Little Bao spiral inward and transfer energy to the surrounding gas. Some of that energy escaped as light, making Big Bao shine brighter.

Then, it was time to dig into what caused the eruption. If the outburst threw enough of the shared gas into space, the individual stars could have survived in an even tighter orbit. But the team estimates that only about a tenth of the giant’s outer gas escaped. The energy carried by that fast-moving gas also suggests that Little Bao reached Significant Bao’s core. Together, those clues point to a merger.

Recent findings suggest that still, too much dust clouds the system to directly see what remains. And it won’t settle for years or even decades, although Karambelkar and his colleagues will be watching.

They’ll be looking for more examples of this type of merger, too. “Now we can go and try to look for similar systems,” Karambelkar notes, “and hopefully aim to catch more of these systems even before they erupt.”.

Why are the spiral arms of this galaxy glowing?

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Webb’s infrared portrait of NGC 2283 reveals where young stars light up clouds of hydrogen gas in a galaxy 45 million light-years away.
  • Today’s Image of the Day features NGC 2283, a spiral galaxy in the constellation Canis Major.
  • Industry observers note that A few bright white stars catch the eye first.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Webb’s infrared portrait of NGC 2283 reveals where young stars light up clouds of hydrogen gas in a galaxy 45 million light-years away.

Today’s Image of the Day features NGC 2283, a spiral galaxy in the constellation Canis Major.

Industry observers note that A few bright white stars catch the eye first. Behind them, reddish clouds wind around a golden center, tracing the arms of a galaxy about 45 million light-years away.

The James Webb Space Telescope collected the data for this portrait in just 17 minutes of total exposure time.

What makes the image worth a longer look is how much is happening inside those arms.

The bright knots scattered along them show where young stars are already changing the clouds they formed from.

Elsewhere in the same galaxy, a massive star exploded in 2023, returning material to the space between stars.

The large white stars with long, sharp spikes belong to our own Milky Way.

They lie between Earth and NGC 2283 and appear in the picture because they happen to sit along Webb’s line of sight.

It has been revealed that their spikes come from the way light bends around parts of the telescope. Once you look past them, the galaxy’s shape is easier to pick out.

Two loosely wound arms curve away from an elongated band of stars that crosses the center.

Astronomers call that central structure a bar. Our own galaxy has one, too, but we observe the Milky Way from inside its disk.

Webb sees NGC 2283 almost face-on, giving us a clear view of how its bar and arms fit together.

Webb built this view from six exposures taken through different infrared filters.

Its Near-Infrared Camera and Mid-Infrared Instrument recorded different parts of the light coming from the same patch of sky.

In a recent development, combining those observations lets astronomers see several things at once. Some filters pick up light from stars or from clouds of hydrogen energized by young stars.

Others detect the glow of carbon-rich molecules called polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, which are also found in soot on Earth.

Image processors assign visible colors to those infrared measurements.

The result lets us follow details that would otherwise be invisible to our eyes, including the uneven distribution of gas and dust along the arms.

Industry observers note that the spiral arms look almost continuous from a distance. Look closer and they break up into bright clumps, wisps, and darker gaps.

The brightest knots include dense clouds of gas lit up by young stars.

A star begins forming when part of a cold cloud becomes dense enough to collapse under its own gravity. As material falls inward, the growing star heats up.

Some of the most massive young stars release enough ultraviolet light to energize the hydrogen around them, making the surrounding gas glow.

That glow gives astronomers a way to find places where star formation has happened recently.

In NGC 2283, the glowing clouds and young clusters make it possible to trace the arms even where dust hides some of the stars.

On January 28, 2023, astronomers discovered a supernova in NGC 2283.

Known as SN 2023AXU, it was a Type II supernova, the kind that can occur when a massive star runs out of fuel in its core.

Once the core can no longer support itself against gravity, it collapses. The resulting explosion throws the star’s outer layers into space.

Over time, material from explosions like this can mix with surrounding gas and become part of clouds that form latest stars.

That process changes the ingredients available to later generations.

Elements such as oxygen and sodium can travel far from the star that released them, then end up in another star or in the material that gathers around it.

NGC 2283 is one of 55 nearby galaxies Webb observed in a program designed to study how stars, gas, and dust interact.

These galaxies are close enough for Webb to distinguish individual star clusters and gas clouds, allowing astronomers to compare conditions from one part of a galaxy to another.

It has been revealed that in this portrait, the spiral arms may be the first thing you notice. The small knots along them are what make the scene worth coming back to.

Each marks a place where young stars are already leaving a visible imprint on the material around them.

Image Credit: ESA/Webb, NASA & CSA, A. Leroy.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sensors carried by six narwhals highlighted warm Atlantic water reaching deep into remote East Greenland fjords and areas near glaciers.
  • Greenland’s glaciers do not melt only from warm air above them.
  • Ocean water can also reach their underwater edges and melt ice from below, where the process is much harder to measure.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sensors carried by six narwhals highlighted warm Atlantic water reaching deep into remote East Greenland fjords and areas near glaciers.

Greenland’s glaciers do not melt only from warm air above them.

Ocean water can also reach their underwater edges and melt ice from below, where the process is much harder to measure.

Industry observers note that this matters because melting glaciers release freshwater into the North Atlantic. That water can change ocean layers, currents, and climate patterns far beyond Greenland.

According to recent reports, yet many East Greenland fjords are difficult to reach. Sea ice, harsh weather, and long distances often keep research ships away, leaving major gaps in ocean records.

Six narwhals have now helped fill some of those gaps in data from fjords. Sensors carried during their normal dives showed warmer Atlantic water reaching deep fjords and glacier fronts far inland.

Scoresby Sound lies on Greenland’s east coast and forms the world’s largest fjord system.

It has been revealed that fjords are long, narrow arms of the sea that reach deep into the land. Narwhals can move through fjord areas that ships rarely reach.

Professor Mads Peter Heide-Jørgensen of the Greenland Institute of Natural Resources helped lead the work.

“The narwhals have been in parts of the fjords where very few measurements have been taken before. And there, 300 kilometers from the coast, we find traces of Atlantic water.

“It is completely upcoming that we can show this,” mentioned Professor Heide-Jørgensen.

According to recent reports, local hunters helped capture and tag six narwhals near Scoresby Sound. The tags measured water temperature, salt level, depth, and location for between 85 and 332 days.

Between 2017 and 2020, the animals collected 2,060 ocean profiles.

Each profile recorded water conditions at several depths during a dive, giving the team repeated readings from remote waters that ships rarely sample directly.

Some readings came from more than 4,900 feet (1,500 meters) below the surface.

Professor Susanne Ditlevsen of the University of Copenhagen helped analyze the large collection.

“Now we suddenly have measurements from places we can use in our models, giving us a much more complete picture of the ocean. It is absolutely fantastic to use the animals in this way,” mentioned Professor Ditlevsen.

East Greenland has cold Polar Water near the surface and warmer, saltier Atlantic water below it. Salinity simply means the amount of salt in water.

The team combined the narwhal readings with more than 2,200 older profiles from the World Ocean Database.

It then built a model, which is a math tool that finds patterns in large amounts of data.

“We used the two large datasets to build a robust model showing how temperature, salinity and depth are related,” explained Professor Ditlevsen.

“The models show that the layer consisting of Atlantic water has become thicker, while the upper layer of Polar Water has become thinner,” she added.

The results point to a stronger Atlantic influence in the region.

The Blosseville Basin warmed over the study period, with summer records showing warming in both the colder Polar Water and the warmer Atlantic water.

It has been revealed that the shape of the seafloor controls where deep water can travel. Shallow ridges may block it, while deep channels can carry it toward glaciers.

Atlantic water became the main water type below about 820 feet (250 meters) in the Blosseville Basin.

It also crossed an underwater ridge and moved into the remote inner parts of Scoresby Sound.

The warmer water reached glacier basins about 186 miles (300 kilometers) from the coast.

Glaciers in deep basins faced warmer and saltier water than glaciers along the shallower Blosseville Coast.

This shows why fjord depth matters. A glacier can sit far inland and still receive Atlantic water when a deep route connects it to the open sea.

The team compared ocean conditions with the amount of ice that broke away from glaciers. This process is called iceberg discharge.

Where water at 1,310 feet (400 meters) was warmer and saltier, icebergs accounted for a larger share of the glaciers’ total summer ice loss.

“This is the water that helps melt the glaciers. We show how the warm water can contribute to accelerating the rate at which glaciers lose ice,” remarked Professor Heide-Jørgensen.

Ocean heat can reach the ice from below, but the results do not show that warm water caused every change in glacier loss.

Air temperature, surface melting, seafloor shape, and local glacier conditions also matter, so the pattern does not point to one simple cause.

Only six narwhals carried sensors, and the animals chose their own routes.

Because narwhals prefer cold water, they may have spent less time in the warmer Atlantic layer.

Sources indicate that the older ocean records were also uneven. Few measurements came from some fjords before 2010, so long-term changes inside Scoresby Sound remain difficult to judge.

According to recent reports, the tags were not recovered after use. The team could not check them again for small changes in accuracy, especially in the salt readings.

It has been revealed that winter findings need extra care because narwhals provided most of the recent winter measurements. Their routes may not represent the whole region.

Climate models use real measurements to estimate how Earth may change.

Better ocean records can improve estimates of future glacier melt in Greenland, a point that Professor Ditlevsen connected to the larger climate question.

Sources indicate that “In the large climate models used to predict future climate change, glacier melt plays a major role. That is why it is crucial that we improve our understanding of it, particularly because Greenland contains so much ice.”.

The newly introduced data can strengthen future climate estimates. Narwhals cannot replace ships, satellites, or long-term ocean stations, but they can reach waters that people struggle to measure.

Their dives revealed a clear route for warm Atlantic water into remote fjords.

The study is published in the journal Science Advances.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When Jonquel Jones picks up the phone to chat with us at Condé Nast Traveler, she’s in the back of her team bus, having just arrived in Minneapolis with the New York Liberty. In two days, she and her teammates will make WNBA history, defeating the Minnesota Lynx in Game 1 of the 2026 Playoffs. Their win will be the first time a No. 8 seed—the lowest-ranked team to qualify for the playoffs—beats a No. 1 seed, the league’s top-ranked team. But for Jones, such a victory will hardly qualify as new territory.

The 32-year-old Upcoming York Liberty center has spent the better part of the last decade breaking records: She has taken home all four major MVP honors, became the first international player named All-Star MVP, and helped lead the Liberty to their first-ever championship in 2024.

Sources indicate that an athletic career like hers means rarely staying in one place for long—a reality reflected in the setting of our conversation. Between WNBA seasons and stints playing overseas, Jones has built a life where traveling has become a part of the game (off the court, of course). But no matter how far basketball takes her, there’s one destination that brings her back to herself: her home country, the Bahamas.

In a recent development, when her schedule finally allows for a pause, returning to the islands offers Jones a different kind of home-court advantage—and a chance to reconnect with the places and people that matter most to her. We caught up with the WNBA All-Star to talk through a typical trip back to the Bahamas, from the comforts she packs before leaving New York City and her in-flight essentials to the Bahamian delicacy she never returns without—plus how to make it yourself!

What trip are you unpacking for us?A trip to Grand Bahama, where I grew up.

Tell us about the itinerary: Where did you stay? What were the highlights?I always stay at my condo, which is close to where my family lives. I have homes both in the Bahamas and in New York. My grandmother, parents, cousins, nieces, and nephews are all still on the island. Aside from two of my siblings, pretty much my entire family still lives in the Bahamas, so getting to spend time with them is really special.

According to recent reports, how often do you visit?I try to go back whenever I can, but it all depends on my schedule. This year’s off-season gives me a few months off, so I’ll be spending at least two months back home. During the FIBA Women's Basketball World Cup, though, I was only able to go for seven days. It really varies from year to year.

According to recent reports, who were you traveling with?I always bring my dog Rylo with me when I go back home. He’s a seven-year-old poodle mix, and he loves the Bahamas. I got him in 2019, right before COVID. I grew up around a lot of dogs—mostly yard dogs—and I’ve always had a special connection with animals.

In a recent development, growing up, I had a dog named Princess, and she was my dog, for real—no pun intended. She went everywhere with me. Whether I was riding over to my grandmother’s house, walking to the beach, or playing basketball, she was always right there. She’d sit on the sidelines and watch me play, making sure I was okay. Princess was my first experience with unconditional love, and she’s the reason I fell in love with dogs.

On this trip, did you overpack, underpack, or get it just right?I’m definitely an overpacker. I like bringing little comforts from home in Upcoming York, like my favorite matcha and coffee beans. I’m a big matcha fan, so I’ll even bring my entire matcha set. There’s a Japanese market called Midoriya Japanese Grocery on Fifth Avenue in Brooklyn that has amazing matcha, and I always stock up before a trip. I’m also a big fan of Stumptown Coffee; Hair Bender is my go-to blend. It’s nice to have a few pieces of my everyday routine with me. They help me settle in.

Sources indicate that what drugstore essentials do you always have in your backpack?Claritin! I have to have it with me. I have terrible allergies, and something about the pine trees in the Bahamas make them go crazy. I actually recently brought a friend back home with me, and the two of us spent the entire trip passing the bottle back and forth. Without my Claritin, it definitely takes me longer to acclimate.

What is a little luxury you always bring with you?A nighttime face mask. I love having something I can use to pamper myself during a little girls’ night in. A good overnight mask is my go-to when I want to firm up my skin or wake up with a little extra glow.

Recent findings suggest that do you have a favorite item of travel clothing to fly in?Comfort is definitely my priority when I travel. I'm not just looking after myself, but Rylo, too, so I want to make sure we're both comfortable. Dogs can pick up on nervous energy, and I don't want him to sense that from me. I try to stay in a relaxed, zen state so we can both enjoy the trip.I'm a Nike athlete, and I love their top and bottom sets. They have great two-piece options that are simple but fashionable, which makes them perfect for traveling.

In a recent development, what's one piece of home you always pack?I’m probably going to sound crazy, but I’m a gamer, and bringing my PlayStation 5 console is a big part of how I get comfortable and settle in when I get back to the Bahamas. I have a whole gaming setup waiting for me at my condo, so all I have to do is plug in my PS5 and I’m ready to go. It’s one item I never travel home without.

What's your go-to snack to keep on hand for long travel days?It’s probably not the healthiest choice, but I grew up eating Cadbury Crunchie Bars. I loved them as a kid, then went through a phase where I stopped eating them. For some reason, though, I’ve recently fallen back in love with them, and they’ve become my go-to. Now they also make Cadbury Crunchie Rocks, which are bite-size, cluster versions of the bar that come in a resealable bag, making them a little easier to travel with. I also love Cadbury Dairy Milk Fruit & Nut. Oh my god, that bar? So good. I feel a little like a granny saying this, but it’s one of my favorites. It has almonds, raisins, and dried fruit—it's delicious. My mom used to buy it when I was growing up, and as a kid, I couldn't understand why she liked it so much. But, lo and behold, I get it now.

Recent findings suggest that what's your in-flight routine like?I’d say either my Steam Deck, a portable gaming system, or a good book. I’m a big reader and use it to escape. I especially love fiction and fantasy. I recently read The Sword of Kaigen: A Theonite War Story, which has a similar feel to Avatar: The Last Airbender. It’s such a great book, but fair warning: the fight scenes are brutal, so prepare yourself. It’s worth it, though.I also can’t travel without my Bose headphones. Those are an absolute must.

What's a fragrance that never leave home without?I love, love, love the LV Lovers fragrance by Pharrell Williams in collaboration with Louis Vuitton.

Industry observers note that last question: What souvenirs do you bring home?Whenever I leave the Bahamas, I always bring back conch. It’s a Bahamian delicacy that you’ll find in every dish, and can be prepared in so many different ways. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that for more than 150 years, a burial found on the grounds of Westminster Abbey remained a mystery.
  • If you went only by the inscription carved on the limestone sarcophagus excavated on the North Green at Westminster Abbey in 1869, you’d understandably assume it held the remains of Valerius Amandinus, a wealthy Briton who lived in Roman Britain around 300 C.E.
  • Sources indicate that it certainly didn’t help that a written account in 1873 declared the skeleton lost.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that for more than 150 years, a burial found on the grounds of Westminster Abbey remained a mystery. Clues from the coffin itself, not to mention the skeleton inside, puzzled experts until Westminster Abbey’s consultant archaeologist, Warwick Rodwell, identified the deceased as a high-ranking medieval monk. He went one step further, determining the bones belonged to Aelfwig, an abbot of the Abbey’s Benedictine monastery, although Rodwell left open the possibility that the occupant was another abbot.

If you went only by the inscription carved on the limestone sarcophagus excavated on the North Green at Westminster Abbey in 1869, you’d understandably assume it held the remains of Valerius Amandinus, a wealthy Briton who lived in Roman Britain around 300 C.E. Archaeological research isn’t that simple, though. A Latin cross dated to the 10th or 11th century was also carved across the lid, likely when the coffin was reused, so with conflicting symbology muddying the waters, the identity of the person entombed on the Abbey’s grounds remained unknown for generations.

Sources indicate that it certainly didn’t help that a written account in 1873 declared the skeleton lost. In 2016, however, conservators found the bones where they had presumably been all along: inside the coffin.

Industry observers note that rodwell worked on the puzzle for years, eventually publishing a study in the Journal of the British Archaeological Association explaining how the evidence led him to two abbots who served at the monastery. His first candidate, Aelfwig, died around 1020, but the second option was Aelfwig’s successor, Wulfnoth, who died 29 years later.

“We have two viable contenders for the occupant of the sarcophagus,” Rodwell noted in a statement from the Abbey. He ruled out Aelfwig’s predecessor because that abbot left the area and died elsewhere. “We do not know the date of birth of either. But either would fit equally well if we assume the abbot was in his early 20s when the appointment was made and close to 50 when he died. The fact Aelfwig was already a monk of Westminster might favor him.”.

Recent findings suggest that the sarcophagus’s own history reveals little. The limestone probably came from Oxfordshire, England. But Rodwell wrote that no clues link the sarcophagus to its original burial site or explain why it was later moved, even though the inscription clearly ties it to a Briton who lived about 1,700 years ago. Identification is further complicated by the Anglo-Saxon cross added to the lid centuries later and by Rodwell’s belief that grave goods were stolen in the early 19th century.

To learn more about the man himself, Rodwell worked with James Young Langhorne, a human bone specialist from Pre-Construct Archaeology. They determined that the man was between 35 and 49 years old and stood about 5 feet, 9 inches tall. That contradicts the 19th-century assessment, which described him as a “robust young man” no older than 30 and about 5 feet, 7 inches tall. The analysis also revealed osteoarthritis in multiple joints, two healed rib fractures, and signs of an old infection in one leg. There was no obvious cause of death.

It has been revealed that radiocarbon dating by the Scottish Universities Environmental Research Centre placed the bones between 987 and 1052 C.E. This confirmed that the sarcophagus had been reused, and the date range matches the Saxon-period cross on the lid. With that range established, Rodwell looked more closely at the possible candidates.

It has been revealed that he concluded the man was an abbot because he was “honored” with burial in a “fine sarcophagus”: his wooden coffin was packed in lime and placed inside the stone casket. To support his theory further, Rodwell wrote that he believes the “prestigious burial” first took place in the eastern arm of the abbey church. The sarcophagus would have been fully buried, with the recut lid serving as a cross-slab in the church floor. Then, after Henry III began rebuilding the abbey in the 1240s, workers moved the sarcophagus into the “newly constructed sacristy courtyard” in 1258.

Today, the sarcophagus is on permanent display in the Abbey’s museum, The Queen’s Diamond Jubilee Galleries.

#111584. Tech Report: Where is freshwater wildlife under the most pressure? A newly introduced map offers surprises

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1056 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Where is freshwater wildlife under the most pressure? A newly introduced map offers surprises

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1056 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A global study maps 45 threats to 21,490 freshwater species and reveals where conservation plans based on land wildlife can miss areas of high risk.
  • Rivers, lakes and wetlands are home to nearly a third of all known vertebrate species.
  • A latest global study maps where 45 human pressures, from crop farming to dam construction, are most likely to affect freshwater wildlife.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A global study maps 45 threats to 21,490 freshwater species and reveals where conservation plans based on land wildlife can miss areas of high risk.

Rivers, lakes and wetlands are home to nearly a third of all known vertebrate species.

A latest global study maps where 45 human pressures, from crop farming to dam construction, are most likely to affect freshwater wildlife.

A team led from McGill University analyzed 21,490 species and found that freshwater threat hotspots often differ from those on land.

For the threats compared, freshwater mammals generally faced greater pressure than land mammals, with a smaller gap for reptiles.

Christophe Brabant, a doctoral student in biology at McGill University, led the work with biology professor Lars Lønsmann Iversen, a member of McGill’s Bieler School of Environment.

The researchers drew on expert assessments to identify the threats facing each species.

They combined those assessments with species’ known ranges to map where the threats are most likely to affect them.

The researchers identified three threats that were especially widespread.

Across river sub-basins worldwide, they estimated that each affected roughly one in four freshwater species present, on average. Farmland growing crops came first.

Dams and other water management came second, and runoff from farms and forestry third.

Europe and northwestern Africa’s Maghreb region carry the heaviest combined load of all 45 threats. In Europe, the dominant problem is pollution from cities, farms and industry.

In a recent development, in the Maghreb it is pollution plus dams and heavy water use. Other hot spots include the Nile, the Niger Delta and the Rift Valley lakes of East Africa.

The lightest loads are where few people live, in Siberia and northern Canada, and in the Sahara, Arabian and Australian deserts.

According to recent reports, global averages hide big differences between animals. Fish are mainly hit by fishing across 37% of their range and by dams across another 30.5%.

Farming was the leading threat across 45.8% of amphibians’ combined range and 31.45% of the combined range of dragonflies and damselflies.

The authors linked this pattern to the animals’ reliance on both land and water at different stages of life.

It has been revealed that freshwater reptiles and mammals face a different enemy. Hunting and other direct use are the main threat across 37.8% of reptile ranges and 43.4% of mammal ranges.

That covers the wildlife trade, traditional medicine, animals caught in fishing gear and animals killed on purpose.

In an interview with Earth.com, Brabant noted that dams, farmland, and farm pollution are widespread, but their weight changes from region to region and group to group.

“This means there is no one-size-fits-all approach to freshwater conservation,” he remarked.

The raw material was the Red List kept by the International Union for Conservation of Nature, which records for each assessed species the threats experts have seen affecting it.

The team took five groups that have been assessed in full: amphibians, fish, mammals, reptiles, and the dragonflies and damselflies.

For each species, they combined its range map with its threat list.

“By combining this data, we could calculate, for any sub-watershed, the probability that a species occurring there is affected by a particular threat,” Brabant mentioned.

One map per threat per group made 225 maps, which the team stacked into a single index of combined pressure.

Species with small ranges were given more weight.

A threat recorded for a species found in one lake can be placed on the map with confidence, while one recorded for a species spread across a continent can’t.

To test whether the maps mean anything for survival, the team compared them with two separate records.

In the 5% of river basins where extinction risk is modeled to be highest, 71% of the 45 threats were more likely to affect a species than their global average.

The second record was the Living Planet Index, which tracks counts of individual animal populations over time.

Across 2,568 freshwater vertebrate populations from 600 species, populations were shrinking faster in basins with a heavier combined threat load.

Neither record was used to build the maps, so the match is not circular.

The authors wrote that it suggests the maps capture where threats are already pushing freshwater species toward decline.

The study also lined up the freshwater maps against earlier ones made the same way for land vertebrates.

For all seven threats that had been mapped on land, freshwater mammals were more likely to be affected than land mammals.

Freshwater reptiles showed the same pattern with a smaller gap, which the authors put down to the time reptiles still spend on land.

The hot spots were in different places, too. Where freshwater fish and frogs are under the most pressure is not where land vertebrates are.

In a recent development, “What surprised me most was how different the geography was,” Brabant told Earth.com. Conservation planning has often relied on information about land species, he said.

That is why freshwater species and their threats need to be written into plans explicitly if the plans are going to reach them.

The Red List treats each threat as if it acted alone, and the authors wrote that many of them combine in ways that could make the damage worse.

The maps estimate how likely species are to be affected in each area. They don’t measure how much harm each threat causes.

Range maps describe where species live today, so places a threat has already emptied may not show up.

Asked which places he would look at first, Brabant said threat alone isn’t enough. Europe and northwestern Africa lead on accumulated threats, while many tropical regions stand out for the number of species affected.

“Areas of high richness and high threat suggest that threat mitigation is most urgent, whereas areas of high richness and low threats would be most suitable for proactive protection,” he stated.

What would help most right now, he remarked, is reducing the pressures: cleaner water, protected habitat and rivers reconnected. But the most useful action depends on the place and the species.

The next step is matching each basin’s threats to the conservation actions that address them, which the maps alone can’t do yet.

The full study was published in the journal Science.

You Can Build All the Power Plants You Want. Without This Overlooked Machine, None of Them Will Matter.

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (783 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popularmechanics

💡 Key Takeaways
  • As humanity entered the 21st century and the ravages of climate change became more and more apparent, the push toward electrification (replacing gas-powered cars, furnaces, and stoves with electric versions) really gained steam.
  • But building out an electrified future isn’t as easy as sticking wind turbines in the ocean and vast solar arrays in the desert and calling it a day.
  • According to recent reports, in a upcoming study published in the journal Cell Reports Sustainability, researchers at Johns Hopkins University report that critical grid equipment, such as transformers and converters, could become the bottleneck in powering a rapidly electrifying society.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As humanity entered the 21st century and the ravages of climate change became more and more apparent, the push toward electrification (replacing gas-powered cars, furnaces, and stoves with electric versions) really gained steam. At the same time, the electricity supply itself has been getting cleaner. According to Pew Research, solar power accounted for only 0.01 percent of the world’s electricity production back then, but fast-forward a quarter of a century, and that number is now nine percent and rising.

But building out an electrified future isn’t as easy as sticking wind turbines in the ocean and vast solar arrays in the desert and calling it a day. These new forms of renewable energy also need to connect to the grid before they can supply us with that much-needed new power. Expanding the grid’s capacity to meet this ballooning demand was already going to be a tall order as more and more electric cars, ovens, and heat pumps came online. Now, the rise of power-hungry AI data centers has transformed that difficult task into a borderline impossible one for the simple reason that the U.S. may not have enough of the equipment—or the materials to make said equipment—to build the required infrastructure.

According to recent reports, in a upcoming study published in the journal Cell Reports Sustainability, researchers at Johns Hopkins University report that critical grid equipment, such as transformers and converters, could become the bottleneck in powering a rapidly electrifying society. According to the researchers, demand for electricity isn’t anything new. In fact, it’s been steadily rising since Thomas Edison flipped the switch on the Pearl Street Station in 1882. But due to the rise of AI data centers, the electricity industry has entered a whole new era of demand growth.

Recent findings suggest that “When the demand for electricity started to grow faster than expected, it started to amplify all the cracks in the industry,” Yury Dvorkin, a Johns Hopkins researcher and co-author of the study, noted in a press statement. According to Dvorkin and co-author Boyu Yao, electricity demand historically ticked up a percent or two each year. But now, largely because of data centers, demand is projected to grow 21 percent overall by the end of the decade.

If this rapid demand growth persists, it will put considerable strain on supplies of specific materials, including copper, steel, nickel, aluminum, and manganese, needed to build the necessary transformers, which step up or step down the voltage of alternating current on the grid.

Industry observers note that “This type of equipment was taken for granted, but without it, you can build a data center or a power plant but it won’t be powered because you cannot connect it to the grid,” Dvorkin mentioned. “By 2030 we’re likely to have transformer shortages even without the most aggressive power demand growth.”.

Sources indicate that according to their projections, copper will run short in 2027, followed soon by steel and nickel, which will affect not just grid utilities but wind power infrastructure and electric vehicle charging stations. This shortfall isn’t necessarily news: a study by S&P Global earlier this year found that copper could experience a 10 million metric ton deficit by 2040. This deficit isn’t caused by a lack of copper in the ground, since the planet holds abundant copper resources. Extraction is where the industry is facing a crucial bottleneck.

“Copper is abundant in the ground, but there’s not enough being extracted to be able to meet the demand,” authors of a copper market analysis wrote for The Conversation earlier this year. That’s because investors want higher and more reliable returns than copper mines currently offer, and the industry faces complex permitting processes and can’t find enough workers.

This new study suggests that under its baseline scenario, the U.S. might be able to produce enough transformers yet still fall 16 percent short on other grid-related equipment. But with AI data centers supercharging demand, the study’s “high power demand” scenario is more likely. That scenario projects a 15 percent shortage of transformers and a 30 percent shortage of all other equipment. The authors also note that roughly two-thirds of this expected shortage can be attributed to AI data centers.

Recent findings suggest that “Utilities will compete for transformers with the data center industry,” Dvorkin remarked. “Transformers will first be delivered to whoever can pay the highest premium. Will it be a mom-and-pop utility or a big data center corporation?”.

I think we already know the answer to that question.

#111580. Tech Report: Why does Webb see so many giant galaxies in the early universe?

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1102 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Why does Webb see so many giant galaxies in the early universe?

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1102 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Lumina simulation traces how stars and quasars transformed gas in the early universe and explores why Webb sees so many massive galaxies.
  • The first stars and galaxies gave off ultraviolet light that stripped electrons from hydrogen atoms between galaxies.
  • Quasars later began stripping helium of its last electron, a process that took more energetic light and was still underway long after most of the hydrogen had been ionized.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Lumina simulation traces how stars and quasars transformed gas in the early universe and explores why Webb sees so many massive galaxies.

The first stars and galaxies gave off ultraviolet light that stripped electrons from hydrogen atoms between galaxies.

Quasars later began stripping helium of its last electron, a process that took more energetic light and was still underway long after most of the hydrogen had been ionized.

A new computer simulation called Lumina tracks how gas, dark matter and light interacted through both changes.

It models a region that would span about 1.6 billion light-years on each side at today’s cosmic scale, giving astronomers a way to test their predictions against observations from the James Webb Space Telescope.

Oliver Zier, a fellow at the Center for Astrophysics | Harvard & Smithsonian, led the project.

Aaron Smith of the University of Texas at Dallas was a co-author, along with colleagues at MIT, York University and the Max Planck Institute for Astrophysics.

“With JWST, the early universe has become an exciting newly introduced frontier in astrophysics,” Zier mentioned. “To understand what we are seeing with this telescope, we need to translate our theories into detailed predictions.”.

It has been revealed that A simulation is that translation. Astronomers feed in the laws of physics and the universe’s starting conditions, then let a supercomputer calculate how everything develops over time.

It has been revealed that they compare the result with real telescope images. A match gives astronomers more confidence in the model. A mismatch can show where its assumptions need more testing.

Lumina covers roughly the first 2 billion years, following the earliest galaxies and the thin gas between them.

The simulated cube is about 1.6 billion light-years on a side, more than 100 times the volume of comparable simulations.

The team divided its contents into 432 billion pieces of gas and dark matter, and each piece of gas has about 3.6 million times the mass of the Sun.

Galaxies grow where the dark matter gathers, strung along the filaments of the cosmic web.

The team ran Lumina on Frontier, a supercomputer at Oak Ridge National Laboratory in Tennessee.

The simulation used 7,536 graphics accelerators, just over 20% of the machine, and about 600 terabytes of working memory at its peak.

Smith described what that size makes possible.

“For the first time, we can follow along as both hydrogen and helium changed into their modern form across such an enormous volume of the universe, while still resolving the galaxies and other luminous objects driving that transformation,” he said.

In a recent development, earlier simulations of this kind, including the Thesan project, stopped before helium began to clear. Lumina’s cube is 144 times the volume of Thesan’s.

According to recent reports, the first stars and galaxies cleared the hydrogen slowly and unevenly. In Lumina, bubbles of cleared gas open around the biggest galaxies first and grow until they merge. Regions far from any galaxy stay foggy longest.

The team divided the simulation into 125 regions and tracked how swiftly the hydrogen changed in each one.

In a typical region, nearly all of the hydrogen gas between galaxies had lost its electrons by about 1.1 billion years after the Significant Bang. In the slowest regions, that took about 1.3 billion years.

Astronomers see the same late finish in the light of distant quasars, which still indicates absorption by hydrogen gas at that time.

Stars did nearly all of this work. Quasars supplied about 15% of the hydrogen-clearing light near the end.

Clearing helium takes light about four times more energetic than clearing hydrogen, and ordinary stars give off very little of it. Quasars do.

A quasar is a supermassive black hole pulling in gas so fast that the gas shines with intense ultraviolet light.

In Lumina, the brightest quasars began stripping helium of its last electron about 900 million years after the Massive Bang. The process was about halfway complete by 1.5 billion years.

By 2 billion years, the regions where helium still held its last electron accounted for less than 1% of the space Lumina modeled.

The bubbles around quasars grew larger than the hydrogen bubbles that formed around galaxies.

Each clearing also heats the gas. The thin gas between galaxies warms to roughly 18,000°F to 36,000°F (10,000°C to 20,000°C) while the hydrogen clears.

It cools as the universe expands, then warms again when the quasar light reaches it.

Measurements of the helium clearing are scarce. Most studies of it rely on fewer than about 25 quasars with a usable line of sight, and Lumina’s timing agrees with those measurements.

According to recent reports, lumina also grows galaxies, and here it fails a test. At about 1.2 billion years after the Substantial Bang and earlier, the simulation produces fewer very massive galaxies than Webb has found.

The shortfall grows the further back in time the comparison goes.

The team wrote that this confirms a known problem: galaxy models tuned to the nearby universe undercount the giants Webb sees in the early one.

Stars might form more efficiently in the earliest massive galaxies, or the masses astronomers read off Webb’s images might be less certain than assumed.

The simulation can’t settle that on its own, but it marks where the standard picture falls short.

Some of Lumina’s agreement with observations is built in.

Sources indicate that the authors set the share of each galaxy’s hydrogen-clearing light that escapes into space at 18%, a value chosen so that hydrogen clears on a realistic schedule. So the timing of that clearing is partly a tuning choice, not a prediction.

The team also slowed the speed of light in the calculation to a fifth of its real value, because the full speed would have made the run unaffordable.

That shortcut may keep hydrogen fog in remote voids a little too long. And the detailed comparison with real quasar spectra, the one that would say whether the helium timing is right, is still to come.

Recent findings suggest that zier’s team aims to release the full Lumina data in 2028. Companion studies are already using it to work out how patchy clearing marks the afterglow of the Major Bang, and how many quasars of each brightness the early universe held.

Observations from Webb and future surveys by the Roman Space Telescope will help astronomers test whether Lumina can explain how the earliest massive galaxies formed.

The full study was published in the journal Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society.
