A dinosaur found by a Montana rancher on her land in 2019 sold for $47.3 million, over five times its top estimate

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (867 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A Nanotyrannus skeleton nicknamed Jodi sold for $47.3 million at Sotheby's in 2026, raising concerns about scientific access to rare fossils.
  • A Nanotyrannus skeleton nicknamed “Jodi” sold at Sotheby’s in New York on October 27, 2026, for a final price of $47.3 million.
  • Jodi Pierson found the skeleton in 2019 on her privately owned land near the town of Jordan, in Garfield County, Montana.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A Nanotyrannus skeleton nicknamed Jodi sold for $47.3 million at Sotheby's in 2026, raising concerns about scientific access to rare fossils.

A Nanotyrannus skeleton nicknamed “Jodi” sold at Sotheby’s in New York on October 27, 2026, for a final price of $47.3 million. Its pre-sale estimate was $6 million to $9 million.

Jodi Pierson found the skeleton in 2019 on her privately owned land near the town of Jordan, in Garfield County, Montana.

According to recent reports, six bidders competed for more than 12 minutes, the auction house said. Jodi is now the second most valuable dinosaur ever sold at auction.

The record belongs to “Gus,” a Tyrannosaurus rex skeleton that sold at Sotheby’s Upcoming York for $50.1 million on July 14, 2026.

According to Guinness World Records, Gus broke the record set by “Apex,” a Stegosaurus also sold at Sotheby’s Fresh York. Apex fetched $44.6 million on July 17, 2024.

Sotheby’s reports its results including the buyer’s premium, the fee added to the winning bid. The hammer price for Jodi has not been made public.

Jodi was the only lot in its own dedicated sale. Neither the buyer nor the seller has been named.

Its listed provenance is a private collection that acquired the skeleton in 2021.

According to recent reports, sotheby’s lists Jodi as Nanotyrannus cf. lancensis, from the Hell Creek Formation, about 67 million years old. The abbreviation “cf.” marks a provisional identification.

A crew of seven, including Pierson and Clayton Phipps, dug up the skeleton in a single field season. It comprises about 191 fossil bone elements from one individual.

Sources indicate that its virtually complete skull has 53 bones and roughly 50 teeth. The rarely preserved wishbone is intact, and about half of the belly ribs, or gastralia, survived.

Missing parts were restored with 3D-printed and sculpted elements, and the mounted skeleton measures about 19.6 feet (6 meters) from nose to tail. It stands about 9 feet 6 inches (2.9 meters) tall, not 6 feet 5 inches (2 meters) as first listed.

The auction house describes the animal as an adult, based on its overall size and degree of bone development. It cites no peer-reviewed study of the skeleton.

At the Frieze Masters art fair in 2023, the same skeleton was exhibited as a juvenile T. rex.

For decades, many paleontologists argued that Nanotyrannus fossils were simply young T. rex. The debate centered on a skull collected in Montana in 1942 by the Cleveland Museum of Natural History.

In 1988, a team that included museum curator Dr. Michael Williams named it Nanotyrannus lancensis. In December 2025, a study in Science found that the skull’s throat bone had stopped growing, indicating a mature animal.

In October 2025, a study in Nature concluded that the tyrannosaur in the “Dueling Dinosaurs” fossil was a fully grown Nanotyrannus lancensis. Growth rings and fused vertebrae put its age at about 20 years.

Sources indicate that that animal had larger forelimbs, more teeth and fewer tail vertebrae than T. rex, the North Carolina Museum of Natural Sciences reported.

After examining more than 200 tyrannosaur fossils, the researchers also named a second species, Nanotyrannus lethaeus, after the River Lethe of Greek mythology.

“This fossil doesn’t just settle the debate. It flips decades of T. rex research on its head,” Lindsay Zanno, head of paleontology at the North Carolina museum and a co-author of the study, said in 2025.

According to recent reports, before the Gus auction, the Society of Vertebrate Paleontology issued a statement on scientifically significant fossils. It called for them to be permanently curated in accredited museums, universities and other public research institutions.

Sources indicate that without provisions for long-term access, private ownership may permanently diminish opportunities for future research, education and public engagement, the society warned. It also recognized the key role of private landowners, amateur fossil enthusiasts and commercial excavators.

“The discovery of an vital fossil is only the beginning of its scientific story,” noted Kristina Curry Rogers, the society’s vice president at the time.

“Many of the most significant advances in paleontology have come years or even decades after a fossil was collected,” she noted. New analytical methods and technologies allowed scientists to ask entirely new questions of specimens already housed in museums.

After the Jodi sale, Curry Rogers and Zanno published an opinion piece on fossil auctions. They wrote that they hope the latest owner will make Jodi available for scientific study and public education.

Under Montana law, fossils are part of the surface estate, so they normally belong to whoever owns the land.

According to recent reports, the provision, enacted in 2019, says the word “minerals” does not include fossils unless a deed or other instrument clearly states otherwise. A landowner can sever fossil rights from the land through a clear and express grant.

Sotheby’s offered Jodi with full rights and documentation certifying its condition, authenticity and the legality of its ownership.

The federal Paleontological Resources Preservation Act of 2009 does not apply to state, private or Indian lands, according to the Bureau of Land Management.

The information was obtained from Sotheby’s.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • What happens when more than 100 members-elect descend on Capitol Hill a week after Election Day?
  • As Rep.-elect Dan Koh, D-Mass., put it, “It really is like high school — but it’s fun high school.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that A group of incoming members of Congress and staff arrive on Capitol Hill for upcoming member orientation on Monday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

What happens when more than 100 members-elect descend on Capitol Hill a week after Election Day?

As Rep.-elect Dan Koh, D-Mass., put it, “It really is like high school — but it’s fun high school.”.

Trainings and guest speakers aren’t everyone’s idea of a fun time, but Democrats are feeling good about this year’s new member orientation. Giddy, even.

Industry observers note that the incoming freshmen will pose for a class photo on the House steps. They’ll test their luck in a lottery to see who lands the best office space. And everywhere they look, they see signs of the blue wave that swept over the country.

“I think — well, I hope — that we will be doing a lot of exceeding expectations in this caucus. The American people deserve it and expect it,” stated Rep.-elect Sam Forstag, D-Mont., as he headed to lunch after an orientation session on Monday.

It has been revealed that forstag is the first Democratic congressman from Montana in 30 years, succeeding retiring GOP Rep. Ryan Zinke. A former smokejumper who parachuted into remote forests to put out wildfires, Forstag won by more than 3 points in a district President Donald Trump carried by double digits in 2024.

“I think there’s a lot of folks who didn’t expect us to,” he said of his win. “Nobody knew who we were this past December when I was still working at the smoke jumper base in Missoula.”.

Democrats are still digesting their larger-than-expected wins, which saw them flip more than 40 House seats and oust a number of high-profile incumbents, including National Republican Congressional Committee Chairman Richard Hudson, R-N.C.

Sources indicate that “It’s like drinking out of a firehose,” said Rep.-elect Rebecca Cooke, D-Wis., who unseated incumbent GOP Rep. Derrick Van Orden in Wisconsin’s 3rd District.

Recent findings suggest that cooke and her opponent clashed during the campaign over his use of AI-generated ads that she described as deepfakes. Now, they have to work together to make sure the transition goes smoothly.

It has been revealed that “The congressman mentioned that he’s willing to be helpful in that transition. I think it’s notable that we make sure that the casework is transferred over, that constituent service is a priority, and that nothing falls through the cracks for people,” she said.

The 120th Congress will be full of history-makers, and a record-breaking number of women are set to serve in the House.

Industry observers note that “This is a Congress with the most women ever to be a part of this chamber,” Cooke mentioned. “And a lot of [Democrats], frankly, from the Midwest, and so I’m excited to build that sort of power from the Midwest to make sure that our interests are represented.”.

The math isn’t lost on Republicans navigating a freshman class where they have fewer peers than they hoped.

Recent findings suggest that “I thought that it would probably go a little bit different. I think a lot of people did, but it is what it is. You work with what we have,” remarked Rep.-elect Mark Lamb, R-Ariz.

But just like high school, everyone’s trying to make friends. As incoming members filed into the Capitol Visitor Center on Monday morning, Rep.-elect Cait Conley, D-N.Y., introduced herself to Rep.-elect Sydney Gruters, R-Fla.

Meanwhile, Rep.-elect Claire Valdez, D-N.Y., who describes herself as a “proud democratic socialist,” walked by chatting with Del.-elect Robert White, who will become only the third person in the modern era to hold the title of D.C.’s nonvoting delegate.

“I’m sitting next to a teacher right now; I’m sitting next to the mayor of Scranton … good, nice people,” said Rep.-elect Zack Mullock, D-N.J., who said he was surprised by how many “regular people” he was meeting among the incoming class.

Rep.-elect Brad Lander, D-N.Y., who ousted fellow Democrat Dan Goldman in a Brooklyn-based primary before cruising to victory in the general election, was also making friends.

“I was hanging out with Donavan McKinney yesterday in orientation, and I’m just really excited to meet all the amazing people. Micah Lasher, we were hanging out last night. Jacqui Irwin, so we’re just trying to get to know each other,” he noted.

It has been revealed that after arriving on Sunday with suitcases in hand, the future freshmen got a chance to set foot inside the House chamber later that day. Lander remarked he’d been there before to see Rep. Greg Casar, D-Texas, a friend of his, get sworn in four years ago. But Sunday was his first time on the floor itself.

“It’s obviously a lot different when it’s you,” he said.

Koh agreed, saying “everyone in that room, Republican or Democrat, had a lot of reverence for where they were.”.

“I think it was just a good reminder about how despite all the division, that’s what we’re going to focus on — trying to figure out how to get things done for the American people,” he stated.

Members-elect were trying their best to navigate their new workplace on Monday, many of them donning backpacks as they came to terms with the realities of their new job.

“We just have to get back to class,” noted Rep.-elect Ed Gallrein, R-Ky., to a crowd of reporters trying to flag him down as he left orientation to use the restroom.

They’d have Italian food for lunch, after a session in the CVC auditorium where many of the future members typed notes on their laptops.

“They’ve got a packed agenda for us all week, really helping us figure out how to get started. Build our team, set course, understand where the bathrooms are — large and small. We got a lot to learn,” Lander mentioned.

Industry observers note that more U.S. women are taking menopause hormone therapy, latest prescription data suggest.

In a recent development, monthly dispensing of hormone therapy for women aged 40 to 74 more than doubled since 2023, growing from 2 million to 4.9 million, researchers report November 19 in JAMA. The analysis of U.S. pharmacy dispensing data revealed that this increase began in 2024. The rise continued in 2025, before and after the Food and Drug Administration’s November removal of the black box warning from packaging, and into 2026.

Although the data in the new study are aggregate, the researchers used population data to estimate the dispensing rate for this age group, which jumped from 28 prescriptions per 1,000 women to 67 prescriptions per 1,000 over the period studied.

The new study wasn’t designed to determine what’s behind the increase. It’s possible that the evidence regarding hormone therapy’s safety and effectiveness for the treatment of menopause symptoms, such as hot flashes, is reaching more women. Medical groups such as the Menopause Society have recommended menopause hormone therapy for women with symptoms who are younger than 60 or within 10 years of the start of menopause, absent certain risk factors including prior breast cancer and stroke.

“Greater attention to women’s health, updated medical guidance supporting individualized menopause hormone therapy and social media may all be contributing to increased interest,” notes Dana Sarnak, who studies sexual and reproductive health at Johns Hopkins School of Medicine. Anecdotally, her clinician colleagues report more patients seeking menopause care, she says.

Many women and physicians turned away from hormone therapy in the early 2000s after a large study called the Women’s Health Initiative raised safety concerns, which were later considered overblown. Research since then has provided a more nuanced understanding of the benefits and risks of menopause hormone therapy at different ages.

Sources indicate that there are safer formulations, including patches and gels, of estrogen today then at the time of the Women’s Health Initiative, for which participants took a pill. The new study found that product use increased for transdermal and vaginal estrogen and for progesterone products — women who have their uterus need to take progesterone along with estrogen. The use of oral formulations remained stable. There has been a shortage of estrogen patches in the United States this year, which the U.S. Food and Drug Administration attributes to increasing demand.

The redistricting fights that underscored this year’s battle for the House could continue into the 2028 election cycle, although lessons from last Tuesday will likely shape those efforts.

House Republicans had hoped that new congressional maps in seven states would help them limit losses in the face of an unfavorable political environment. But nearly a week after the election, the GOP appeared on track to flip just three redrawn seats while losing a host of seats in Texas, Florida, North Carolina, Ohio and Alabama that were reconfigured in their favor.

“The question is whether the results have let some air out of the [redistricting] balloon or not,” remarked Erik Nisbet, a professor at Northwestern University’s School of Communication.

Republicans may question the utility of redrawing more state maps in the 2028 cycle, while Democrats will need to weigh how to spend their political capital. But the latest lines approved over the past year could still prove more favorable for Republicans in future elections.

“This was a wave election, and there’s no guarantee that the Democratic generic ballot would be D+13 — which is the reason why redistricting didn’t work for Republicans — in the next cycle,” Nisbet added.

According to recent reports, latest maps appear possible, if not likely, in at least a few states. Maryland voters last week approved an amendment that would clear the way for new boundaries ahead of the 2028 elections. Democratic Gov. Wes Moore, who easily won a second term last week, stated he hopes to see a new map, citing the threat of President Donald Trump continuing to push for friendlier lines in GOP-led states. Maryland Democrats could draw a map that would favor them in all eight of the state’s House seats, including the Eastern Shore district of Rep. Andy Harris, the state’s lone Republican in Congress.

Advocates for a latest map in Wisconsin got a boost last week when Democrats flipped both the state House and state Senate, setting up a Democratic trifecta. Gov.-elect David Crowley remarked he would sign a bill redrawing the state’s congressional map if legislators sent one to his desk.

Republicans in recent years have had a lopsided edge in the congressional delegation for Wisconsin, a perennial battleground state. But Democrats flipped two House seats last week, with Rebecca Cooke and Mitchell Berman unseating GOP Reps. Derrick Van Orden and Bryan Steil, respectively, bringing the state delegation to an even 4-4.

Democrats could also look to redraw the lines in Upcoming York and Virginia. Earlier this year, voters in the commonwealth approved a new map that would have given Democrats up to four pickup opportunities, but the Virginia Supreme Court later struck it down on procedural grounds. Even without the new map, Democrats flipped two House seats in Virginia last week and came within 2 points of flipping a third.

Democrats in Fresh York, meanwhile, took initial steps toward mid-decade redistricting earlier this year, but 2028 is the earliest they could hold elections under a new map.

On the Republican side, several states have been mentioned as candidates for latest maps in 2028.

Officials in GOP-led Mississippi have held hearings this year on redistricting, which could target Democratic Rep. Bennie Thompson. Republicans are also aiming to redraw the state’s legislative lines ahead of next year’s off-year elections.

In a recent development, it’s not clear whether states that were unsuccessful in redrawing their district lines for 2026 will try again when their legislatures convene next year. Republicans in both South Carolina and Indiana fell short in their push to pass new maps and could decide to revisit the issue. But Democrats flipped a House seat in each state last week, and some Republican incumbents won reelection by narrower margins than usual. Still, Republicans maintained their legislative majorities in both states, though Democrats broke their supermajorities in the South Carolina and Indiana state houses.

An analysis by DecisionDeskHQ offers a potential warning sign for Republicans in the Palmetto and Hoosier states: Under the GOP-drawn maps that were not adopted for 2026, Democrats could have flipped even more seats last week.

Redistricting appears off the table in a handful of states where fresh maps for 2028 had once been considered possible.

Georgia’s outgoing Republican governor, Brian Kemp, remarked last week that he would not call a special session to address redistricting before the end of the year, after Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms was elected to succeed him.

There were no House flips in the Peach State in the midterm elections, though several Republicans won by closer-than-anticipated margins.

According to recent reports, in New Jersey, Democratic Gov. Mikie Sherrill told the New Jersey Globe that she also did not “see a path forward for redistricting right now.”.

Sources indicate that democrats flipped two House seats in the Garden State last week. Navy veteran Rebecca Bennett defeated Republican Rep. Thomas H. Kean Jr., while Cape May Mayor Zack Mullock scored a surprise win over GOP Rep. Jeff Van Drew.

With their newly introduced majorities in Washington, Democrats could propose legislation to ban partisan gerrymandering.

That’s something John Bisognano, the president of the National Democratic Redistricting Committee, anticipates happening, but he said Democrat-led states should be prepared to respond to new maps drawn in Republican-controlled ones.

“If they are going to continue to take those actions, Democrats in states across the country need to be prepared to respond, and we, of course, now have significantly more opportunities than we did before Tuesday to respond to those states,” he remarked.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • WASHINGTON — A part of the brain famous for listening is vital for talking, too.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

WASHINGTON — A part of the brain famous for listening is vital for talking, too.

Data collected from people as they listen and try to talk show that this brain region, a small spot inside a larger area called Wernicke’s area, has a more expansive job than researchers thought when it comes to communicating. The results may help efforts to restore people’s voices. The results presented November 15 at the annual meeting of the Society for Neuroscience and published November 19 in Science.The study provides convincing evidence that this brain spot is critical for speech production, says neurologist and language researcher Jeffrey Binder of the Medical College of Wisconsin in Milwaukee. “My hope is that this study will help scientists and clinicians accept a more accurate interpretation of this focal area” as an early stop on the pathway to saying a word.

A small part of the brain, just above the left ear, was first described in 1874 by a neurologist Carl Wernicke as necessary for making sense of speech. People with damage there had trouble comprehending words. But some people also had trouble producing them. “Sounds were swapped, words were replaced with near misses,” Edward Chang of the University of California, San Francisco, said in a news briefing. “The basic question has been, ‘Why would damage to a hearing area of the brain break the ability to speak?’ That question has been open for 150 years.”The newly introduced research offers an answer: A small bit of Wernicke’s area (to be extremely specific, the left posterior superior temporal gyrus or lpSTG ) becomes active just before a word is spoken. “Every word that you have said today began in that small part above your left ear about a quarter of a second before you said it,” Chang said.

In a recent development, the finding adds to growing evidence that brain areas are more complex than people have appreciated, says neuroscientist Leigh Hochberg at Brown University in Providence, R.I. “I believe that one of the things we are going to learn over the next five, 10 years of this research, is that each part of the brain that, we were taught as a med student or a grad student, does this, probably does that and a whole lot more.”.

Scientists measured brain activity in 28 people before they had surgery for epilepsy or tumors. They were able to see that this brain region kicked on as a person listened to words, and also just before they attempted to speak. Cells there had preferences for certain sorts of words, long ones, for instance. “It’s more active when you’re about to say the word caterpillar than when you’re about to say the word cat,” said Matthew Leonard, a cognitive neuroscientist at UCSF.

Electrical stimulation to this small bit of brain also interfered with people’s ability to talk. “What we found was that stimulation, really only in this lpSTG area, disrupted this speech production when it was delivered just prior to speaking,” mentioned UCSF bioengineer Alexander Silva.

In a recent development, some efforts to make implanted devices that can help restore speech to people who no longer talk focus on the motor cortex, a part of the brain that controls the movements required for speech. This bit of Wernicke’s area offers an additional spot to consider, Silva said. “What if you could target a single brain region and gain access to the full spectrum of speech, from listening all the way up to speech production?”.

Experimental brain implants in two volunteers with paralysis were able to detect both what they heard and what they were trying to say, the researchers report in the study.

The discovery may help scientists better understand situations that involve both hearing and speaking, such as speech or comprehension differences in people with autism, or how children first begin learning to talk, Chang remarked.

In a recent development, rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., took to the House floor Monday to unveil a resolution that would impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, and a vote on the matter could occur by Wednesday.

A draft resolution that Massie read aloud on the House floor on Monday accused Hegseth of eight violations of law or the Constitution, including that he violated the 1973 War Powers Resolution in his prosecution of the Iran war and acted illegally in military campaigns in Venezuela, Yemen, the Caribbean Sea and the eastern Pacific Ocean.

Massie's resolution also charges Hegseth with disregarding protection of civilians in wartime and suppressing the free speech of a U.S. senator.

Massie announced his intention to file the resolution as a matter of the privileges of the House.

Industry observers note that speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., will now have to rule as to whether the resolution constitutes a proper question of the privileges of the House. There is precedent from prior instances when impeachment was found to be valid as it relates to the House’s constitutionally granted powers.

He must schedule a vote to occur within two legislative days. Assuming that the speaker rules that Massie's resolution is privileged, the House could vote on the resolution itself, or on a motion to table it or refer it to committee.

If the House were to impeach Hegseth under this process, it would mark a historical anomaly. According to the Congressional Research Service, recent attempts to impeach an official as a matter of the privileges of the House have not resulted in approval of the resolution. In cases in which an official has been impeached, the House has nearly always chosen to conduct an investigation first.

Industry observers note that in an interview on Oct. 26, Massie put the chances of his resolution being adopted at 50-50.

In comments to reporters outside the Capitol after his floor remarks, Massie said he suspected some Republicans may back his resolution but he indicated he has neither asked for nor received any such assurances from any of them.

According to recent reports, he predicted there could be some GOP support in the Senate if Hegseth is impeached and it goes to trial. He noted that if the trial does not start until 2027, any Republicans who might vote to convict Hegseth would presumably be joined by most if not all of a more sizeable Senate Democratic caucus.

Massie's odds of success for his resolution may now be greater than his previous 50-50 prediction given the results of the Nov. 3 midterm elections, which gave Democrats control over both chambers in the next Congress — a vote motivated largely by opposition to the Iran war and its inflationary impact.

In a recent development, the questions now are, first, how many House Republicans will defy President Donald Trump and vote to impeach Hegseth; and, secondly, how many incumbents who lost their reelection bids on Nov. 3, a cohort that is disproportionately Republican, might be absent for the impeachment vote?

Massie said some Republicans who lost their reelection bids may feel freer to vote to impeach Hegseth. And he also said Republicans who were reelected and will have to face voters in 2028 may also think about how their vote on an impeachment resolution would reverberate politically.

"It's going to be everybody's conscience, and then they'll have to live with that vote," Massie stated. "And they're going to have to live with that vote two years from now if they're not part of the retirement caucus. And if they were part of the retirement caucus, what do they have to lose?".

Asked why he did not bring articles of impeachment against President Donald Trump, Massie said: "I think the president needs to see one of — this is a metaphor — one of his horses shot out from under him, and then maybe he'll he will see things differently.".

If the House does vote on Massie’s resolution, Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., who is expected to become the House speaker in the next Congress, stated on ABC’s “This Week” on Sunday that he would be a “hard yes” on it.

Hegseth has “got to go,” Jeffries noted. “The so-called secretary of Defense has abused his power, undermined our national security and engineered this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran, which has skyrocketed prices on the American people and made the country less safe.”.

Most if not all House Democrats are expected to agree.

In a recent development, last week, Rep. Adam Smith, D-Wash., the ranking member of the Armed Services Committee and its likely chairman in the next Congress, indicated in an interview with The Newly introduced Republic that he would support Massie’s impeachment resolution, and he predicted it would be adopted.

Sources indicate that referring to Massie’s measure, Smith mentioned, “By every estimation, it will pass and he will be impeached. And off that goes to the Senate. Then the Senate is legally required to spend all of their time dealing with that until it’s done with.”.

Sources indicate that "Every second Pete Hegseth remains at the top of the Pentagon, our servicemembers are at risk," Rep. Jason Crow, D-Colo., a senior member of the Armed Services Committee, said in a post on X on Sunday.

Also on Monday, Everett B. Kelley, the national president of the American Federation of Government Employees, a union that represents some 820,000 federal and D.C. government employees, sent a letter to House members urging a “yes” vote on Massie's Hegseth impeachment resolution.

The letter cited the risks Kelley remarked the Iran war has posed to the lives of the Defense Department's uniformed and civilian personnel, and the missive noted Hegseth's stripping of workplace rights and protections for the department's civilians.

"By adopting Rep. Massie’s resolution, the House can begin the long overdue bipartisan effort to reclaim its constitutional powers and authority, restore checks and balances, and take responsibility for the lives of military personnel and civilian employees that Mr. Hegseth’s capricious leadership has jeopardized," Kelley wrote.

Industry observers note that massie announced in mid-September his intention to file an impeachment resolution against Hegseth. But Johnson adjourned the House before the vote would have occurred.

Massie’s new resolution is substantially the same as his earlier one, with the same eight articles of impeachment.

The first three of these alleges that Hegseth’s conduct of the Iran war violated the War Powers Resolution.

Massie's measure says Hegseth prosecuted the Iran war without congressional authorization and in the absence of an attack on the United States or an imminent threat.

Further, the measure alleges that Hegseth continued the war despite the House and Senate adopting in June a concurrent war powers resolution calling for the withdrawal of U.S. forces from the fight.

And, the resolution states, Hegseth continued the Iran war after the expiration of the War Powers Resolution’s 60-day termination period and any potential 30-day withdrawal period.

Massie’s measure further asserts that Hegseth:.

Recent findings suggest that the House has only voted twice to impeach a member of the Cabinet. In 1876, Secretary of War William Belknap was impeached over allegations of corruption, and his abrupt resignation likely contributed to his acquittal in the Senate.

In 2024, the House voted 214-213 to impeach Alejandro Mayorkas, then-secretary of Homeland Security, for “willful and systemic refusal to comply with the law” and “breach of public trust.” The Senate dispensed with the charges without a trial.

What satellites leave behind

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3249 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Astronomy

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It was the lithium that gave it away, notes Daniel Murphy, an atmospheric chemist at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
  • It was early 2023, in Fairbanks, Alaska, in the deep blue of winter, and Murphy and his colleagues had just sent a plane through the stratosphere, the atmospheric stratum 6 to 31 miles (10 to 50 kilometers) above Earth’s surface where the protective ozone layer lies.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It was the lithium that gave it away, notes Daniel Murphy, an atmospheric chemist at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.

It was early 2023, in Fairbanks, Alaska, in the deep blue of winter, and Murphy and his colleagues had just sent a plane through the stratosphere, the atmospheric stratum 6 to 31 miles (10 to 50 kilometers) above Earth’s surface where the protective ozone layer lies.

Industry observers note that their experiment came as interest was growing in controversial proposals to cool the planet by injecting certain aerosols into the atmosphere — a form of geoengineering. The team hoped to get a baseline measurement of the chemistry of the upper atmosphere, before any geoengineering experiments altered the hard-to-reach atmospheric layer.

The lithium showed they were too late.

According to recent reports, the team expected to find trace amounts of metals naturally deposited by meteoroids, which constantly bombard and burn up in Earth’s atmosphere. But their data highlighted way more lithium in stratospheric particles than is typically present in meteoroids.

It has been revealed that “That’s what led us to the other metals,” Murphy says. Analyzing their samples, they also found higher than expected levels of aluminum, plus significant amounts of other metals like copper and lead that are scarcely found in meteoroids and must have come from some other source. Then there were the more exotic metals like niobium and hafnium, which appeared in their samples in the same ratio as in an alloy used to manufacture rocket engine nozzles.

Sources indicate that the data pointed to an obvious culprit: human-made objects such as satellites and spent rocket stages that fall back to Earth from orbit and reenter the atmosphere. On the way down, they wear away and disintegrate under the heat of friction — a process known as ablation.

Later that year in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS), Murphy and his colleagues reported that 10% of stratospheric aerosol particles carried metals from spacecraft.

In a recent development, the number was shocking, but not altogether surprising. Reentries have been rising sharply in recent years as corporations and countries began launching megaconstellations of thousands of satellites, like SpaceX’s Starlink. And all those satellites will inevitably deorbit.

Industry observers note that since Murphy and his colleagues’ 2023 report, it’s become clear that human-made satellites are now dumping more of certain metals into the upper atmosphere than meteoroids naturally do. This influx has raised concerns that the metals might catalyze chemical reactions that destroy ozone, alter cloud formation, or boost or buffer the greenhouse effect.

According to recent reports, researchers say it’s too soon to know for sure if the metals are a serious environmental problem. But megaconstellations are growing faster than our ability to close these knowledge gaps.

Industry observers note that at the same time, the uncertainty over whether regulators might have to act presents a substantial risk to the space industry, states Martin Ross of the Aerospace Corporation, a research and development nonprofit based in El Segundo, California, and a co-author of the 2023 study. “We would call it an enterprise risk,” says Ross, “in that the longer we wait to see if there is something going on, the bigger the mitigation will be — if there needs to be any mitigation — down the line.”.

From our vantage point on Earth, space may be incomprehensibly vast, but the orbital environment is not.

Six years ago, according to the U.S. Space Force’s public catalog, there were some 13,700 trackable objects circling in low Earth orbit; last year, the number had climbed to nearly 25,000. Disposing of satellites in the atmosphere reduces overcrowding and the risk of uncontrolled objects crashing into each other — and potentially setting off a chain of collisions that wipe out key space-based technologies or turn Earth orbit into an impenetrable debris field.

RELATED: Our increasingly cluttered skies.

According to recent reports, “Reentry is the only sustainable, short-term way of cleaning up the orbital environment,” says José Pedro Ferreira, a doctoral candidate in astronautical engineering at the University of Southern California (USC) in Los Angeles, who left an industry job for academia in the early 2020s when it became clear that reentry could have unintended consequences. “We need to do it, otherwise we may undermine our capability of accessing orbit.”.

But operators are also typically held responsible by their national regulators for any damages their spacecraft cause on the ground, and for decades the industry has designed spacecraft to burn up as much as possible in the atmosphere to minimize the risk to lives and infrastructure on the ground, a principle known as design for demise.

As a result, the space industry has long perceived its impacts to Earth as minimal. But in the age of megaconstellations, that’s no longer the case.

“As with everything, we live in a closed system,” states Ferreira, “and things do not disappear.”.

SpaceX debuted its first 60 satellites into orbit in May 2019 to bring internet to even remote regions of the globe; less than a decade later, Starlink’s constellation is more than 10,000 satellites strong. Starlink already comprises roughly two-thirds of active satellites, and SpaceX aims to grow it to as many as 42,000. Other countries and corporations are not far behind: Amazon Leo is authorized by the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) to operate roughly 7,700 satellites; China has plans to deploy some 28,000.

Not only are we launching more than ever, but we’re also bringing spacecraft back down faster than ever before.

For decades, spacecraft have been designed to burn up as much as possible upon reentry to minimize risks to those on the ground. As a result, the space industry has long perceived its impacts to Earth as minimal. But in the age of megaconstellations, that’s no longer the case.

Historically, satellite operators had what Ferreira calls a “gentleman’s agreement” to deorbit their spacecraft within 25 years of mission termination to prevent orbital clutter. Recently, some national authorities have begun enforcing even tighter timelines. The FCC, for example, now enforces a five-year window.

“If you have 50,000 satellites in orbit, which is almost surely going to be reached in the not too distant future, with a design lifetime of five years,” Murphy indicates, “that would mean a satellite would be reentering and burning up in the atmosphere on average more than once an hour.”.

According to recent reports, operators of megaconstellations may use even shorter timelines for deorbiting satellites, according to Ferreira, bringing them down at the first sign of malfunction. “Which is great from a standpoint of orbital sustainability,” he says, “but it starts raising the question more and more about what the impacts are in the atmosphere.”.

There are reasons to be concerned.

In a recent development, aluminum, for example, which makes up the bulk of most spacecraft, may form aluminum oxides as it breaks down during ablation, which can kick-start a chain of chemical reactions that eat away at ozone, Earth’s main shield against UV radiation. Some atmospheric models suggest that metals from spacecraft in stratospheric particles could seed polar stratospheric clouds, further accelerating ozone depletion.

Injecting aluminum into the upper atmosphere is also the basis of many controversial geoengineering aims. Aluminum compounds would block radiation from the Sun, which could cool down our warming planet. But they might also entrap radiation reflected off the surface of the ocean, which could increase surface temperatures. Opposition to geoengineering has so far stymied any field experiments, but with the number of reentries rising from a few hundred to many thousands per year, an uncontrolled geoengineering experiment on a grand scale may have already begun.

Sources indicate that “The metals are at the same altitude range as the ozone layer, so we have to be concerned about what they would do,” Murphy says. “We don’t know it’s bad, but we don’t know it isn’t bad either.”.

One reason it’s so difficult to predict the impacts of ablation is that we don’t yet understand what happens to spacecraft during ablation. “We reenter things all the time and we have been since the moment we started launching spacecraft,” notes Stijn Lemmens, a space debris mitigation analyst at the European Space Agency (ESA). “It’s fascinating, for something which is so ubiquitous, how little we actually know about it, and how little we used to care about it.”.

Operators have long been incentivized to design spacecraft to burn up as much as possible in the atmosphere, and decades of this design for demise ethos has given the space industry a solid idea of how much material — or how little — will make it to the ground when objects burn through the atmosphere.

But in terms of that material that is ablated, “we’re really in the dark,” says Ross. Previous studies have suggested that around 90% of the bodies of orbiting satellites and spent upper stages could be vaporized, later condensing into the nanosized particles the team detected. But, says Ross, “we really don’t understand how these vehicles melt, how they break apart, how they form smoke trails.”.

To quantify the impacts on the atmosphere, researchers start with atmospheric models and then add ablated material, examining how those particles interact with the natural stratospheric background via complex chemical reactions and physical processes like mixing. But the outputs of the atmospheric models are right now held back by our limited understanding of the fiery, complex process of ablation — details like what compounds are being emitted and what size particles are being formed. “We’re basically guessing at this point,” Ross states. “And we’re getting to the limit of what we can do with guessing.”.

In a recent development, to do better, scientists are developing upcoming models of the physics and chemistry of ablation itself. At USC, Ferreira and his colleagues model how ablation produces aluminum oxides in the upper atmosphere, providing atmospheric researchers with inputs for both emissions and particle size. In a 2024 study in Geophysical Research Letters, the team reported that a 550-pound (250 kilograms) satellite — about the size of your average megaconstellation satellite — could deposit some 66 pounds (30 kg) of aluminum oxide nanoparticles in the upper atmosphere. Such particles could remain aloft for upwards of 30 years, potentially catalyzing ozone-destroying reactions as they settle throughout the stratosphere for decades after reentry.

Industry observers note that but state-of-the-art ablation models don’t always agree on what products are being formed, according to Ross. A model from researchers at the University of Leeds in the U.K. suggests that aluminum hydroxide, rather than aluminum oxide, may be the main byproduct.

According to recent reports, to validate ablation models and get more useful data from atmospheric models, we need more measurements from reentries. How an object breaks apart as it tumbles through the air is a messy process — a product of astrophysics, fluid mechanics, materials science, and engineering. “You cannot reproduce it on Earth,” Lemmens notes. “There is no facility large enough to, in one assessment, combine all the effects.”.

That means scientists need to measure ablation where it’s actually taking place — “take instruments and put them on airplanes and go out and watch these things reenter,” Ross states.

Since the beginning of the Space Age, these kinds of measurements have only been taken a handful of times. Observing space objects from an airplane as they streak through the atmosphere is difficult work — and potentially dangerous. Most reentering objects are uncontrolled, making it hard to predict exactly where the object will hit the atmosphere and how much of it will burn up in the process. Researchers need a degree of certainty to avoid sending a plane full of scientists and sensors up into a debris field. “These types of reentries, which are destructive and still predictable so that you can get close, are extremely rare,” Lemmens claims.

But in 2024, ESA got lucky. The first of four Cluster II satellites — debuted in 2000 to study Earth’s magnetosphere — was poised to reenter the atmosphere, and the agency had a pretty good idea of exactly where and when it would break up over the southern Pacific Ocean.

Recent findings suggest that “We could get close,” Lemmens claims. “The drawback is it was in broad daylight, which had not been attempted before on this level of detail.”.

In daytime, the team would have no visual confirmation of reentry, and it would be harder to get clean data than at night. The team had to trust they were pointing their instruments at the right spot, and then look at their data after the fact to see if they caught it. “In the end, it’s a leap of faith,” Lemmens indicates. “You predict as well as you can, you fly the plane as well as you can, but in the end, you do it all in the blind,” he says.

It has been revealed that on Sept. 8, a team of scientists took off from Easter Island on a modified Dassault Falcon 900 business jet packed with instruments, and pointed their cameras just above the bright blue horizon roughly 500 miles (800 km) away.

The team used spectroscopic instruments to identify which vapors were coming from the ablating satellite. Since the team knew the material makeup of the satellite, they could gauge its surface temperatures during reentry, as the appearance of specific ions would indicate a certain material had reached its melting point.

It has been revealed that altogether, they captured about 20 seconds of the reentry. Two more satellites from the same cluster were set to reenter within 24 hours of each other on Aug. 31 and Sept. 1, 2026, giving ESA another opportunity to capture more of the reentry process and to fully reconstruct the breakup.

For researchers, one upside to the rapid and unmitigated increase in satellite reentries is more opportunities to capture the process in action.

Some of the best data yet to come will be collected by ESA’s Draco mission, in which the agency looks to build and launch a satellite with the “sole purpose of falling apart again,” says Lemmens. Draco will launch in 2027 with an indestructible capsule that will survive reentry, protecting the data collected from the surface of the satellite as it’s torn apart by the atmosphere.

Recent findings suggest that researchers will be able to combine these onboard data with remote observations, using them to improve or validate existing models of ablation. “That means we, for the first time, will actually have the full story without any ambiguities,” Lemmens notes.

Once a scientific consensus is reached, then mitigation measures, whether technological or regulatory, can be deployed.

Industry observers note that if research confirms that one material or another in spacecraft is particularly damaging to the atmosphere, for example, space operators can remove and replace it. “That was the basis of the success of the Montreal Protocol,” states Ross.

Recent findings suggest that after scientists discovered a hole in the ozone layer in the 1980s, every country in the world signed on to the Montreal Protocol, an international agreement to control the ozone-depleting substances humans were emitting into the atmosphere. The hole has been shrinking ever since. Signed in 1987, the agreement is widely considered one of the most successful environmental treaties to date. Since then, however, other global climate agreements have not fared as well.

Industry observers note that still, many remain optimistic, including Ross. He points to the commercial space industry’s track record of working with regulators and astronomers to reduce space debris and light pollution. “There is some current flowing in those lines,” he states.

RELATED: Can robots save Earth orbit?

Recent findings suggest that some operators have already expressed a commitment to acting on whatever guidelines come out of research on the atmospheric risks. “The difficulty that I have as a responsible operator is, in this particular case, I don’t know what to do,” Vijay Thakur, a technical authority at French satellite corporation Eutelsat, stated at an October 2025 panel at the Secure World Foundation’s 7th Summit for Space Sustainability in Paris. There are clear brightness limits he can follow to mitigate impacts to the astronomical community, he noted, but no such guidelines exist yet for atmospheric impacts.

Sources indicate that “I want to put the right technical requirements, for me as the operator customer, onto industry so they can build what I need to operate and take it up and bring it back down without damaging anything from 0 kilometers to the von Kármán line,” Thakur stated, referring to the commonly accepted boundary of outer space at 62 miles high (100 km). “Help.”.

There are some design tweaks presently available that could reduce emissions and help more of each spacecraft survive reentry, including non-ablative heat shields and inflatable aerodynamic decelerators, according to Adam Mitchell, a materials and processes evaluation engineer at ESA.

Of course, the more of a spacecraft that survives reentry, the greater the risk on the ground during uncontrolled reentries — and most reentries are uncontrolled. “There is this balance between sustainability and safety, but when it comes to human safety, there is no compromise at all,” Chris Young, space sustainability senior lead at the U.K. Space Agency, remarked at the same Secure World Foundation panel. “Design for demise has to take priority.”.

Satellite builders could also consider replacing problematic metals — but that comes with its own trade-offs. In 2024, the world’s first wooden satellite, LignoSat, rolled out to orbit in a partnership between Kyoto University and Japanese logging firm Sumitomo Forestry. A cube of magnolia wood panels, LignoSat will give researchers insights into how well wood holds up in the space environment, and how cleanly it burns up in the atmosphere. Carbon fiber is another material of interest, according to Ferreira. But these organic materials may release black carbon into the upper atmosphere, which may absorb sunlight or reflect it, depending on the structure the carbon takes.

According to recent reports, ross thinks we can close the remaining knowledge gaps in short order — and that those lessons can be applied almost immediately. “We can do that before the next generation of satellites comes along,” he says, “but we just need the resources.”.

It has been revealed that A cultural revolution is coming for the industry, regardless of what’s discovered about the impacts to the atmosphere. “The one-use, nonrecyclable culture that we have in space, of, ‘We’ll launch something to space with rare Earth minerals that are of limited supply and then burn them all up in the atmosphere after one use,’ that is unsustainable,” said Young.

Sources indicate that A sustainable future — one that balances both Earth and space sustainability — will involve creating something we haven’t quite nailed yet in our earthbound industries. “We need to move beyond the single-use mindset that currently defines much of spacecraft design and accelerate the transition toward an in-space circular economy,” Mitchell claims.

Can we do in space what we’ve failed to do on Earth? Right now, researchers are gathering data as fast as they can, as fast as resourcing allows, to inform models of ablation and atmospheric processes that will eventually be validated by measurements taken during reentry.

Then, equipped with actionable data, we can act.

Kate Wheeling is a freelance journalist based in Santa Barbara, California. She writes about the environment and humans’ relationship with the natural world. Her work has appeared in The Atlantic, Smithsonian magazine, The Daily Beast, and Mother Jones.

#111557. The Sky This Week from November 20 to 27: Uranus at opposition

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2075 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Astronomy ↗ Open Full Page

The Sky This Week from November 20 to 27: Uranus at opposition

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2075 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Astronomy

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, friday, November 20The Moon passes 5° north of Neptune at 8 A.M.
  • In the northeast, Auriga the Charioteer is above the horizon by 7 P.M.
  • Recent findings suggest that why are these called the Kids?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, friday, November 20The Moon passes 5° north of Neptune at 8 A.M. EST, then passes 7° north of Saturn at 8 P.M. EST. They remain visible all evening, forming a triangle in southern Pisces and northern Cetus. The Moon and Saturn are visible to the naked eye, but Neptune will be invisible without binoculars or a telescope. Check out last week’s column for more details on how to view the celestial trio.

In the northeast, Auriga the Charioteer is above the horizon by 7 P.M. local time. Its brightest star is Capella, which shines at magnitude 0.1 and sits some 43 light-years away. Just southeast of this star, you’ll find another triangle in the sky tonight. This small shape is an asterism about 2.7° long, known as the Kids. It consists of Epsilon (ε), Zeta (ζ), and Eta (η) Aurigae, which range from 3rd (Epsilon and Eta) to 4th (Zeta) magnitude.

Recent findings suggest that why are these called the Kids? Capella’s name essentially means “She-Goat,” according to the late stellar expert Jim Kaler. These fainter stars cluster close by the brighter star like goat kids around their mother.

Mercury reaches greatest western elongation (20°) at 7 P.M. EST; it will be visible before dawn tomorrow morning, so keep reading for more details.

Sunrise: 6:51 A.M. Sunset: 4:40 P.M. Moonrise: 2:04 P.M. Moonset: 2:12 A.M. Moon Phase: Waxing gibbous (84%) *Times for sunrise, sunset, moonrise, and moonset are given in local time from 40° N 90° W. The Moon’s illumination is given at 10 P.M. local time from the same location.

Industry observers note that saturday, November 21If you’ve got a viewing site with a clear eastern horizon, this morning offers a great opportunity to spot the solar system’s innermost planet. Look for Mercury about an hour before sunrise, when it reaches 7° high and shines at magnitude –0.5. The planet reached its greatest western elongation from our Sun yesterday evening, and is now 20° west of our star in the sky.

Industry observers note that located in Libra, the tiny world sits to the far lower left of bright Venus, higher in the sky. Venus is in the constellation Virgo, standing just north (to the upper left) of the bright star Spica. Another bright star, Arcturus in Boötes, hangs to that pair’s far upper left.

According to recent reports, pull out a telescope to check out the size and phase of each planet. Start with Venus, whose disk spans a hefty 46” — right now larger than Jupiter’s apparent size in our sky. Despite its impressive width, however, the disk of Venus appears as just a sliver, only 19% lit. Slide down to Mercury for comparison, and see that its phase is much larger — 62% — while the planet’s overall apparent width is much smaller, just 7”.

If you’re able, keep watching Mercury day by day in the morning sky. Its gibbous phase will continue growing, reaching 84% lit by the end of the month.

According to recent reports, sunrise: 6:52 A.M. Sunset: 4:39 P.M. Moonrise: 2:29 P.M. Moonset: 3:22 A.M. Moon Phase: Waxing gibbous (92%).

According to recent reports, sunday, November 22With the Moon not far from Full, its western limb is now coming into view as the Sun rises across the lunar landscape. The large, flat-floored crater Schickard is prominent in the southwest, near the small, circular Mare Humorum. Because the nearly Full Moon is so bright, you may want to use a Moon filter before you turn your telescope toward our satellite tonight for a closer look.

According to recent reports, zoom in on Schickard to discover that its dark floor isn’t perfectly smooth, but pockmarked by smaller craters that came after the initial, larger crater’s formation. Its outer walls are shallow and beaten down, also showing off their age. Look closely at Schickard’s western wall to see how it has slumped, particularly compared to the eastern side of the crater rim. Also compare the texture of the southwestern portion of the crater floor, which appears quite rough, to the rest of the crater, which is smoother. The difference arises because most of the crater was flooded by lava, which didn’t quite reach its southwestern regions.

Industry observers note that stretching about 130 miles (210 kilometers) across, Schickard is roughly 4 billion years old and was formed by a giant impact. Because it sits so near the limb of the Moon, it often looks oblong from our vantage point on Earth — but from above, orbiters have shown it is really quite circular in shape.

Recent findings suggest that sunrise: 6:53 A.M. Sunset: 4:39 P.M. Moonrise: 2:59 P.M. Moonset: 4:34 A.M. Moon Phase: Waxing gibbous (97%).

Sources indicate that monday, November 23A few hours after sunset, the house-shaped constellation Cepheus stands on the point of its roof in the northern sky, above the Little Dipper. Cepheus is home to several lovely double stars, including Xi (ξ) Cephei, also known as Kurhah.

Glowing at magnitude 4.3, Kurhah is not one of the stars in the house’s outline, but lies within the boxy base. You can find it about midway between Alderamin (Alpha [α] Cep) and Iota (ι) Cep, the western and eastern points in the house’s box, respectively. Kurhah’s two components are separated by just under 8” — once you find the star in binoculars or your finder scope, any telescope will split them. The pair consists of a brighter magnitude 4.4 primary, which glows white, and a fainter magnitude 6.5 secondary, which appears to many observers as yellow.

According to recent reports, if you happen to have a large telescope, you may want to give a nearby deep-sky treasure a try: planetary nebula NGC 7139 sits just 2° west-southwest of Kurhah, but it requires a large scope (8 inches at least) to spot, as this bubble of gas glows at magnitude 13.3. If available, an Oxygen-III filter will help bring it out by dimming the nearby stars.

Sources indicate that sunrise: 6:54 A.M. Sunset: 4:38 P.M. Moonrise: 3:37 P.M. Moonset: 5:52 A.M. Moon Phase: Full.

Tuesday, November 24Full Moon occurs at 9:54 A.M. EST, bringing us our second Super Moon of the year. A Super Moon occurs when the Moon reaches Full phase close to perigee, its closest point to Earth, making our satellite appear larger and brighter than average. The November Full Moon is also called the Beaver Moon.

Recent findings suggest that A few hours earlier, before dawn, the Full Moon passes through the Pleiades star cluster (M45) in Taurus, occulting several of its bright stars. This is an easy event to watch, visible to the naked eye — or you can get a closer view with binoculars or a telescope (just note that you may want a Moon filter if available, as our satellite is so big and bright). The timing of the event will depend heavily on your location; note that it begins right around sunrise along the East Coast, so observers there may only see the Moon approaching the famous group of stars.

The 5th-magnitude star Celaeno (16 Tauri) disappears behind the Moon’s leading edge just moments before 6 A.M. CST, followed minutes later by 4th-magnitude Taygeta (19 Tau). Next to vanish is 4th-magnitude Maia (20 Tau) just before 6:20 A.M. CST, followed promptly by Sterope (21 Tau) a few minutes later. The latter two may be difficult to catch from the Midwest without optical aid, as sunrise is fast approaching. If you are using binoculars or a telescope in this region, make sure to put them away several minutes ahead of sunrise from your location. Celaeno reappears around 6:40 A.M. CST, 15 minutes or so before sunrise.

For specific timings from your location, visit the International Occultation Timing Association at http://www.lunar-occultations.com/bobgraze/index.html.

In a recent development, the Moon then passes 5° north of Uranus (also in Taurus) at 2 P.M. EST. Over in the constellation Leo, Mars passes 1.8° north of Regulus at 5 P.M. EST.

Recent findings suggest that sunrise: 6:55 A.M. Sunset: 4:38 P.M. Moonrise: 4:24 P.M. Moonset: 7:10 A.M. Moon Phase: Waning gibbous (99%).

In a recent development, wednesday, November 25The Moon reaches perigee, the closest point to Earth in its orbit, at 4:01 P.M. EST. At that time, our satellite will stand 223,288 miles (359,347 km) away.

Recent findings suggest that the distant ice giant Uranus reaches opposition tonight at 6 P.M. EST. Opposition is the best time to view a planet in our sky, and it’s visible roughly from dusk until dawn. Because Uranus is faint — magnitude 5.6 — you’ll want to give it a few hours after sunset to climb away from both light pollution and turbulent air near the horizon. Around 10 P.M. local time, you’ll find Uranus midway between the bright star Aldebaran and the Pleiades star cluster in Taurus the Bull, about 60° above the southeastern horizon. It sits some 1.5° south of 4th-magnitude 37 Tauri.

Although Uranus can be visible to the naked eye under clear, dark conditions, the bright waning Moon is nearby, so pull out binoculars or a telescope to view the far-off planet tonight. Once you land on its location, look for a “flat,” grayish-colored star. Uranus’ disk spans 4”, so you will likely be able to tell it is circular, rather than a pinpoint of light like any background stars.

Sunrise: 6:56 A.M. Sunset: 4:37 P.M. Moonrise: 5:24 P.M. Moonset: 8:26 A.M. Moon Phase: Waning gibbous (96%).

Thursday, November 26Celebrate Thanksgiving with a celestial turkey: The famous Orion Nebula (M42) is also playfully known as the Turkey Nebula because it looks to some like a turkey, particularly in deep astrophotos. But whether you’re a photographer or not, this bright deep-sky treat is easy to enjoy tonight while dinner digests.

Industry observers note that by about 9 P.M. local time, Orion the Hunter has risen above the eastern horizon, his recognizable three-star belt standing in a vertical line. The lowest star in that line is Alnitak (Zeta [ζ] Orionis), and the Orion Nebula lies just 3.7° south-southwest of this star, to its lower right on the sky this evening. You might be able to spot its glow without optical aid, although the bright Moon nearby may make that difficult. Binoculars or any telescope will easily show it.

According to recent reports, at 4th magnitude and spanning some 85’ by 60’, the Orion Nebula is a huge and bright star-forming region that sits roughly 1,350 light-years from Earth. In the brightest portion of the nebula lies a small grouping of young stars called the Trapezium Cluster. Take your time with this gorgeous sight, scanning around the region to pick out detail in the nebulosity. And if you are an astrophotographer, consider turning the view into a Thanksgiving memory to share for years to come.

Sources indicate that sunrise: 6:58 A.M. Sunset: 4:37 P.M. Moonrise: 6:35 P.M. Moonset: 9:33 A.M. Moon Phase: Waning gibbous (91%).

According to recent reports, friday, November 27The Moon-free window for observing Comet 161P/Hartley-IRAS reopens tonight, the same day the comet reaches perihelion, the closest point to the Sun in its 21½-year orbit. It has been a fairly stable 10th to 11th magnitude, and although it has no appreciable tail, the nucleus’ green glow has been notable in recent astrophotos.

Recent findings suggest that you’ll find Hartley-IRAS in the west a few hours after sunset. Around 7 P.M. local time it is still 30° high, well above the turbulent air near the ground that can muddy astronomical views. Tonight the comet is in western Sagitta, about 6.3° north-northeast of 3rd-magnitude Zeta (ζ) Aquilae. Even a small (4-inch) scope will net you a view, but larger apertures will show more detail around the nucleus, allowing you to look for features such as a sharpened southern flank as it flies into the solar headwind.

Sources indicate that while you’re in this region, make sure to sweep just 2.1° northeast of the comet’s location to spot the famous Coathanger asterism in Vulpecula. This 1°-long grouping of stars looks just like its namesake, with the hook on the southern side of the hanger’s arms.

Sources indicate that sunrise: 6:59 A.M. Sunset: 4:36 P.M. Moonrise: 7:53 P.M. Moonset: 10:26 A.M. Moon Phase: Waning gibbous (82%).

Sources indicate that alison Klesman is senior editor of Astronomy magazine. She holds a Ph.D. in astronomy and has studied a variety of topics, from minor planets to supermassive black holes.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Sources indicate that tired of using loud and unsightly window air conditioners or clunky and underpowered portable air conditioners? Even if you don’t have the means to install a fully ducted HVAC system in your home, you can still upgrade to a more powerful cooling system with a ductless air conditioner.

Ductless air conditioners, often called mini-splits, cool targeted areas of your home without relying on the ductwork. Instead, they connect a compact outdoor condenser to one or more indoor air handlers, which are usually mounted on a wall or ceiling.

Sources indicate that to help narrow down the best ductless air conditioners, I compared models across capacity, efficiency, installation requirements, noise level, smart features, and overall value. I also spoke with HVAC expert Kim Lincoln, who has 25 years of industry experience, for guidance on how mini-splits work, when they make sense, and what shoppers should know before buying.

It has been revealed that to ensure that our list of ductless air conditioners caters to a wide range of needs, I looked at units from well-respected brands like Pioneer and Senville and selected models of various sizes at different prices. Many come with features like programmability, dehumidification settings, and, in a few instances, smartphone functionality.

Sources indicate that as an added perk, most of these contraptions also double as heaters—which is useful during cooler months. I leaned on my experience with different types of cooling units, as well as product specs I reviewed during my research. The final list below represents the best in each category, including best budget and best for DIY installation.

Recent findings suggest that for this enhancement, I relied on the expertise of Lincoln, as well as my own experiences with several types of ductless air conditioners. I asked her a variety of questions about mini-splits, touching on topics like the differences between this type of air conditioner from other units, installation, and more. I also updated the products I recommend to reflect recent advances in smart home technology and energy efficiency.

This highly-rated AC unit from Senville comes in a number of sizes, ranging from 9,000 BTUs all the way up to 30,000 BTUs, and it comes in 120- and 230-volt models. It has 4-in-1 functionality, working as an air conditioner, heater, dehumidifier, and fan, and it operates at just 34 decibels, making it a tranquil option for a bedroom or nursery.

You can control all of its settings via the included remote. The air conditioner comes with an installation kit, including a communication cable and copper lines, but it’s key to note the brand requires professional installation for the unit’s five-year warranty to be valid.

This ductless air conditioner is perfect for small rooms and spaces, with a coverage that can handle areas between 200 and 500 square feet. Great for climate control storage and small bedrooms, the WYS009A-20 is an Energy Star-certified machine that’ll help you save money year-round. It cools as low as -13 degrees F and heats up to 122 F.

Recent findings suggest that it has a permanent washable air filter and a remote control for easy operation—though you have to buy an additional remote to use Wi-Fi capabilities. It also operates at only 25 decibels, making it one of the quietest machines on this list, and it has four modes: cooling, heating, dehumidification, and ventilation. After installation, Pioneer provides free tech support and five-year coverage on replacement parts and the compressor.

Sources indicate that this model from Della is a great value. It delivers 24,000 BTUs/hour, making it suitable for rooms up to 1,500 square feet. It’s also the sleekest model we found.

In a recent development, in addition to cooling, this unit has settings for heating, dehumidification, and ventilation, and that versatility extends to its selection of impressive features, including a 24-hour timer, sleep mode, energy-saving mode, and multiple fan speeds. You can easily adjust all of these using the included remote control and the Della+ app. The app allows people to control the settings, set timers, and control various Della units from one screen for whole-house control.

Sources indicate that the Della Mini-Split comes with a full installation kit, including a line set, and it operates at 51 decibels. Some installers report the directions are confusing and have had to rely on online guides for extra help, but most reviewers are happy with this unit.

According to recent reports, suppose you want the ability to adjust your air conditioning from your smartphone. In that case, this model from Senville includes built-in Wi-Fi connectivity, allowing you to operate it remotely from an Android or iOS device.

It’s suitable for large spaces, thanks to its four-zone setup and 36,000-BTU output. Plus, it also has heating, dehumidification, and fan settings.

The unit has a turbo mode for even more versatility, and it automatically switches from cooling to heating based on the ambient temperature. The Senville Mini-Split comes with an installation kit that includes a 16-foot line set for your professional installer.

The large, rectangular indoor units that come with most ductless air conditioners can be a bit cumbersome on your wall, and if you prefer a more streamlined appearance, this unit uses a ceiling cassette instead.

In a recent development, the 9,000-BTU system can be used for heating and cooling in spaces up to 350 square feet, and it comes with a 16-foot line set and all necessary installation equipment. The system has a 24-hour timer, sleep mode, turbo function, and three indoor fan modes. It operates at 31.5 decibels, making it ideal for bedrooms.

In a recent development, if energy usage is your top priority, DELLA’s 12,000-BTU mini-split is one of the most efficient systems commonly available online. Its efficiency rating sits around 22–23 SEER2 (which is a newer efficiency standard that prioritizes real-world performance), and that means it uses significantly less electricity than many other entry-level mini-splits.

In a recent development, the inverter compressor automatically adjusts output instead of cycling on and off, which helps the unit maintain steady temperatures and reduces power consumption. (You’ll really notice this feature during periods of extreme weather that tend to spike utility bills.).

The unit is well-sized for bedrooms, offices, or small living areas, and it cools and heats spaces up to about 600 square feet. The built-in Wi-Fi control and quiet operation round out the package.

One drawback: While DELLA has great reviews, it’s a smaller tech giant and may offer less customer support, based on some user feedback.

It has been revealed that if you’re looking to cool a smaller space like a bedroom or home office, Costway Blast Series is a solid pick for a bedroom, office, or other small room where you want more permanent cooling than a window unit can provide. Its 9,000-BTU output is sized for spaces up to 450 square feet, so it’s a better fit for modest rooms than the larger 18,000- or 24,000-BTU systems in this category. It also offers quiet operation, a display-off function, a timer, and a remote control you can use from bed.

Like many of the units we looked at, this product is more versatile than a cooling-only AC, too. It has cooling, heating, dry, fan, and sleep modes, plus ECO, turbo, and iFEEL settings. The washable filter and self-cleaning function are also helpful for keeping routine maintenance manageable.
