  • Senate Majority Leader John Thune was reelected as the Republican leader on Tuesday and will steer the conference through their time in the minority.
  • The South Dakotan ran uncontested despite a push from some of his colleagues to delay the leadership elections following Republicans’ stunning defeats last week in the midterms, which saw them lose at least seven seats and the majority.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., leaves a meeting in the Capitol on Tuesday, before his election as incoming minority leader later in the day. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

Senate Majority Leader John Thune was reelected as the Republican leader on Tuesday and will steer the conference through their time in the minority.

The South Dakotan ran uncontested despite a push from some of his colleagues to delay the leadership elections following Republicans’ stunning defeats last week in the midterms, which saw them lose at least seven seats and the majority.

According to recent reports, “Obviously, the election result was not what we hoped for,” Thune told reporters, referring to the midterms. “But I think it’s key that we take the lessons from that and internalize the message the American people were sending to us.”.

While he and the rest of the leadership slate sailed through the conference contests by voice vote, it wasn’t without drama.

Before the leadership elections began in the Old Supreme Court Chamber early Tuesday morning, the conference held a meeting at the request of a group of GOP five senators, led by Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis.

The conversation, which several senators described as “frank,” ended up pushing back the leadership elections by a few hours. But they were not postponed to another day as some had hoped.

“This has never been anything against John Thune,” remarked Johnson, as he made good on his commitment to leave the room early if the conference proceeded with its election. “What I didn’t agree with was holding the election right away, giving nobody an opportunity to really challenge any leadership position.”.

Industry observers note that “Part of the issue here is who wants the job? God bless him for serving,” Johnson added.

The conference conversation Tuesday morning turned into an “open-mic” with both conservatives and those who lost their elections speaking, according to senators.

Recent findings suggest that sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., told reporters, “To rush into this and to just ratify all the same leadership — I mean, what message does that send?”.

But no contender to Thune emerged despite the angst, and a motion to proceed to the election, introduced by Thune’s fellow South Dakotan Sen. Mike Rounds, was accepted.

It has been revealed that sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., said voters who rejected Republicans last week were reacting to high gas prices, the war in Iran and the cost of living, not to how Senate leaders were running the conference.

“I don’t think anybody in Texas who voted for the Democrat governor was voting against John Thune. If you diagnose that as a problem, you’re misdiagnosing the problem,” Paul mentioned.

Whip John Barrasso, R-Wyo., was reelected to his position, as was the chairman of the Senate Republican Conference, Tom Cotton of Arkansas. Sen. James Lankford of Oklahoma was again selected as vice chair of the conference, while Sen. Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia was reelected as Republican Policy Committee chair.

In a recent development, “Our first step is to make sure the American people know that we heard what they noted, and the American people’s priorities are our priorities. That’s the way we regain their trust,” Barrasso said afterward.

Industry observers note that sen. Bernie Moreno of Ohio got the nod to chair the National Republican Senatorial Committee, meaning he will helm the campaign arm as the party looks ahead to the uncertain waters of 2028.

Moreno mentioned, “I was in the retail automobile business, so when you don’t listen to your customers, your customers punish you. I think we have to own it, and I think we have to learn from it.”.

It has been revealed that sen. John Kennedy, R-La., said on Monday evening, “What we as a conference right now need is honesty. We need focus. We need to try to reach a consensus on what we need to change.”.

Kennedy was among those pushing to delay the leadership elections and told reporters on Tuesday he voted present instead of yes on whether to proceed to them.

Recent findings suggest that sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., who ran for GOP leader twice — once in 2022 against Sen. Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., and in 2024 against Thune — declined to run again to challenge Thune. But in a Dear Colleague letter on Monday, he detailed what he’d like to see in the lame-duck session before Democrats take power, including confirming every nominee President Donald Trump has sent to the Senate, funding the government without an omnibus, banning stock trading, passing the permitting bill that is advancing this week in the Senate, passing the National Defense Authorization Act, balancing the budget and pushing through a sweeping voter ID bill known as the SAVE America Act.

Senate Republicans on Tuesday also voted on a resolution on their path forward that was spurred by a motion from Scott, aides said.

“It is the sense of the GOP Conference that we will maximize the 54 days we have with congressional majorities, to confirm every judicial nominee and every executive nominee that the conference approves of, to pass our core Republican priorities, and to do everything humanly possible to pass a reconciliation bill before Jan. 3,” the resolution reads in part.

That long list of goals highlights the expectations Thune has faced as leader, where he led one-third of Republicans’ trifecta in Washington. In the next Congress, Democrats will hold the majority in both chambers of Congress after their larger-than-expected wins, while Trump finishes out his term as president.

Thune mentioned he told his conference: “As I look back on the last couple of years, my question is, what would you have me do differently?”.

“Given the constraints we had to deal with, all the stuff that was coming at us on a daily basis, a narrow margin in the House, the White House, the Democrats over here who were obstructing two long government shutdowns — I think we came out of it as well as could have been expected, and got a lot of stuff done,” Thune told reporters.

“If you believe the exit polls, it was the war, it was the economy, it was inflation, it was fuel prices,” Thune added. “So no, I wasn’t apologizing for anything that we did. And I think on the political side, I don’t know what else I could have done.”.

Scientists Studied Thousands of Ancient Skeletons and Found a Strange Truth About Human Progress

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It does a body good” slogan has some historical backing, at least in Europe.
  • It has been revealed that “When children and adolescents have access to sufficient, high-quality food, they grow taller, within the constraints of genetic factors,” Manon Stephan, an economic historian at Germany’s University of Tübingen, said in a statement.
  • To test that idea, Stephan and colleagues at Tübingen and the Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology examined 18,457 bones from 783 sites in 45 countries.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The dairy industry’s “Milk. It does a body good” slogan has some historical backing, at least in Europe. That’s one of the more surprising takeaways from a large study that used ancient skeletons to track how well people lived across Europe and Asia over the past 7,000 years. The researchers based their analysis on one telling measurement: human height.

It has been revealed that “When children and adolescents have access to sufficient, high-quality food, they grow taller, within the constraints of genetic factors,” Manon Stephan, an economic historian at Germany’s University of Tübingen, said in a statement. “Therefore, height enables us to draw conclusions about living standards.”.

To test that idea, Stephan and colleagues at Tübingen and the Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology examined 18,457 bones from 783 sites in 45 countries. In the study, published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, the team estimated people’s heights from their long bones. They then tracked how average height changed in each region and compared those changes with shifts in population density and technology.

In China, men were taller 7,000 years ago, averaging 5 feet 10 inches. Over time, however, their height steadily declined, reaching a low of just 5 feet 3 inches on average in the 19th century. Chinese women’s height also declined, though less drastically, falling from an average of 5 feet 2 inches 7,000 years ago to 4 feet 10 inches in more recent times.

In a recent development, trends like these would be nearly impossible to trace through written records alone. “In many parts of the world, any written sources that would allow us to draw conclusions about economic development appear quite late on our timeline and are patchy in their distribution,” Stephan said. “That’s why we rely on bones.” The bones in question came from 22 Asian and 23 European countries and were taken from the graves of commoners in both densely populated and rural regions.

Sources indicate that in Europe, by contrast, the trends went in a different direction. Around 5,000 years ago, men in northern Europe averaged just 5 feet 4 inches. However, the study authors wrote, as pastoralist peoples migrated from the steppes of Eastern Europe and western Siberia, they brought with them more advanced dairy farming and the genetic trait of lactose tolerance. This led to greater consumption of dairy products, which the study identifies as a leading factor in increased height. Average heights in northern Europe continued to climb into the early Middle Ages, but sometime between 500 and 1000 C.E., they began to decline, a trend that lasted until the end of the 19th century.

Women’s heights followed a similar pattern. China and Japan experienced the steepest declines, while Europe saw a rise, though a less steep one than among men.

In a recent development, the authors wrote that “human stature is a valuable indicator of nutritional status and health.” Reconstructing this indicator offers insight into which societies provided better health and nutrition to their people. Surprisingly, technological progress did not prove to be a major factor in improving either.

Industry observers note that “Our study also confirmed that technological progress does not automatically lead to greater height,” noted Jörg Baten, a professor of economic history at the University of Tübingen. “In China, for example, fresh, higher-yielding rice varieties and other innovations were introduced in the 11th century [C.E.]. While the higher yields enabled the empire to remain the dominant power, they did not subsequently lead to a better standard of living for the general population. Instead, population density increased: People had more children because this was seen as a form of security in old age. This meant, however, that each individual had not more to eat, but less. And importantly the quality declined, for example, in terms of high-quality protein.”.

In a recent development, europe’s findings on technology mirrored Asia’s. Improved technology helped support denser populations, but it didn’t increase average height or necessarily improve the nutritional value of food.

Going forward, the authors hope to link more of these changes in height to shifts in social conditions or developments in agriculture. “This requires further research,” mentioned Mark Hudson, an archaeologist at the Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology. “However, the statistical data reveal trends and provide clues as to when these changes occurred.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that in an increasingly fire-prone western North America, Jennifer Grenz, an ecologist and member of the Lytton First Nation, looks at fire with a holistic eye. She considers her work with landscapes recovering from catastrophic wildfire to be “deliberately unfocused,” spanning soil microbial ecology, restoration ecology, invasion biology and historical biology.

It has been revealed that grenz analyzes historical ecological records, like how Indigenous people have shaped and cared for ecosystems over time, to paint a comprehensive picture. “I’m interested in how those histories leave ecological legacies and hints of the stewardship of the past,” says Grenz, who leads the Indigenous Ecology Lab at the University of British Columbia in Canada. “What changed on the land that made it more vulnerable?”.

Grenz spends time with many kinds of specialists, such as archaeologists, anthropologists and Indigenous elders who provide oral histories.

Industry observers note that moving forward, her lab will examine ecology below ground, including soil, microbial communities and root networks. The goal is to understand the role of underground ecology in critical topics like carbon sequestration, climate change, biodiversity and sustainable management.

“My motivation is in our interior Salish Territories in the southern interior of British Columbia, where my ancestors rest and where my people are,” Grenz claims. “The responsibility I feel to them and to our Tmícw, which means our lands, [is] to not take us back to the past, but to show that we have the deep knowledge to help us move forward.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that FCC nominee Danielle Thumann Severs waits to testify during her confirmation hearing with the Senate Commerce Committee on Tuesday.
  • President Donald Trump's Republican nominee to the Federal Communications Commission faced opposition Tuesday from Senate Democrats who fear the commission could be controlled exclusively by Republicans under Chairman Brendan Carr, who they vowed to investigate in the next Congress.
  • Appearing before the Senate Commerce Committee, nominee Danielle Thumann Severs limited her commitments to independence from Carr, including on regulating broadcasters based on their content decisions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that FCC nominee Danielle Thumann Severs waits to testify during her confirmation hearing with the Senate Commerce Committee on Tuesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

President Donald Trump's Republican nominee to the Federal Communications Commission faced opposition Tuesday from Senate Democrats who fear the commission could be controlled exclusively by Republicans under Chairman Brendan Carr, who they vowed to investigate in the next Congress.

Appearing before the Senate Commerce Committee, nominee Danielle Thumann Severs limited her commitments to independence from Carr, including on regulating broadcasters based on their content decisions.

Much of the hearing focused on Carr and his threats to use the FCC to punish broadcasters he disagrees with.

Sen. Ben Ray Luján, D-N.M., said that he expects Carr will not last long in his position once Democrats take control of Congress in the new year.

In a recent development, “Mr. Carr, if you're listening now, know you're going to be in this body once a month, if not more, and in the House of Representatives as well, answering questions … so we can get to the bottom of the nonsense and the cover-ups that have been taking place,” Luján said.

The nomination of Thumann Severs, who currently serves as senior counsel to Carr, has led to consternation among Democrats due to continued vacancies at the FCC. The five-member commission is intended to have three members of the president’s party, including the chair, and two in the minority.

At the moment Carr serves alongside fellow Republican Olivia Trusty and Democrat Anna M. Gomez, whose term expired earlier this year. Gomez may continue to serve through next year under the law if a replacement is not nominated and confirmed.

Democrats are concerned that if Thumann Severs were to be confirmed, the commission’s three Republican members could constitute a quorum on their own, allowing Trump to fire Gomez.

According to recent reports, sen. John Hickenlooper, D-Colo., mentioned Senate precedent is to move pairs of one Democratic and one Republican nominee for the FCC and that he “strongly” believed the Thumann Severs nomination should have been paired with a renomination of Gomez in order to continue having “both parties at the table.”.

“A bipartisan FCC is essential to avoid things like large-scale media consolidation [and] I think also, more fundamentally, to protect a free and diverse press [that] serves everyone,” Hickenlooper stated.

In addition to urging Trump to renominate Gomez, Democrats underlined the need for a second Democratic member of the commission.

Hickenlooper highlighted Thumann Severs’ close work with Carr, who Democrats and some Republicans have been critical of for comments about using the FCC’s public interest standard against television stations airing programming Carr disagrees with.

Thumann Severs’ work at the FCC right now focuses on the Wireline, Public Safety and Homeland Security, and Consumer and Governmental Affairs bureaus, rather than the Media Bureau.

According to recent reports, committee Chair Ted Cruz, R-Texas, has also been critical of Carr’s comments. On Tuesday, he listed the FCC’s request for ABC-owned stations to submit early license renewals alongside earlier incidents in which he said Democrats encouraged the weaponization of the FCC against conservative voices.

“The First Amendment places notable limits on the government’s ability to regulate speech,” Cruz stated. “The FCC possesses significant regulatory authority over communications, so there is always a risk that it could weaponize its authority against Americans with whom it disagrees.”.

Thumann Severs committed to Cruz that she would base licensing decisions on “the law and the record” and not use the FCC’s authority to “pressure or punish” broadcasters for protected speech.

According to recent reports, however, when Sen. Edward J. Markey, D-Mass., questioned Thumann Severs on whether the FCC could punish broadcasters the president disagreed with, Thumann Severs repeated one of Carr’s arguments in discussing the FCC’s role.

Recent findings suggest that “Broadcasters are subject to public interest obligations as part of the public trustee model in exchange for the licenses that they hold,” she stated. “As part of those public interest obligations, they are subject to many different rules and requirements, and the FCC is charged with enforcing and investigating the public interest standard against broadcasters.”.

Under repeated questions from Markey about Carr’s previous remarks, Thumann Severs said she would base her decisions “in the facts and the law and the record.”.

Luján also asked Thumann Severs to name issues where she had disagreed with Carr or Trump. While she said her decisions would be her own, she declined to name any examples of disagreement.

In addition to questions about Carr, Democrats asked the nominee about the FCC’s E-Rate program, which provides low-cost connectivity for schools and libraries, and the Universal Service Fund, which funds the E-Rate program and other programs.

Recent findings suggest that thumann Severs said that she believes the E-Rate program has been successful and that the FCC has a statutory obligation to provide some kind of discounted service to schools and libraries. But she was less forthcoming on whether the FCC could shut down the program as it currently exists without congressional approval or whether the program should be restricted only to rural areas.

Late last month, Democratic members of the House Energy and Commerce Committee, led by Communications and Technology Subcommittee ranking member Doris Matsui, D-Calif., sent a letter to Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., and Cruz urging Gomez’s renomination with any move to confirm a Republican nominee.

“Commissioner Gomez has shown the experience and judgment to continue that work,” the members wrote. “We therefore ask that the Senate pair any new Republican nominee with her renomination to a full term, consistent with the bipartisan design Congress built into this agency.”.

On Monday, the Leadership Conference on Civil and Human Rights also sent a letter to committee leadership urging a delay on the hearing and any vote on Thumann Severs’ nomination until Gomez can be renominated.

“Independent agencies should not be extensions of presidential will: their leaders should exercise independent judgement based on their expertise and statutory mandates,” the group wrote.

Cruz did not indicate Tuesday when the committee might vote on Thumann Severs’ nomination, and no markup has yet been confirmed by the committee of hers' and those of three others for two posts at NASA and one at the Transportation Department who also testified.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is Write Here, a column where authors and literary luminaries tell us about the travels they took to find inspiration and create their latest books.

Industry observers note that in this installment, author and n+1 editor Chad Harbach describes his love for Block Island, Rhode Island, and a 2016 trip that informed a keystone part of his latest novel The Brightness. In the book, a bildungsroman that tackles topics like campus politics, the discourse around sexual assault, and the anxiety of being in one’s twenties, Block Island serves as the dramatic setting for a long, eventful wedding night that alters the lives of Harbach’s characters—particularly that of Pella Affenlicht, who originally appeared in Harbach’s 2011 debut The Art of Fielding. Below, Harbach recalls gathering his own friends for a summer holiday on Block Island as an excuse to refamiliarize himself with the destination as he began to write it in fiction—and the local peafowl that nearly made it into the book.

“In the early stages of writing The Brightness, one of the first things I decided was that the book’s centerpiece, the big wedding of the character Owen, would be located on Block Island, Rhode Island. I wanted the scene—which is now this 150-page stretch of the story, when all sorts of crazy things happen over a single, almost Shakespearean night—to be on the island’s eastern shore where houses are positioned at the top of these stone cliffs. I pictured an outdoor dance floor overlooking the beach and the ocean with the moon in the distance. Essentially I wanted to write the destination wedding I desperately wanted to attend. But as I was working on it, I realized I needed to go back there to check if my memories of the place were accurate, to have it fresh in my mind.

My then-partner and I organized a trip to Block Island with a large group of friends in the summer of 2016. We rented a massive house and folks came from places like New York, Philadelphia, California, and Amsterdam. It felt like a wedding in that sense—everyone gathered for this joyous celebration in a beautiful place. We didn’t do all the terrible stuff to one another that’s maybe required for the juicy plot of a novel, but we did spend eight days cooking together, playing the piano, singing songs, drinking a lot, and staying up very late.

It has been revealed that but we couldn’t sleep in very late because, well, there were these peahens. There was a sort of farm with animals, maybe a petting zoo, near our house, and their peahens liked to come and roost in the trees on our property. Every morning at 5 a.m., after we had been up until 2 or 3 a.m., the peahens would just start. I don’t know if you’ve ever heard the squawking of peahens, but suffice to say it was awful. It’s funny: When I started doing publicity for The Brightness, an announcement mentioned that part of it is set on Block Island. I got texts from friends who were on that trip, saying, congrats, we’re so excited, the fucking peahens better be in there. I initially did have this whole bit about the peahens, but there was so much going on in the plot that I cut them—not without really trying to make it work first.

Other than the loud birds, it was a great trip. The place struck me as just as magical as it had when I first went at 19 years old, when I was in college. I had a friend whose grandparents had a house there. I’ve visited several times since, and always loved it. But this was the only time I’ve ever gone somewhere for book research, and I was able to lock in some granular details like what the downtown looks like, the shape of the buildings, the sight of the marshlands, and what it’s like to bike out to the airport.

I was also excited to find that the feel of it was exactly as I remembered. Block Island has this rugged, natural beauty—it’s a rocky, tree-filled place surrounded by ocean, where everyone just rides bikes around, and part of it is a protected nature preserve. It’s sort of the forgotten sibling of Nantucket or Martha’s Vineyard. Some people don’t even know that Block Island exists, which keeps it from changing too much, even though it was settled by Europeans in the mid-1600s. The cemetery there has the tombstones of families that date back centuries, long before the United States became a country. I think some of those same families still live on the island now. So there’s this sense of continuity and timelessness.

According to recent reports, even before you reach Block Island, there’s just something about climbing on to the ferry and heading out into the open water, this freedom and openness that’s very inspiring to me. I grew up in Wisconsin, on Lake Michigan, which isn’t an ocean but looks like one, and I’ve always loved that feeling of vastness and mystery that comes with a massive body of water—that literal depth. It reminds me that we as humans actually haven’t mastered everything, and there are many things in this world that are not easy for us to touch.

All of this made Block Island a helpful setting in The Brightness. What happens on this wedding night propels the characters toward life paths that are very different from what they thought they were going to have, and having the story be imbued with the island’s sense of openness, possibility, and what might be feels fitting. As a writer, that can be part of the work: tapping into that feeling or gestalt of a place. It can be very easy to do at times, and difficult at others. And, you know, sometimes it’s just hard to write. So it was a great help writing about somewhere I love visiting literally and creatively. Instead of resisting sitting down at my desk, I’d be like, I’m ready to go to Block Island. It’s this setting I could picture well, enjoy being in, and keep traveling to—even if it was just in my imagination.” —As told to Matt Ortile.

The 6 Best Smart Thermostats to Keep Your House Comfortable and Save You Money

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • Sources indicate that just like Wi-Fi-enabled lights and plugs and locks, smart thermostats give you the ability to automate an element of your home for increased convenience.
  • Using a companion app on your phone, you get intuitive and nuanced controls, including the ability to customize temperature schedules remotely.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Sources indicate that just like Wi-Fi-enabled lights and plugs and locks, smart thermostats give you the ability to automate an element of your home for increased convenience. In this case, it’s your temperature controls. These devices tend to be a bit pricier than conventional thermostats, but it’s an upgrade that can pay for itself over time thanks to increased energy efficiency.

Using a companion app on your phone, you get intuitive and nuanced controls, including the ability to customize temperature schedules remotely. That comes in handy when, let’s say, you want to warm up the house earlier than usual if you head home from work early. You’re also able to track your usage with monthly energy reports, which can help you bring down your bills.

Sources indicate that for the past few months, my colleagues and I have been steadily testing smart thermostats throughout in our homes, including models from Google Nest, ecobee, and Honeywell Home. These are the models we tried, plus a few more we recommend based on our research and reviews. We’ve also included some expert advice on what to consider before you buy.

The ecobee covers the standard lineup of smart thermostat features, with climate control and money-saving that are commonplace among any of the top options, but sets itself apart with a wider range of smart features.

Industry observers note that it doubles as a security base for your home security, serving as the arming and disarming mechanism. It also features a built-in air quality monitor that alerts you to poor air quality and sends reminders when you need to replace air filters in your furnace.

In a recent development, the ecobee comes with a separate smart sensor for precision control, allowing it to fine-tune the temperature in the rooms where you spend the most time. Though it comes with a single sensor, you can purchase more to add that precision throughout the house.

It also provides free Eco+ Software which works on your smartphone and generates energy reports that further maximize your energy savings.

Sources indicate that the smart thermostat also comes with a host of standard smart features. After connecting to a Google assistant or Alexa, the smart speaker built directly on the thermostat itself can take voice commands and even play music. It also comes with a three-year warranty from date of purchase.

Each purchase comes with a full converter kit as well, so if you aren’t right now in a home with a C-Wire, you can add one by following the kit instructions.

In a recent development, for a smart thermostat that better fits a tight budget, Amazon has its own option that comes with many of the same energy-saving features at a lower overall price tag. Through the connected app, the thermostat tracks and reports your energy usage and peak time periods throughout the week and month.

Sources indicate that through Alexa, you can also set home, away, and sleep temperatures that you can schedule throughout the day and week in order to further maximize savings on your energy bill and optimize your air conditioning to your exact schedule. You can also set the temperature remotely from your phone through the Alexa app.

Beyond the controls, by using an Amazon product, the organization will pass along potential rebate and saving opportunities that you could take advantage of by owning a smart thermostat.

As for upfront costs, the device is designed specifically for easy DIY installation so there is no need to hire an HVAC technician unless you want one.

The Honeywell T9 is a great choice if your primary concern is reducing energy use and lowering your bills. You need to pair it with one of Honeywell’s smart room sensors to take advantage of the thermostat’s full functionality, which is an extra hurdle, but the sensor only costs about $30, so it’s a short one.

One of the key ways the T9 saves money is through virtual fencing. Using your phone’s GPS, the thermostat automatically switches between home and away mode as you come and go. So, when you leave your house, energy usage is reduced across the board.

Sources indicate that honeywell also provides monthly usage reports that point out areas where energy can be reduced for a lower upfront cost. Adding more room sensors can increase the accuracy of those reports, giving you more chances to optimize your heating and cooling system.

The Honeywell T9 doesn’t have the same wide spectrum of features as our other recommendations, but it’s core functionality is very solid.

The newest generation of the Google Nest Thermostat has impressed our team as an easy-to-install, easy-to-use option that reduces energy use and is compatible with most HVAC systems. Like previous models, the smart thermostat builds a schedule, learns your temperature preferences, and reduces energy when it isn’t needed.

Sources indicate that reviews Editor Danny Perez installed the Nest in his own home and absolutely fell in the love with nearly every aspect of it. “To say I like this thermostat is an understatement: It lights up when I pass by to show me the interior temps, as well as local weather and humidity (it’s nice to know my presence is acknowledged, not gonna lie),” writes Perez.

Sources indicate that beyond the basic features, Perez also pointed out how much he likes the actual display and design of the thermostat. “Sure, other thermostats and window a/c units have similar smart features, but they don’t blend into my home the way the Google Nest thermostat does. I genuinely enjoy looking at it. I light up when I pass by it.”.

Read Full Nest Thermostat Review.

With a large, responsive touch screen, this basic Honeywell thermostat is easy to see from across the room, thanks to a large, custom-color display. It’s a versatile option, compatible with multiple smart home assistants. Like other models, it’s Energy Star-certified, which means that using one can help you save even more money through local rebates.

In a recent development, while the smart thermostat is great for easy scheduling and reading, it lacks the learning software of the Google Nest or the virtual fencing adjustments that many other smart thermostats have. That remarked, it’s also considerably cheaper.

Most smart thermostats aren’t compatible with baseboard heating and cooling systems. This Mysa unit is the rare exception, and designed specifically to work with electric baseboards. Combine that with compatibility across every major smart home system, and the Mysa becomes one of very few thermostats with such capabilities.

While the compatibility alone makes this a tempting choice, it also has many of the same high-end smart features as the competition. This includes virtual fencing, so when you head out for the day, the thermostat automatically reduces energy use.

It has been revealed that another key feature is its temperature monitor. Unlike many other devices, which only provide you with degrees, the Mysa smart thermostat also measures and reports humidity levels.

Traditional thermostats only require power through the four classic wires while smart thermostats typically require low- voltage power all day in order to run the display screen and some basic functions. This low-voltage power comes from an additional fifth wire called the “common” wire or C-Wire. The biggest potential issue you may have with installation is if your home lacks this wire.

According to recent reports, if this is the case, it’s probably time to step away from your weekend home project and call an HVAC technician. While installing a common wire isn’t an incredibly difficult undertaking if you’re somewhat handy, it’s one that likely requires the expertise of a trained professional.

Some smart thermostats include installation kits that provide equipment and step-by-step instructions for adding a C-Wire to your current wiring. This can be a helpful addition to the handier among us, and may circumvent the need for an HVAC technician entirely, though you may want to keep one waiting in the wings if anything goes wrong.

Once you've wired and installed your smart thermostat, you can connect it to other devices in your home via Wi-Fi or occasionally Z-Wave. Most units are compatible with many major smart home ecosystems. While they’re compatible with many systems, I would still take a moment to check and make sure that a thermostat works specifically with the smart home setup you use at home.

Along with scheduling heating or cooling programs from the convenience of your phone, there are a handful of features that set smart thermostats apart from their traditional counterparts. Most smart models automatically adjust the temperature based on peak usage and some automatically respond to outdoor temperatures and set ideal temperatures indoors.

Industry observers note that other models use geofencing, or virtual fencing technology. This creates a radius around your home and detects how close or far away your smartphone is from it. With this, the smart thermostat eases energy use when you aren’t home, and ramps back up as you reenter the virtual boundary.

It has been revealed that several smart thermostats we cover use external sensors to expand the reach of temperature readings. Setup is typically no more complicated than placing the sensors around the house and syncing them up with the rest of the system.

Recent findings suggest that they’re great for maintaining different temperatures in rooms, like keeping bedrooms and bathrooms warm and offices and laundry rooms cool. More precise temperature control also increases the potential for saving energy. Smart thermostats that include sensors as part of their systems often come with one, though some models require purchasing sensors separately.

In a recent development, the Popular Mechanics Gear Team has tested several of these recommendations over the course of several months, including the ecobee Smart Thermostat Premium and the Google Nest Learning Thermostat. We installed these smart thermostats in our homes, set them up, and used them to keep ourselves warm and cool, as the seasons demanded. We gave them our seal of approval based on ease-of-use, installation process, programmable features, and how well the devices integrated with our smart home assistants, mobile devices, and tablets.

A few thermostats, such as the Honeywell Home Smart Color Thermostat, made the list despite the fact that we haven’t tested them yet. In those cases, we picked options from established brands with the specs and features that are comparable to our tested recommendations, and have received strong reviews from customers at online retailers.

We also prioritized options that were highly compatible with other smart devices and offered convenient features for everyday use. Price rice was a major consideration, as well: We chose models ranging from roughly $160 to $250, ensuring that we recommend a range of options that fit every need and budget.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that sens. Bernie Sanders and Elissa Slotkin hold a news conference calling for a “bold direction” for Senate Democrats on Tuesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

Recent findings suggest that more Democrats emerged Tuesday wanting someone besides Senate Democratic leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., to lead their conference in the majority.

But Schumer maintained confidence he would be reelected to the post despite Sens. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., publicly calling for a different leader or a “concrete plan” that provides change.

In a recent development, “I’m confident I will be elected majority leader, and our caucus is really united in focusing on bringing down costs, on ending the corruption, on ending the chaos, on ending the war,” Schumer told reporters Tuesday. “We have great unity in our caucus, and I’ll be proud to lead it.”.

Sanders mentioned during a news conference Tuesday the election was about “change and the need for the Democratic Party to move in a fresh and bold direction.”.

“I personally have known Chuck Schumer for over 30 years, and I like Chuck. Nobody works harder than Chuck Schumer. But in my view the time is now for change, and I will not be supporting Chuck to be reelected as the Democratic leader,” Sanders said, calling for an “economy that works for all, not just the people on top.”.

“Do I think Chuck has been leading in that direction?” he asked. “No.”.

It has been revealed that some incoming members and now incumbents have pointed to Maryland Democrat Chris Van Hollen as one possibility to challenge Schumer. Van Hollen had previously thrown cold water on the idea by saying he was instead “kicking the tires” on a presidential run in 2028 but has recently changed his tune.

A person familiar with Van Hollen’s thinking said he “has received an outpouring of calls on running for majority leader and is now in active listening mode.”.

Slotkin did not endorse anyone for leader but said she had a “really productive conversation” with Van Hollen yesterday.

It has been revealed that “Whoever wants my vote is going to have to show me a concrete plan that’s definitely different. I’m a ‘no’ until and unless I see that from anyone,” she stated, urging her peers to “withhold quorum” when Senate Democrats hold their leadership elections “until you get that plan and you feel like you have a voice in that plan.”.

She urged not just a roadmap for the first 100 days, but ideas for how to “communicate differently.” As for her own future, she noted, “I am not actively seeking this job. I’m seeking change.”.

Asked about his plans Monday evening, Van Hollen mentioned, “It’s not about me, but I am listening to the thousands of people who have been calling for change, but especially listening to our members, with a particular ear to upcoming members who have just come off the campaign trail.”.

“What I’ve said from the very beginning is, we shouldn’t have a coronation. We should have a caucus discussion about what we're going to do with the power and responsibilities that have been invested in us,” Van Hollen said. “I’m in listening mode and haven’t shut the door.”.

In a recent development, van Hollen took it a step further at an event Tuesday in Washington, D.C., criticizing the minority leader and Democrats’ campaign arm over their preferences in some primaries. “Schumer and the DSCC sided with the crypto industry and AIPAC against these candidates,” he said, according to a livestream of the event.

Sources indicate that schumer tried to tamp down the suggestion of a rivalry. “We talk frequently, and we’re united — united in lowering costs, and united in ending this damn war,” he noted of Van Hollen.

Others threw their support behind Schumer ahead of the Democratic leadership elections, which are expected to take place in December.

Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee Chair Kirsten Gillibrand, D-N.Y., praised Schumer for raising money and recruiting candidates like Sens.-elect Sherrod Brown of Ohio and Roy Cooper of North Carolina to help land at minimum seven seats, and potentially nine if Alaska and Mississippi ultimately swing their way.

Sources indicate that “That takes vision. It takes clarity of thought. It takes strategic leadership, and that is what Sen. Schumer has done. And that is why you will see, despite all grumblings, enormous gratitude,” she noted.

Recent findings suggest that gillibrand pointed to candidates like Scott Colom, the Democrat in Mississippi who is currently leading GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in a nail-biter of a race. “That wave doesn’t get created by magic. It gets created by hard work and putting the pieces together over years,” she said.

Colom, however, has been noncommittal, telling MS NOW, “Too many of our leaders are from the same areas of the country,” pointing to the Brooklyn roots of both Schumer and current House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, who is expected to run for speaker on the House side.

Sen. Ruben Gallego, D-Ariz., stated he and Schumer have had their differences. But he implied he backs him for majority leader: “At the end of the day, these are historic numbers. It’s time for us to unify. We are going to work together as a caucus to initiative together about how to move forward for what the country wants us to do, and I think we have the person who I think is going to lead us there.”.

Recent findings suggest that sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., noted Democrats have “an opportunity to do things differently, and I think we will, regardless of who the leader is. It doesn’t really matter whose name is on the door.”.

Industry observers note that “Yes,” he noted of his support for Schumer, noting that so far, nobody has officially stepped up to the plate. “This is a guy that worked incredibly hard over the last couple of years. I know people have other opinions about this. But we have a mandate to do things and get things done for the American people.”.

“And we can do that with Chuck Schumer.”.

Recent findings suggest that mark Schoeff Jr., Paul M. Krawzak and Kelly Livingston contributed to this report.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For a break that balances the buzz of discovering a new city with a good dose of fresh air, Stockholm’s mix of lush parks and eclectic architecture is an enduring choice. The city is formed of 14 islands, meaning you’re never too far from a waterfront to amble along. It's packed with historical charm (head to Gamla Stan to see one of Europe’s oldest medieval cobbled streets), as well as stylish boutiques and museums championing everything from Abba to the world’s best-preserved 17th-century warship. While the city is home to a slew of excellent hotels, from elegant converted townhouses to the former home of Astrid Lindgren (author of the beloved Pippi Longstocking book series), you’ll want to look to Airbnb for a real home-from-home vibe.

Sources indicate that these 11 excellent rentals throughout the city and its outskirts balance top-notch amenities with the freedom that only comes with a private booking. True to Nordic form, there’s a clutch of homes with their own sauna and steam rooms, and all have either sea or skyline views. Below, the best Airbnbs in Stockholm to book for a weekend of weaving through medieval streets, gallery hopping, and lots of cinnamon buns.

We've vetted these listings based on Superhost status, ratings, amenities, location, previous guest reviews, and decor.

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 1.5 bathsWhy we love it: Historic architecture, prime location, dedicated workspace.

Subverting traditional Scandi minimalist sensibilities, this cool retreat in the hip heart of Södermalm channels a moody, more underground kind of charm. On the top floor, light-flooded, open-initiative living areas are packed with rich, creamy furnishings and crisp architectural lines—multiple previous guests say that this is one of the most stylish homes they’ve ever stayed in. Downstairs, two tranquil bedrooms are carved directly into the exposed natural rock, so you can sleep beneath historic vaulted ceilings after a long day skipping from sight to sight. On that note: Södermalm is an eclectic area of town, with plenty of vintage shops and wine bars, after which you can hole up in this cocooning, cave-like retreat, as though you’re stepping into your own secret—and very stylish—bunker.

Neighborhood: SödermalmThings to do nearby: Fotografiska, Riddarholm Church, Stockholm City Museum.

Number of guests: 2Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Forest access, indoor fireplace, outdoor gas grill.

Recent findings suggest that blink, and you might miss this off-grid, A-frame cabin, hidden among a thick swathe of pine trees. It’s worth searching for: Once you make your way through the foliage, you’ll find a truly wonderful Swedish escape for two. The glass-fronted structure invites in all of the elements, while inside, it’s time to switch off—there’s a crackling open hearth where you can grill all of your meals, and precious little noise other than the rustle of wind through the canopy. Fair warning: There’s a very rustic toilet and seasonal shower about a 30-second walk down the forest path, so if you’re not a DIY fan, perhaps look elsewhere. Nonetheless, for more adventurous sorts, the trade-off means absolute tranquility surrounded by happily grazing sheep and twinkly starry night skies—all within a hop and a skip of the capital.

Neighborhood: VärmdöThings to do nearby: Lillsved Beach, Buddharama Temple, Stora Sandön.

Better yet, it’s totally massive, sprawling across three roomy floors, with a prime spot perched right on the peaceful banks of Åkers canal. A snazzy and social kitchen space opens onto a central island and a fireplace, where all the family will want to gather. When it’s time to bed down, there are cozy curtained sleeping nooks and an additional attic dormitory, adding a playful, rustic vibe. You can rent canoes from host Cecile to paddle down the canal, or jump on an e-bike to explore the surrounding nature reserves. When you return, fire up the outdoor grill and gather around the dining table for a long dinner with more endless views.

Dry off and hop into the private wood-fired sauna to warm up. Hop off the boat, and you can sunbathe on the jetty, cook up some local catches on the barbecue, or jump into the complimentary canoe. Grab the kayak from the cupboard and head down to the beach to make the most of this beautiful location. Sources indicate that this spacious waterside cottage is not in Stockholm’s city center, but by compromising on a 30-minute commute into town, you gain something really special. Now, it lies surrounded by pine trees in a nature reserve beside a sparkling, clear lake, with the sea just a few steps further in the other direction. A large porch provides the spot for barbecue dinners and sunbathing sessions in the summer, and there are two spas within walking distance for those looking for their Scandi sweat fix—the sea-facing Skepparholmen Spa, and Japanese onsen-style Yasuragi. Breaking: The Secret Reason Why Ancient Roman Concrete Is So Remarkably Strong—And How One Engineer Has Recreated It

💡 Key Takeaways

  • It has been revealed that the Pantheon, Rome’s unreinforced concrete dome, constructed around 118 to 125 C.E., still stands intact to this day.
  • In a recent development, for decades, researchers credited the inclusion of volcanic ash from Pozzuoli, a city in Naples, Italy, for the unique strength in the mix; others claimed that lime, a calcium oxide or calcium hydroxide binder created from heating limestone, was the key ingredient.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:.

It has been revealed that the Pantheon, Rome’s unreinforced concrete dome, constructed around 118 to 125 C.E., still stands intact to this day. The Aqua Virgo, part of the ancient Roman system of aqueducts, was built in 19 B.C.E., yet still supplies Roman fountains, including Trevi, today. Is it any wonder that ancient Rome still draws our global admiration?

In a recent development, for decades, researchers credited the inclusion of volcanic ash from Pozzuoli, a city in Naples, Italy, for the unique strength in the mix; others claimed that lime, a calcium oxide or calcium hydroxide binder created from heating limestone, was the key ingredient. Massachusetts Institute of Technology’s Admir Masic, a civil and environmental engineering professor, thought there must be more to the story.

Industry observers note that masic established a lab at MIT with the specific goal of researching ancient Roman concrete. First and foremost a chemist, he states he knew there was something beneath the surface of Roman concrete potentially lending it strength. His team of researchers, from MIT, Harvard, Italy, and Switzerland, discovered that ancient Roman concrete gets its strength—and therefore its incredible longevity—from its inherent self-healing properties. As cracks form, the surrounding material somehow fills them back in, over and over.

Scientists commonly suspected that ash, and not lime, was the hero of the Roman concrete-making process, because the Romans were the first to add volcanic ash to the mixture. This hydration-based method gives the mixture additional strength and makes it possible to build in all seasons.

But it didn’t explain the self-healing quality. Another mystery was in the concrete’s apparent crystalline phases, known to take shape only at high temperatures—at least 80 degrees Celsius (or about 176 degrees Fahrenheit). Yet, the Romans wouldn’t have exposed their concrete mixture to those sorts of temperatures.

In a recent development, then, researchers discovered calcium aluminate hydrate being used as a binding agent in ancient Roman concrete, which only created further intrigue. This is where the mystery of self-healing gained its first big clue—trying to learn where the calcium came from, Masic indicates. So his team’s focus shifted to the overlooked role of lime, which is primarily composed of calcium compounds.

Recent findings suggest that masic notes that modern concrete, when mixed with lime, volcanic components, and water, creates a homogeneous mixture—quite unlike ancient Roman concrete, which is studded with tiny, distinct white particles. “How is it possible that every construction site would make this heterogeneous material even though they put so much effort [into] making it very standard in terms of ingredients [and] how to mix it?” Masic wondered.

According to recent reports, the research team decided to investigate the mechanical, structural, and chemical properties of these particles, dubbed “lime clasts,” which were present in every sample they analyzed, Masic says. It led the team to realize “that lime clasts are not an error in mixing, or sloppy mixing, but they are the root of a very specific way of mixing mortars.” Not present in modern concrete, but ubiquitous in the ancient Roman version.

Originally, researchers believed that the Romans added water to the lime mixture to make a slurry. This “slaking” creates a homogeneously structured mixture. However, the presence of the lime clasts didn’t fit into this model.

What the Romans actually did was “hot mixing,” which introduces a novel series of chemical reactions. They ground the stone into tiny pieces of calcium oxide and mixed them with volcanic ash and a dry aggregate. Finally, they added water. “This is where the reaction of calcium oxide with water happens, and the entire mix gets hot, [which] releases energy, and creates hot spots up to 200 to 250 degrees Celsius,” Masic explains.

While lime and the ash formed the basis of the mixture, the constellation of millimeter-scale, mineral particles embedded throughout the mortar turned out to be the secret outcome of the hot mixing process. The key to hot mixing is that it doesn’t dissolve all of the lime clasts. Instead, they get systematically embedded into the concrete mix, creating a reservoir of calcium. When the concrete is exposed to water, the calcium spontaneously expands, creating a protective layer of nanoparticles that fill in the cracks before they can spread. Voila, self-healing concrete. Masic’s team published their findings in the journal Science Advances.

The team’s own recreation of Roman concrete healed a crack within two weeks. A modern concrete mixture didn’t heal at all, allowing water to flow through the crack. Eventually, water seepage like this destroys the integrity of modern concrete structures.

Roman self-healing concrete allows the mixture to last longer and requires less maintenance and less new material for construction—which also reduces emissions during concrete production. Standard cement production, the solid binder in concrete, accounts for about 8 percent of global CO2 emissions today.

According to recent reports, our world actually has various forms of self-healing concrete, such as bioconcrete, in which bacterial spores activate and produce calcium carbonate to fill in cracks. However, the high costs of modern methods keep the industry from using them widely, states Masic. Meanwhile the ancient Roman method offers “self-healing at an extremely competitive price,” he says.

Now that we know the secret, should we return to making concrete this way?

In fact, Masic co-founded a manufacturer in 2021, that uses lessons he has learned from studying ancient Roman concrete. Today, DMAT is creating a concrete additive “that increases the lifespan of concrete structures by 50 percent and reduces CO2 emissions to 40% of traditional concrete,” according to MIT’s Climate Portal. As of August 2026, their material is part of underground water tanks, road barriers, and pavement in Italy and Switzerland. DMAT also prepares to expand to U.S. infrastructure projects.

Manasee Wagh contributed to this story.

His favorite interviews have included sit-downs with Roger Federer in Switzerland, Kobe Bryant in Los Angeles, and Tinker Hatfield in Portland.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, dor Minzer remembers sitting in an undergraduate computation class at Tel Aviv University. He was intrigued by his professor and soon found himself pulled into a new world: the mystifying intersection of math and computation, first laid out by Alan Turing during World War II. Working with the professor, Minzer became deeply interested in the limitations of what computers can and can’t do.

“My part is actually to prove not only do I not know how to do it, but I can prove that it’s impossible,” Minzer says. “You have to really be curious.”.

According to recent reports, minzer’s hard work has paid off. In 2018, he proved a theoretical computer science problem called the 2-to-2 games conjecture. It asks whether computers can efficiently distinguish games where almost all rules can be satisfied from those where almost none can be satisfied, when the rules have a strict structure.

In September, Minzer and his two graduate students at MIT posted a 95-page milestone paper on the unique games conjecture, which builds off the 2-to-2 conjecture. The paper wasn’t quite ready, but they published to get ahead of a press release from OpenAI, describing its proof for the same problem, slated for only days later. It’s a situation that many mathematicians have found themselves in this year as AI companies flood the field with findings at lightning speed.

Minzer states it’s critical to remember that math, and all the research and contemplation behind it, is very human. “It’s a human activity,” he says. “Research is sort of a living organism, a living body.”.

Minzer teaches his own students now. Some days, he talks to his class and gets the sense that nobody is paying attention. But other days, he gets a few students that participate. They have ideas, they’re excited, and they remind him of his own days as a graduate student.

According to recent reports, “I feel like now I feel like I’m passing the torch,” he says. “Before you have a Ph.D. adviser, you’re like a new person in a dark room. There are infinite places to go. Your Ph.D. adviser is the person that holds your hand and says, ‘Okay, let’s walk here.’”.

Sources indicate that isabel Angelo spends her days searching the cosmos for exoplanets and signs of extraterrestrial intelligence. But Angelo’s head isn’t in the stars. It’s buried under mountains of 0s and 1s — data from space telescopes old and fresh.

To piece together a fuller picture of what’s out there (alien megastructures around nearby stars, perhaps?), Angelo and her colleagues at the SETI Institute in Mountain View, Calif., are turning to machine learning models. These tools are analyzing the troves of telescope data for anomalies — things that look “weird” in space that we don’t know how to explain yet.

It has been revealed that most of the space weirdos will probably turn out to be total normies — a comet, a newborn star or a star surrounded by lots of gas and dust. “These are things that I would expect [the models] to find,” Angelo says. “But the goal is to find something that’s not even in any of these categories.”.

In the meantime, Angelo keeps her whimsy and wonder for space alive by remembering historic moments, like the reveal of the first portrait of a black hole in 2019. The scientists “put all of these telescopes all over the Earth. They wait for the Earth to rotate. They do all this math to construct this one image,” Angelo says. “I can’t believe how creative and innovative we have to be to learn about space. It’s such a specific and really fun challenge.”.

Ohio Sen. Bernie Moreno will chair the National Republican Senatorial Committee during the 2028 cycle. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call file photo).

According to recent reports, house and Senate Republicans picked their new campaign chiefs Tuesday, tasking Ohio Sen. Bernie Moreno and Georgia Rep. Brian Jack with leading the GOP campaign arms for the 2028 election cycle.

In their upcoming positions, both will spearhead Republicans’ push to win back majorities on Capitol Hill after Democrats seized control of both chambers of Congress by flipping more than 40 House seats and at least seven Senate seats in last week’s midterm elections.

In a recent development, republicans returned to Capitol Hill this week still reeling from their losses but resisted calls to delay Tuesday’s leadership elections. In the Senate, South Dakota’s John Thune was reelected Republican leader without any opposition, while Ohio Rep. Jim Jordan defeated Louisiana Rep. Steve Scalise in a closed-door, secret-ballot election to lead House Republicans next year.

Recent findings suggest that moreno will succeed South Carolina Sen. Tim Scott as chair of the National Republican Senatorial Committee.

“Republicans must enter this next election clear-eyed: the road ahead back to a Republican Senate majority will by no means be easy but the fight has never been so notable,” the Ohio senator noted in a statement.

Speaking to reporters on Capitol Hill, Moreno described his upcoming role as “a hell of a job.” He mentioned Republicans would be “absolute savages” on ending government corruption and continuing “to work for the American people.”.

“I suspect the best tailwind we’ll have is that the Democrats will learn all the wrong lessons,” he told reporters.

Moreno, a close ally of President Donald Trump, is presently serving his first term. He first ran for Senate during the 2022 cycle but dropped out of a crowded GOP primary eventually won by JD Vance. Two years later, buoyed by an endorsement from Trump, he won a contested primary for the state’s other Senate seat and went on to oust Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown that fall.

It has been revealed that brown is poised to return to the Senate after defeating appointed Republican Sen. Jon Husted last week in a special election for the remaining Senate term of Vice President Vance. While Ohio has swung heavily toward Republicans over the past decade, Democrats scored big wins in the Buckeye State last week, winning several statewide offices and flipping three seats in the U.S. House.

But assuming he runs again for a full term, Brown will be on the ballot in 2028, setting up what’s likely to be a tense home-state fight.

Recent findings suggest that in an apparent reference to the returning Brown, Moreno offered some Washington advice Tuesday: “Make sure you rent. Do not buy.”.

The 2028 Senate map gives Republican pickup opportunities in a handful of swing states, including Arizona, Georgia, Nevada, Upcoming Hampshire and Pennsylvania. The party will also be defending battleground seats in Alaska, Iowa, North Carolina and Wisconsin. Also on the Senate ballot are races for Republican-held seats in Kansas and South Carolina, where Democrats scored surprise wins last week.

It has been revealed that on the House side, Jack defeated Indiana Rep. Rudy Yakym III to become the next chairman of the National Republican Congressional Committee. He takes office after one of the worst elections for the GOP in recent decades and will succeed outgoing NRCC Chair Richard Hudson, who lost his own North Carolina seat last week.

It has been revealed that house Republicans face the tough task of cutting into Democrats’ 40-plus-seat majority next cycle. But the party will have a slew of pickup opportunities, given the sheer number of seats Democrats won in historically red territory this year.

Like Moreno, Jack was first elected to Congress 2024, leveraging a close relationship with Trump to win an open seat outside Atlanta. He previously was White House director of political affairs during Trump’s first term and was a senior adviser to the president’s 2024 campaign. Over the past two years, he served as the NRCC’s recruitment chair.
